div.head: KONTRIBUTERS.
div.p: KONTRIBUTERS.
SUM NOATS ON THERE WAYZ. Ex THE OFFIS BOY.

Kontributers is mi speshal avershon—in utber wurds, i detest the hole specshiz from the inmost recessiz ov mi 'art, so 2 speke. in the let plaice, they think that the paper can't git along withowt 'em, and in the 2nd they 'ave no bowells ov kom- pression 4 a pore offis boy witch 'as to karry the letters up a endless flite ov stares.

Their are different klassiz kontributers. There are kontributers 2 the pails ov our valuable and widely red jernel---as the editor sez; and there are kontributers 2 the waste-paper baskii. i may insi- dently menshun that the latter konsiderably out- number the 4mer.

But the kontributers'2 the baskit are not with- I owt there use in a well-organized kommunity—and this town is well organized, barrel-organized. in fact-4 if it wos not 4 them, wear wood a modest offis boy git 'is pockit munny from now that a 'ard- arted kasheer keeps sich a argue i on the stampsand petty-kash ? 2 resoom. The kontributer is as dosile as the un- born babe until lov 'is lubrikashons is rejeckted, and then 'is 'atred ova mild benignant editor, and a staff that is overflowing with milk and 'oney ov 'uman kindness, is as implakable as the law ov the Meads and Prussians. 'e rites letters 2 the papers abowt the malignant inflewense ov a litterally ring, witch is awl kast in-2 the kapashus maw ov the W.P.B.—witch is short 4 " Ritin' pays badly." 'e kalls the editor several names that are 2 be found in nacheral 'history books, & if 'e kan ketch 'em 'e' its unoffendin' offis boys on a plaice wear the bones aint prominent. Then again, the usual sort ov kontributor is kare- ful 2 selekt as a subjeck 4 'is artickle sum think witch is ov no interest to ennybody under the son, and to trete it in a mannerfthat is direcktlyopposit 2 the style ov the paper 'e sends it 2 'e also rites on unsootable paper. i will 'ere give wood-be kon- tributers a useful 'int—always rite on good thick foolskap, it is much the best 4 rappin' butter up in, & kommands shire price than eny uther kind ov paper. Kontributers also fancy that they are far better judjes than the editors to wot is sootable & wotie not and they 'ave 'abit ov giving advice on wot they no nothing abowt to people that don't want no teechin'. ThPy 'ave uther pekewliar & unpleasant karakteristikaginch as underlinin' every tither wirrd; & dirtyin' the tuns steps jist after they 'ave been; klened bi one ooze anonymity is disgized under the nom de ploom ov youres truly. But wot angers me most agenst kontributers is that they think no-1 kan tell the truth but them- selves. They go 2 grate pains to diskover wen the editor will be out, & then come & ask if 'e's in. if 'e's over the way samplin' a new brand ov Skotch wine, u tell them that 'e is away on important bizness konnekted \Aids the vintners' industry; if 'as gone to git marrid, u say that famerly troubles detain 'imorich statements are both striktly true,but witch- over reply u make, the kontributer don't beleeve us &if 'e is sarkastikally inklined, 'e kalls you Anania, and tenderly inqwirz after your sister Saflira. I alwayz trete sich ribaldry with the consent it deservz, & the only wurd the baffled kontributer kan git from me is a 'orty stair. I intended 2 say a few wurdz abowt the wayz ov aksepted kontributers, but I 'ave seen so few ov them that it is impossible 3 express an imparshal opinyun. We 'ave sum reg'lar kontributers. They never wish to see the editor ; an interview with the kasheer satisflze there simple wants. It affords sum amusement to observe theirfacea wen told that the kssheer is out. It wood be interestin' 2 quote there remarks on these okkashons, but our paper being essentially a model 1, i am forced to refrane. This is awl about kontributers, & in konklusion, i will merely observe that if these 'umble remarks 'ave unintenshonally offendid eny 1 of the nume- rous army ov kontributers, let im remember, air 'e reeks is venjunse, that it wos not me, but the other , boy that maid. them.—Adapted from the Umpire.

div.head: MAGLSTRATES AND THEIR DUTIES.
div.p: MAGLSTRATES AND THEIR DUTIES.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court,on Mon- day morning, Alderman Sutton said that his atten- tion had been called to a paragraph, headed "A magistrate wanted," which appeared to be going the round of the papers. As the criticisms in that paragraph were calculated to mislead, he thought it only fair that an explanation should be given. It would appear from the paragraph that the whole body of the magistrates were in the habit of neg- lecting their duty, whereas the fact was that cer- tain magistrates were appointed to attend the court on certain days, and most of them attended very regularly. With regard to himself, anyone reading that: paragraph would infer from it that he , should have been there at 10 o'clock on Friday, and that he kept the court waiting until a quarter to eleven. The fact was that the days on which he was appointed to attend were Mondays and Thurs- days, and he thought he attended pretty well on those days, and sometimes on other days. There- fore an explanation should be given, because it was very likely that certain magistrates who ought to attend on certain days were unable to do so. The best plan would be for those magistrates who found that they could not attend to send notice to the Chief Constable in sufficient time, to enable him to get other magistrates to attend, but he did not think it was fair that the whole body of the magis- trates should be blamed because certain of their number do not attend to their duties.

div.head: MEASLES AT -WARRINGTON.
div.p: MEASLES AT -WARRINGTON.

The " Medical Press " says :—ln the midst of these days of supposed enlightenment, it is almost incredible that such a state of things could exist as that which is supposed to be the case at Warring- 'fa The lite; to which we allude are as follows: —An exceptionally lar4 luirnba ,children hay- ing died at Warrington within the last fortnight— i 44, as against 11 in the corresponding period in 1888 —questions were asked at a meeting of the Town Council, if any explanation of this could be given by the Sanitary Committee. The reply showed that many of the deaths had been due to measles, and then the alarming fact was disclosed that there seemed to he an idea prevailing among mothers in the town that their children had to have the measles, and it was necessary to get the disease over. The result of this conviction was that the children were brought into contact with the in- fection upon every available opportunity, to the danger of the community generally. The Com- mittee above mentioned are reported also to have stated that they could not help this state of things. If such an announcement has been made, it is moat regrettable. An ignorant conception such as that under discussion should not be permitted to pro- pagate untold mischief without measures being taken to suppress it. The wise in these matters should make themselves responsible for the guid- ance of the foolish, and it is just possible that they could bring legal pressure to bear upon the latttr in the process. So gross an exhibition of popular ignorance is a disgrace to the age, and we cannot hold those in authority blameless in the matter.— Medical Press."

A WOMAN'S WISH. Would I were lying in a field of clover, Of clover cool and soft, and soft and sweet, With dusky clouds in deep skies hanging over, And scented silence at my head and feet. Just for one hour to slip the leash of worry, In eager haste, from Thought's impatient neck, And watch it coursing, in its heedless hurry Disdaining Wisdom's call or Duty's beck. Ih !it were sweet, where clover-clumps are meeting, And daisies hiding, so to hide and rest; No sound except my own heart's sturdy beating, Rocking itself to sleep within my breast,— lust to lie thete, filled with the deeper breathing That comes of listening to a wild bird's song! Our souls require at times this full unsheathing— All swords will rust if scabbard-kept too long; And I an& tired,—so tired of rigid duty. So tired of all my tired hands find to do! I yearn, I faint, for some of life's free beauty, Its loose beads with no straight string running through! &VP, laugh, if laugh you will, at my crude speech; But women sometimes die of such a greed— Die for the small joys held beyond their reach, And the assurance they have all they need.

The advance guard—A betrothal ring. Miss Adipose refers to her slim lover as a bow and narrow. Fowls cannot be classed as gourmands if they do eat by the peck. Whatever a mistaken vanity may tell us, it is better to please in conversation that to shine in it. I have lived to know that the secret of happiness is never to allow your energies to stagnate. The average horse is a tender-hearted animal. He is always ready to stop and listen to stale of whoa. A Proposal ot marriage should not fail to touch a responsive chord, if there is the right sort of a ring to it. Let fortune do her worst, whatever she makes us lose, as long as she never makes us lose our honesty and our independence. " Ah,' said Jeliokus, taking his friend's baby, "he has got his mother's eyes—and my hair," he added, as the infant grabbed him by the foretop. No one loves to tell a tale of scandal but to him that loves to hear it. Learn, then, to rebuke and silence the detracting tongue by refusing to hear. "You ask for the hand of my daughter? What ex- pectations have you ?" " Why—none at all." "Neither has my daughter. Take her and:be happy." ";Father." said a lad, "I have often read of people being poor but honest. Why don't they sometimes say rich but honest ?" "Tut, tut, my son, nobody would believe them." "Jones," said Brown, as he watched a couple strolling near, "that it is a first love affair." "How do you know?" "I just heard her make him promise not to smoke or drink." Horse-dealer: "That horse! Why, Mr. Fox, that horse has gone a mile in a good deal less than three minutes !" Customer, after a critical examination of the animal: On what railway ?" Important Passenger: "What's the boat stopped for?' Pilot: "Too much fog." I. P.: "But I can see the sky overhead." Pilot: "Well, unless the boiler bursts we ain't goin' that way." Bertha: "This is the very day to ask papa's consent. Arthur." Arthur: "Why? Is he in a good humour ?" Bertha: "No; he's frantic over my dressmaker's bill, and will let you take me off his hands at once." Beyond recall another year has flown, to tell the tale of actions left undone. How blest is he whose aim has been to serve his neighbour and his God. Then brightly will the New Year dawn, to strengthen, water, and prosper him. Sir Thomas More had only daughters at the first, and his wife did ever pray for a boy. At last he had a boy, which after, at man's years, proved simple. Sir Thomas "aid to his wife, "Thou prayedst so long for a boy, that he will be a boy as long as he lives."

"Dennis, why don't-you 'strike?" "And phat should Ido that for?" "The work's too hard for the pay you get. The idea of going up that ladder all day long." "But I only go up half the day, sur." "sow can you make that appear ?" "Because, sur, I spend the other half of it coming down." • llumorrn IN Music.—That humour can be introduced into music was well shown by Haydn in his "Farewell" and "Surprise" symphonies. The former is generally supposed to have been intended as an appeal to Prince Esterhazy against the dismissal of his "chapel;" but ' Haydn's real object is now believed to have been to per- suade the Prince to shorten his stay at his castle, and so enable the musicians to join their wives and families. The music began gaily enough, but it gradually became dreamy and wailing, and as oths after another of the performers stopped, turned out his light, and left the orchestra with his music until at last only two violins remained behind, the "hint" was unmistakable. It ' you all go," said the Prince, "we may as well go too," and Haydn's wish lwns fulfilled. In the 'Surprise" symphony the music dies away into the softest pianis- simo, and is just !what is wanted to send the least appreciative members of an audience to sleep; but suddenly the full resources of the orchestra burst Out into a terrible hang! calculated to arouse the sleepiest of mortals out of the deepest of slumbers. Haydn con- fessed to a friend who happened to call upon him as he was composing the andante that he intended to startle the audience. "There," be said, pointing to the passage where the drums were to make their. now well-known explosion, "all the women wil4scream.", 4Wagner's first attempt in the way of musical composition was a blood- thirsty drama, in the course of which 42 characters were 'killed, and the few others to whom he granted a further lease of life were haunted by the ghosts of the slain.— ,C'essea's Saturday Journal. OLD AGE.—I suppose there is scarce a village with us *in Etigland, if it be any whit populous, but it affords some man or woman of fourscore years of age. Nay, a few years since, there was, in the county of Hereford, a Vay-garne, or a morris-dance, consisting of eight men, -whose ages computed together made up eight hundred :years; insomuch that what some of them wanted of an • hundred years others exceeded as much. In the hospital . of Bethlehem, corruptly called Bedlam, in the suburbs of ' London, there are found, from time to time, many mad persons that live to a great age. Not only too goodness pr pureness of the air, but also the equality of the air, is material to long life. Intermixture of hills and, dales is pleasant to the sight; but suspected for jent,": life, A plain, moderately dry, but yet not fner.)'arren or sandy, nor altogether without trees gni shade, is very con- venient for length of life, Ir.oe,quality of air . . . in the place of our dw'elling is naught; but change of 'air by travelling, al'..ter one be used unto it, is good; and 'therefore qes'. travellers have been long-lived. Also those that: nave lived perpetually in a little cottage, in the &Me place, have been long livers; for air accustomed consumeth less; but air changed nourisheth and re- Daireth more. Fair in face, or skin, or hair, are shorter livers; black, or red, or freckled, longer. Also, too fresh a colour in youth does less promise long life than pale- ness. A hard skin is a sign of long life rather than a soft; but we understand not this of a rugged skin, such as they call the goose-skin, which is as it were spongy, but of that which is hard and close. A forehead with deep furrows and wrinkles is a better sign than a smooth and plain forehead. Firm flesh, a raw-honed body, and veins lying higher than the flesh betoken long life; the Chntrary to these, short life. - - • Yaliseetsats. —Clarence Deming contributes to the ' 'Christian Union some characteristics of rural New Eng- land life and speech taken from a note-b ink of twenty- five years' standing. When, many years ago, I asked a rustic citizen of the town, after his first visit to New York, his opinion of the great city, his reply was : o. Waal, I never! Why, there on Broadway it allers seemed 's though rneetin's just out." The note-book abounds in miscellaneous Yankeeisms gleamed from the whimsical characters to be found, in every back town of Yankeedum. Among the oldest of this old species was Mr. D—, a rugged and antique resident of a Western Connecticut village. While driving his cows to pasture, Mr. D— used to address them in most emphatic terms. One day, while the animals were in uncommonly frolic- some mood, lie was overheard to say," Yes, scatter, will ye! Hang ye' if there warn't but one of ye ye'd .50atter !" On a night dark MI Erebus' Mr. D—: (4,00 out excitedly an hors pilfering hi favourite ;re .—" I se.; tr" '• k ve ! Where ; e . I . 119 e pear tree. be ye? Who are ye?" His profanity via OW. srftlgt'i voluble and redundant; but it never reached 4 climax than on an, occasion when he missed the back- , board of his waggon after a five-mile drive, and on going , back for it found that he had been using it as a seat. Mr. B—, before driving from his farm to town, used to delay long delivering, what he called his "last words." His vexed hired man at last broke out, "Mr. 13—, you'd be an awful bad man to die; you'd have so many last words that the undertaker's bill would come in be- fore Ter was dead." One of the oddest native char- acters was Mr. B—, an ardent defender of the doctrine ot election. One day, while" argytying" with a neigh- bour at dinner, lie lifted a morsel of beef on his fork. asserting: "I have no more doubt, sir, of the doctrine of .election than that I should eat that meat." With the ...emphasis of his gesture the meat flew off and was in- ,..ftantly devoured by the family dog. Here are a few -:Yankeeisms, drawn for the most part trom the same ;10cality :—" He butters sausages "—i.e., lives too ex- arsamgantly ; "Back up your cart," for pass your plate; - Waal, that's a huckleberry tew much," "He died of Veiny ;" "Can't let yer have no eggs to-day, we're a Satin' ;" Draw a long scythe (sigh);" "'"'t'hese corns . hurt me so I most want to walk backwards;"" We had a'fine ball last night the r. Ostrich (orchestra) played • for us." Let me close with this rural telegram which, many Years ago, I was permitted to cony, and which 1 pen literally, save the substittition of it spurious name :—" John Smith has broken his lags badley. All

THE NEW VICAR OF PADGATE AND HIS • WATCHMAKING Arp T PRESCOT. PARISHIONERS. The annual congregitional tea-party in connec- tion with Christ Chinch, Padgate, was held, on Thursday evening, in tne schoolroom. About 300 persons sat down to tea. The subsequent proceed- ings, which were presided over by the new Vicar, the Rev. J. J. Langbam, were alsowell attended. The Vicar, who was received-with applause, remarked how indebted he felt to Mr. Royston and others who were associated with him in getting up that tea- party for having given him such an early opportun- ity of meeting the parishioners. Of course, it first of all seemed very strange to a new corner, and, he felt, as he walked about the village, how much he Shot:Lillis to know thenrall individually. That,however.would be a question oe time. He wished to thank them all for the kind way in which he had already been received, and to say that throughout his work there he should endeavour as far as be possibly could to be a friend of them all. (Applause.) He wanted to know them, and he wanted to be useful to them all. He hoped therefore that they would look upon him soon as a friend, and would not scruple to make use of him if he could help them in any way. They had, he thought, commenced their relation- ship in a very harmonious way. He trusted that their relationship with each other would amays partake of that harmonious character, that they should all work together in a kindly and loving Christian spirit, endeavouring to keep the unity ef the spirit in the bond of peace. He knew how very much they were all attached to the Memory of his pre& eessor, Mr. Williams. They had ,reason to cherish his memory with reverence. He thought that that memory would never be quite obliterated, so long as Padgate Church stood. It was a lasting monument of what he had done for that district, and he (Mr. Lang- ham) was touched as he went about the parish, to hear the expressions of affection—which he did hear for their late vicar. It showed that they valued steady and true work, and it was some encouragement to him, for it seemed to say tohim that if he did his best, in time he also might gain their respect and confidence. That would be his earnest endeavour. He should make no promises as to the lines on which he should in future conduct the services. He might, however, say that what they found him to-day, he trusted they would find him five, ten, or fifteen years hence. They need not be alarmed by looking forward to, constant changes. He thought it more honest and more straightforward to show himself as he was. Of course, everyone worked according to his own lines to some extent, but he did not think they would find any changes of moment in the services of the church. He was not an extreme man, and he had learned to look with respect upon every line of thought within their old church. He trusted that he should always deal tenderly and _considerately with those who differed from him on matters of opinion. (Applause.) Afterwards a musical programme was carried out by members of the choir, and by Misses Yates, Royston, and Turner, and Messrs. Davenport, Harding, Bellian, and Manning. The room had been decorated by Mr. Mines and Mr. Naylor, from the Indus- trial schools. Dancing was indulged in after the con- cert, music being supplied by Mr. Walter Bellian

WYCLIFFE CONGREUATIOINAL CHURCH. ENTERTAINMENT IN AID OF THE RENOVATION FUND. On Tuesday evening the members of the Wycliffe Young People's Society, gave a very successful entertainment, in the Wycliffe Hall, in aid of the fund that is being raised for the purpose of carrying out the renovation of the church. There was a good attendance. The pastor of the church, the Rev. John Yonge, occupied the chain and in opening the evening's proceedings remarkedthat he believed that they were about to spend a very paeasant evening. The members of the Young Peoples Society had been at considerable pains to provide , what he was sure they would find to be a very good ' entertainment. Mr. Parkinson's very eclair:able band would assist. After the band, which was. con- I ducted by Mr. J. B. Caldwell, had Played an over- ture, the first part of the entertainment -vas introduced in the shape of an exhibition of "living and moving waxworks." Miss E. Walling- ton, as "Mrs. Jarley," the preprietoress of the "show," appeared to good advantage in that role, mid Mr. J. Podmore, who acted as her 'assistant "was very amusing, and quite at home in the part. The cos- tumes and characters were admirably selected, and the performance was very much enjoyed. The various " figgers " were represented by the following :—Mary Queen of Scotts, Miss Booth ; Italian gid, Miss M. Dick ; Zenobia, Miss A. Atherton ; milkmaid, Miss M. Atherton; Lady Macbeth' Miss Annie l'orritt ; Princess Ida, Miss Ada Porritt ; Mother Hubbard, Miss Jennie Taylor ; Miss Muffett, Miss Nellie Taylor ; gips), queen; Miss Annie Taylor ; Ophelia, Miss E. Sall ; Portia, Miss E. Holme ; Red Riding Hood, Miss M. Skel- land ; fish, wife, Mile C. Skelland ;. mother and dirty boy, Miss E. 13lease and Master Smith; Sleep- ing beauty, Miss M. A.. Naylor; haymaker, Miss M. Podmore ; Shepherdess,. Miss M. Hayes; Cinderella be- fore the ball, Miss L. Wallington ; Cinderella after the ball, Miss S. Wilcox; Topsy, Miss M. Walling- ton; Grace Darling, Miss M. Howard ; Mother Gamp-Mass A. Howard ;Mrs. Winslow, Miss B. Gaunt; Lady Rosamond, Miss A.Beswick ; Florence Nightingale, Miss B. Rathbone • Executioner, Mr. A. B. Lonasbaw, Mrs. Squeers and iloy,Ms.r. Taylor and Master A. Wylie, Faust, Mr. W. Hewitt; Fat Boy, Mr. S. Hewitt; Lord R. Churchill, Mr. P. Hewitt ; Mr. Gladstone, Mr. W. Lowe; Stanley, Mr. S. Rowlands; Macduff, Mr. A. Griffiths; Don, Mr. W. H. Payton; and Santa Claus, Mr. J. F. Brown. After an interval of short duration Mrs. R. H. Pearson sang "A Summer Shower," her ren- dering of which secured an encore, Mr. W. Brown also contributed a song,and Miss M. Podmore,. and Miss E. Wallington sang a duet "What are the wild waves saying." Instrumental selections were the given by the band. The accompanists were also Rev. F. R. Roberts, and Mr. W. H. Payton. At the conclusion of the entertainment Mr. Garland pro- posed a vote of thanks to the performers for the admirable manner in which they had acquitted them- selves, and also to the band for their excellent services. This proposition was seconded by Mit Horden, who thought great credit was due to all who' had taken part. He personally took great interest in the. Young People's Society, and felt especially grateful to them for their services that night. The Rev. Jolla Yong() said ,he was extremely delighted to witness the waxwork exhibition, and be heartily thanked a the members for their assistance. He thought no words of his could too strongly express their gratitude to Vac musical friends who had contributed their porti in to the entertainment. He took it as an extremely kindly act on their part, and he could assure them that he had experienced great pleasure in listening to them. After the singing of the National Anthem, the audience dispersed. It may be added that the interior of the church ia about to undergo a thorough renovation. It is intended to paint and decorate the interior throughout, and effect considerable alterations for thernore complete ventilation of the edifice. The organ which has been affected by heat and other causes, will be cleaned and repaired. Improved heating apparatus has already been put down. The specifications and designs will be the work of Mr. G. F. Armitage, of Altrincha.m, who has gratuitously placed his services at the disposal of the committee. The work is estimated to cost about £4OO. The church was erected fourteen years ago, and since has been onre healitifico

SPEECH OF LORD DERBY. On Saturday Lord Derby inaugurated a new factory at Prescot, built for the Lancashire Watch Company. Until some years ago Prescot enjoyed a great repute for the making of watch movements, but with the introduc- tion from abroad of machine-made work the industry fell off, and the handicraftsmen of Prescot gradually be- came unable to make a decent living. It is to revive the old industry that the Lancashire Watch Company has been formed. The work will now be done, not by hand as in the old days, but with the best machinery, and there is every reason to anticipate success for the new venture, especially as the Merchandise Marks Act will secure that none but English-made movements will be put upon the market in English cases. The Company has a capital of £50,000, of which about £20,000 has been called up. Work has been carried on for some time in old premises, and the dividend so far has been at the rate of 10 per cent. The workmen themselves, by investing their savingsin shares, will be able to share in the profits. At present there is work in the factory for 400 or 500 hands, but it is intended to extend the operations of the Com- pany so as to employ from 4,000 to 5.030 people. Hitherto ' only movements have been made in Prescot, but the new Company will turn out complete watches. The man- aging director is Mr. T. P. Hewitt, and among the share- holders is Lord Derby. Messrs. Stott and Sons, Manchester and Oldham, were the architects and consulting engineers for the new buildings. The cere- mony of starting the steam engine in the new works was performed by Lord Derby. There was a large gathering of Prescot people and other ladies and gentlemen, including Lady Margaret Cecil, Lord Arthur Cecil, Mr. A. B. Forwood,M.P., Colonel W. W. Pilkington, Captain Willis, and others. Mr. T. P. Hewitt, who presided, said the Company had met with a good deal of hostile criticism. Some people said they had started 20 years too late ; others, that the enterprise might succeed, but that it would only benefit the few at the expense of the many. For his own part, he believed that the Com- pany would be a safe investment for those who put their money into it • that it would pay their workpeople good wages and enable them to labour under comfortable and healthy conditions. (Applause.) Lord Derby, who was next called upon, said : It is a saying of ancient wisdom that a man who is only putting on his armour ought not to brag in a way that would be excusable if he were taking it off after a day of success- ful fighting. lam not disposed to think that bragging is in any case desirable, or commendable, but if it is ever to be indulged in it should be when something has been done to justify it ; not on the strength of an under- taking which is still in its earliest stage. Now, this new company is only starting, and all that wean or do claim for it as yet is that it has made a good start—(applausei —that its work, according to the popular asyine, is half done because it has been well begun. Touren know the circumstances under which it was projected,. You know that Prescott, 100 years ago, or even 50 years ago, was a much more important place, relatively though not positively than it is now. Ido not suppose that it has actually lost in jxmulation, though its wealth may have diminished, but other towns have increased while it has remained stationary even if it has not absolutely gone back. Several sources of income have been cut off. In the old posting times it was-the last stage into Liverpool, and a very large amount of traffic passed through it. The railway came,and left rrescot high and dry, pevehed on its hill. Then, again, it was formerly a frequen't and favourite residence for persons, having business in the neighbourhood. In that respect, in regard to residential attractions, it has suffered in various ways, partly from the opening of collieries all round, partly from the fin fluenees of its big but not fragrant neighbours St. Helens, Runcorn, and Widnes—partly, and perhaps principally, from the greater facility of locomotien opening out more picturesque and more attractive dirtnicts. Then came the gradual decadence and decay of the watch trade. Viqr had it here—we had it in recent memery—and why and: how we-came to lose it I have never epaite understood.-: But knelt we did. Seine part of the business want tee Birmingham ; a good deal, I suppose, went abroad ; and as a consequence want of employment, poverty, ancE distress have been severely felt here. That was the state of things fbr which some remedy had to be found. We. could not gather up the spilt cream, acid crying over it would have-been practically useless. (heughter.) But what we could do we have done. We leave Invested in a cow and gone in for a fresh supply. (Laughter and cheers.) Theidea of reviving our perishing industry by setting up a new compenty was first pubiiety announced, I think, in 113M.and in the first instance ileVrna intended to be on a large scale„ vrith a capital of £lOO,OOO. Various circumstances occurred to make that scheme impossible, oral least to- make it seem ten- large to be safely attempted,. and weheve begun in a smaller way, wishing to feel our roadlrand leaving it open to ourselves to extend our operations hereafter. (Hear, hoar.) Of the practical working•of the concern Mr. Hewitt can tell you more than I; butithe reasons why we thoughtand think that it ought to be a success' are briefly and eargly stated. We saw what therAtnericasie had done, and we could see unreason why wein Prescot ahould not do as well. ("Hear, hear," and applause.) Capital is cheaper here than there. That isto Bey, peopttewill invest it here-With the prospect of a. smatter return.. Labour is cheaper here than it can be in a-country whereeveryartiele almost is doubled in price by protective duties—(hear, hear),— and as for industry, inventioueand ingenuity, these are qualities in which Lancashirehaa never been deficient. (Applause.) Then,.againein thiaease things are made easier for us because we have-only to copy, though we hope it may be•with iinprovensents, what has been done elbewhere. I think we may etaim that our success when we succeAd—rwiWnet say if we succeed--will be more than a private an-eleven more-then a local advantage.• do not want to fight the foreigner with unfair weapons; we do net-want to take a cowardly shelter behind prohibitive or protective- tariffs. (Applause.) But if on fair and equalterms we emerproduce at home what is now brought- froin abroad, everybody here will be advantaged and'nehody else- can reasonably complain. Now there is one circumstancein connection with this • business that seems to me eminently favourable to its future. Watcittes-here havnbeen hitherto something oira.luxury. It is only within the lost few years that the art has been discovered of making them so cheaply as to be in reach—l' do not say of the artisan, but of the ordinary daylabourer. They are-so useful, even so necessary, that no person who-can afford one will wil- lingly go without. We have therefore opened to us an immense new market, subject; ,no doubt, to Swiss and American competition, but otherwiee not likely to be nsuch affectedby the ordinaraeffnetuationa of trade. As to the past experience of the COmpany, so far as it has yet goneo I shall lsave it to be-explained by those who have practically carried on its affairs. Everything that I have heard inclines me-to believle- in ita heture. Even if the future were not all that we desire ceexpect, we should . still have the satisfaction a having made an honest effort to give useful employment tineur neighbours and to Increase the prosperity eh. the • district. But I see no reason so far for any but sanguine views, and in any case we may be assured that in- the working of this Company there- has been nothing that will not bear the light. No guinea-pig directors sit on the board.— (Laughter.) lao promoters have filled their empty hpockets at the cost of the Legapfide investor. The shares have not been puffed up to a premium by; speculators intending to sell. again. All has beers simple, straightforward, and above board. If tha• same thing -could be said of many industrial undeee takings in this country—undertaisings on a mgcb larger scale,—there would n,ir be so many iii- gained fortunes and so ,many. burnt fingers among the investing public. (Applause.) It is an old story that there are some speculations like a cold bather- they are wholesome if you don't stay in too long. Ours is not one of that sorteand I mean to stay in it, and shall invite my friend., to do- the same.—(Applause.) These premises look like business, and Mr. Hes dt's report is very promising. I don't think lam letting any cat out of the bag, or saying anything I oughtnot tossay, when I bell you that as. far as I can make out fromethe flgureseupon the capital actually emyloyed in the beset- ness there has already;hi a year when things are not yet in full work, been earned aedividener of 10 per• coat. —(Applause.) 1 don't say you will get it—it may be wiser to make provision for the future; and in point of fact, until the affaire-of the CcmiDany are in a more ad- vanced state I don't think it would be prudent tngo in- to any details; bub, as far aan can see, I believe. we are in &fair way for success, and Darn sure we hue*: done all that is possibleto deserve it. (Loud applause) The ceremony cf• starting the steam engine-was then' performed by Lord:Derby. The spectators cheered and & bandin attendance played " Rule Britannia.' Colonel Pilkington said the men at the head were largely interestedan its success, and if the ship sank they would all sink together. But if such a. waft were allowed to sink—svell, it would servo them right.-- (Laughter.) Mr. A. B. Forwood, M.P.eproposed a votrent thanks-to Lord Derby. (Applause.), Mr. gartley-(chairman of the Directors)lseconded the ' vote of thanks. He said the Company hal,paid £lllOOO in wages during the past year, and had raade a prsfit of ne 10 per cent enthe capital, invested. Lord Derby, in acknowledging the te of thanks, agreed with, Mr. Forvrood that it would be a very pleas-' ant thing to see the weakpeople themsenees takin.x.up the shares. He would be glad to know thatetlione who turned , out the work participated in the profits.. There need be no entreating of the public to take sip the shares; tne dividends would speak for themselvn A vote of thanks tothe Chairman, moved by Mr. T. Worthington, and seconded by Mr. Ashcroft,. closed the proceedings.

"Mary, darling, if you don't keep still you'll surery tumble down and be killed, and then what will papa do for a little girl ? "

The speaker was a ship captain just back in port after a long voyage. He was sitting in a chair by an open window, in the lower part of the city of New York, more than twenty-five years ago. On the window-sill by his side was the child, five or six years old. She was delightedly watching the vehicles and passers-by in the street, and rattling on with her chatter, once in a while giving a jump almost out of her father's arms,

After this warning, however, she was quiet for a few minutes, and then, seeing a team of goats come along, with a boy driving, Mary at once forgot the peril of the perch, leaped up with acry of pleasure, slippea from her father's grasp, and fell upon the stone pavement six feet below, where she lay as if dead.

When picked up and examined, one of her hip bones was found to be so badly broken that it was doubtful whether she could ever walk again. I. Alexander Mott, one of the most eminent surgeons of his time, took the case in hand, and did all that could be done for the poor little sufferer, but she was doomed to be a cripple for life. Many weary months, full of pain,. went by before she was able to stand and look out at the window again. 13y this time her loving father was; in a distant land, and Mary missed him more than words can tell. After this sad event Mary was a witness of the active plays and sports of other children rather than aTartaker in them. She grew up to womanhood, but her lameness has always prevented her from taking the outdoor exer- cise necessary to good health and spirits. And that is not all, as from time to time there has been a discharge from the crushed bony structure, which has greatly weakened herand run her down. Not long ago she. had ' occasion to refer to the accident of her childhood' in at letter to a friend, from which we are permitted to ,make. the following extract. She says : " Besides the lasting injury done me by the' fkll' from the window, I have been troubled with an in- herited tendency to scrofula. My blood has alwtoys- beee thin and lacking in vitality. Any hurt or wound healed very slowly. Of late years I have suffered ter4 ribly from indigestion and dyspepsia, so that at times-D didn't know What to do with myself. Two or three times a weekT watdd have splitting headaches, read much distress in my chest and hack, and :on the right' side, in tke regfon of the liver.
"I had' to be so mush shut ur in the house that I fell into a state of worry and nervousness I can hardly

scribe; sorietiines r would faII4 tar tbe floor insensible with attack" like epileptic fits. r have been in this dition for tow years. Now,. you. must remember, thaC, :besides the prescription' of the dector, I took almost, ...,`every sort of patept medColime; which) seemed ts have any- )l,earing on my case.
conH
"The last thing I trietiwas Mottles Seigel's Curativs 2yrup, and lan right grad I didtay it. It suits me as lathing ever did before. Irdtives aiway my headaches, and gives me avi appetite.. was-

" Years ago P used to sihg all day Tong when I Ching my work.. After I got sick I lost all wish to make- music, but now when I fear dull anxil out of sorts I take: a deioe of 4 Seigers,'. and in, an hour or two I break otetr siesging like a lark; al "Tell other women for me that this simple medicin its:worth as muchin the house•as food or drink.

CHAPTER XLVII. mOTRPIR AND DAUGHTER. CLELAND had not recognised her father in the short encounter that took place that evening, but the woman with her had done so, and told her daughter whose hand had struck her to the earth. "Never mind, mamma. He is an with me for leaving him; I forgive him." So sobbed the girl when they were alone in the squalid lodgings Mrs. Faunce had taken for them. "He has good reason to he angry with me." she continued. "for he will never know why I left him. He loved me so dearly, and was always so kind, and gentle to me ever since Ross died; and so wa& she, mamma—indeed, she loved me very much." " Don't tell rae,. child no one ever loved you but your poor. ill-treated mother. Oh, Cleland ! your father has been a shocking man, to treat his own flesh and blood as he has treated me. But you shall make up for it, my darling, I know. When you are one-and-twenty you will have such a fortune, Cleland, that I need be poor and dependent no longer. You, will live with me, and keep me from starving then, my child, will you note Here she began to weep, in maudlin fashion ; but • the simple girl took her tears to be very real. She threw her arms round her mother, and .wept, too most sorrowfully. "I will keep you all my life, mamma, gladly— most gladly, if you will only promise not to touch that horrid drink any more; if you will only try and refrain when you find yourself tempted to take it. Indeed, mamma, you don't know what a difference it makes in you; you are not at all like a lady then, yoit are not like yourself. Promise me, mamma—do premise!" The "lady" wept profusely, Shook her head plain- tively, and pressed her small white hands over her heart. Then she sighed. rallied a little, teok out a ragged Lace pocket-handkerchief, and carefully wiped , the extreme corners of each eye. After this process she seemed to grow better, and gave the required promise with melancholy fervour. Cleland was delighted, and kissed her mother thankfully, firmly believing the good intentions she expressed. Then she commenced putting the untidy room tidy, with an awkwardness that showed how unaccustomed she had been to such a task. This was the afternoon of the next day, and the two had just dined. Mrs. Faunce, as she still styled herself, lying back, with all the grace imaginable, on a dirty chintz sofa, watched the awkward movements of her daughter with a languid smile, but still uncon- scious of any shame in the fact of the poor child labouring in such fashion for her comfort. And when Cleland had done as much as she knew how to do, and given the rest over in despair, she sat herself down near the uaswept grate, took the dog in her lap, and consoled herself with its moist kisses and affectionate play. The two together made a simple and pretty picture, but its quiet beauty was soon disturbed by the mother, with these words— " Cle, you are growing quite a nice-looking girl (but you have not my hair and eyes; it is very hard both my children should take after their father); I must see about getting you a husband, Cle—a nice, rich husband. I think I know one." "Mamma, I shall never marry. I moan to remain single and take care of you, because you have been so unkindly treated all your life. I will try and make therest of it havov."

div.head: DEATH OF MR. ADAMSON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. ADAMSON.

Mr. Daniel Adamson, head of the celebrated firm rof engineers, and one of the earliest and most enthusiastic advocates of the Manchester Ship Canal, died at Didsbury on Monday morning. Mr. Adamson was in the seventy-first ytar of his age. He was ex-president of the Iron and Steel Institute O f Great Britain, and the inventor of many useful mechanical appliances. The deceased spent the years of his early life at Stockport, occupying a cottage at Lancashire-hill with his wife and family. At this time, about 1850. he was foreman at the Stockport Boilermaking Works, and is remembered Us a smart, industrious workman. Mrs. Joseph Leigh, ex-Mayoress of Stockport, is Mr. Adamson's daughter. She was born at Lancashire-hill. Mr. Adamson, though distinguished as a mechan- ical engineer, will be best known to this district from his connection with the Ship Canal scheme in its early stages. The conception may not have been his, but to him at any rate belongs the credit of having put the machinery in motion which made that practicable which, -tor more than halt a cen- tury, had been a cherished dream. In June, 1882, he invited some of the leading citizens to meet at his residence, The Towers, Didsbury, " to consider the practicability of constructing a tidal waterway to Manchester, and to take such action thereon as may be determined on after a full discussion of the subject." A Committee was appointed at that meeting, Mr. Adamson being chairman, for the carrying out of certain schemes, of which the out- lines were submitted. It was found upon inquiry that any scheme for making a tidal waterway to Manchester from the sea was impracticable, and Mr. Leader Williams's scheme for constructing a canal With a series of locks was the only one to which,from a practical point of view, attention could be given. The subsequent history of the movement scarcely need be recapitulated. The popular agitation in favour of the canal, the parliamentary proceedings,' the repeated disappointments arising from the rejection of the Bill by the Committees of both Houses, and the final triumph, after an exhaustive inquiry by Mr. W, E. Forster's Committee in 1885, 'Will be fresh in the recollection of our readers. In all this agitation., and in the struggles before the Parliamentary Committee, Mr. Adamson threw his 'Whole energy. The actual work of cutting the canal was begun on the 11th November,lBB7, at Eastharn, and has been prosecuted with such vigour that there is a moral certainty of its being completed Within the four and a half years which formed the limit of Mr. Walker's contract. Everyone will regret that the gentleman to whom more than any other belongs the honour of having given shape to that gigantic undertaking has not lived to sea its

eemPletion. Mr. Adamson was the chief partner in the firm oi Messrs. Adamson and Co., engineers and boiler Makers, Hyde Junction. He was largely connected with the employment of the Bessemer steel, and as metallurgist and mechanical engineer enjoyed high distinction. He WAR president of the Institute Of Civil Engineers in 1887—her Majesty's jubilee Year--and was, in the early part of that year, pre- sented with the Bessemer gold medal. In the fol- lowing year he was elected president of the Iron and Steel Institute, and presided at its autumnal Meeting in Edinburgh. Born at Shildon, in the county of Durham, in 1818, he was 71 years of age at the time of his decease. His early engineer- ing experience was gained upon the Stockton and Darlington Railway. Ile was for a time managing draughtsman and superintending engineer of the 'rnzapany's works at Darlington. Subsequently he l'eesrue general manager of the Shildon Engine Works, and in 1850 entered upon business on his own account. Ile became engaged in several Prrlsperous concerns, and finally settled in theneigh- neurhood of Hyde, where he has carried on for number of years the engineering:business which is known over a great part of the civilized world. The late Mr. Adamson was a Liberal in politics. Mr. Adamson was a type of the keen-witted, clear-sighted man of business, who is no rarety in co, mrnercial life. He bronght to bear upon the work in which he was engaged a practical and earnest mind. In carving out a fortune for himself he was not regardless of the obligations which wealth engenders. He desired to benefit the city in which mast of his wealth was acquired, and in the pro- ject of making Manchester a port, he saw an oppor- tunity of rendering useful service to the commu- nity. After his severance from the active work of the Ship Canal Company, Mr Adamson lived an unobtrusive life at his residence, Didsbury. When the Local Government Act created County Councils, Mr. Adamson was induced to come forward as a eandidate for the Heaton Norris district of the llncashire County Council. He was, however, dfeated, and since then has not essayed to fill any -her Public h ters. position. Ile leaves a widow and two Aldg The elder daughter is the wife of Mr. erman Leigh, the ex-Mayor of Stockport, and the second daughter married Mr. W. .J. Parkin, the managing partner of Mr. Adamson's extensive 'engineering works at Dukintield. The death of Mr. Adamson has caused a painful shock to the people of Connah's Quay and dis- trict Last year Mr. Adamson became possessed of Wepre hail, Flintshire, and of the estate owned by the late Mr. James Freme. In order to make him- self personally acquainted with the tenantry and to betterconsult their interests, Mr. Adamson recently 'gave a banquet at Connah's Quay. There was a large attendance, and the new proprietor gave a long address, in the course of which he spoke of his -earnest desire that every tenant upon the property Should be prosperous and contented. Their rents would not be increased or their positions altered in Any way, and if they had any complaint to make he would personally give it his best consideration. Mr. Adamson's address was cordially received, and his health was drunk with much enthusiasm. Up to the period of his recent illness there was every promise that the relationship between him and the tenantry on the Wepre Hall estate would be of a thoroughly harmonious nature, and his death is greatly lamented.
THE FUNERAL.

The funeral of the late Mr. Adamson, took place, on Thursday morning, at the Southern Cemetery, Withing,- ton. Everywhere in the village there were :signs of anourning. the blinds of most of the private houses being ,drawn, and many of the shops being altogether closed. The whole route from the Towers to the cemetery was lined With persons anxious to show the estimation and vespect in which they held the late Mr. Adamson. The snuffled bell of the Didsbury Wesleyan Chapel was tolled for some time before the procession left the house and 'during its progress to the cemetery. The cortege left the Towers shortly after eleveno'clock in the following order: --Mrs. Adamson's brougham, with wreaths and flowers ; Mrs. Adamson's landau, with drawn blinds ; Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Leigh (Stockport) ; and Mr. Parkyn (daughter and safl-in-law); Masters F Adamson Leigh, T. IL Leigh; Gswold Leigh, Egerton Leigh ;and Daniel AdanasoriLeigh, Mr. Joseph Adamson, Mr. Daniel Adamson (Gee Cross) and Mr. John Home, of Wepre Hall, Flintshire; Mr, John Hunt (Hyde), Mr. Hunt, jun.. _ Mr. E. J. Parkyn, and Mr. A. Parkyn-, Dr. Douglas Moir and Mr. W. Marshall, of Ashton-under-Lyne ; Rev. C. Dunlop Smith and Rev. W. Thompson; Mr. H. Taylor and Mr. W. Marsland ; Mr. J. Keighley and Mr. R. Hoyudes ; Mr. Henry 'Bard- sley and Mr. F. 'Buckley; Mr. J. Turner and Mr. John y°den; The Corporation of Manchester was represented ~„uy the Mayor (Aldernian Mark) and the Town Clerk .(Mr. yv • H. Talbot), and there were present as representir4 thC Manchester Ship Canal, Mr. Alderman Bailey, Mr. Marshall Stevens, and Mr. E. Leader Williams. The cemetery was reached about noon, and here a large crowd of persons had gathered, including 200 of the nricpeople of the late. Mr. Adamson. There were also 4ePresentatives present from many .of the institutions 7ith which Mr. Adainson was connected during his (Hee Arne • The service at the cemetery was conducted by r,,e Roy. C. Dunlop Smith and the Rev.. W. Thompson, of -'-ndsbury,

div.head: ENGLAND AND PORTUGAL.
div.p: ENGLAND AND PORTUGAL.

THE ULTIMATUM. An ultimatum from the British Government was deli- vered to the Portuguese Government, on Saturday, de- manding the recall of all its iorces, officials, and expedi- tions of any kind from the banks of the Shir 6 river, beyond the confluences of the Ruo, and s.sutli of the Zam- besi and Makololand, and requesting an answer within 24 hours, failing which the British Minister at Lisbon and the whole staff would be removed from the country. The Council of Ministers, held under the presidency of the King, thereupon decided to comply with the British demand, while at the same time reserving all the rights of the Portuguese Crown to the territories named. ATTACK ON THE BRITISH LEGATION. RESIGNATION OF THE CABINET. LISBON, SUNDAY NIGIIT. Great excitement prevails in this city to-night. Dis- orderly bands of people, including a number of students, have been parading the streets shouting " Down with the Ministry !" which cry was also uttered by a number of people outside the Belem Palace. An excited mob assembled outside the British Consulate, and, in spite of the fact that it was guarded by police, broke the win- dows and threw the escutcheon bearing the Royal Arms to the ground. The windows of several Ministers were also broken. The British Legation is guarded by police. The people afterwards dispersed quietly. Some of the Opposition newspapers attack the Cabinet ! for its surrender to the British Government, but the Ministerial journals approve the action of the Govern- ment, considering that the Ministers were impelled to it by force of circumstances. Excited groups el people are parading the streets to- night, crying, " Viva Serpa Pinto ! Viva Portugal !" LISBON, MONDAY, 11 A.M. The Ministers have tendered their resignation to the King.

LISBON, MONDAY, 2 10 P.M. Senhor Barros Gomez yesterday personally expressed to Mr. Petre the regret of the Portuguese Government at the outrage committed at the British Consulate last even- ing. The British Minister to-day received a Note from the Government again expressing regret at the incident, and assuring him that the escutcheon should be replaced and the damage repaired. The actual author of the out- rage, a Spanish coal miner, who was s.ccompanied by a crowd of young students, will, adds the Note, be handed ever to the proper tribunal.

5 50 P.M. The King has entrusted Senhor Serpa Pimentel with the formation of a new Ministry, and it is expected that he will submit the list of his Cabinet to His Majesty to- morrow. LISIION, TUESDAY, 6 P.M. The new Portuguese Cabinet has now been constituted as follows :—Premier and Minister of the Interior and of War, ad interim, Senhor Serpa Pimental ; Minister of Justice, Senhor Lopo Vaz ; Minister of Finance, Senhor Franco Castello Branco ; Minister of Marine, Senhor Arroyo; Minister of Foreign Affairs, Senhor Frederic Aronca. It is possible that some alterations may yet be made in the above list before the new Ministers present themselves in the Chamber of Deputies to-morrow. Senhor Serpa Pimental this afternoon had an audience of the King. Mail advices received to-clay at the Ministry of the Colonies, from Mozambique, confirm previous announce- ments that co7nplcte tranquility prevailed on both banks of the Zambesi. OPORTO, TUESDAY, 8.50 A.M. Last night noisy crowds paraded the streets of this city cheering for the independence of Portugal and the integrity of the country, and shouting "Down with England." Stones were thrown at the British Consulate, which is now guarded by police. The mob dispersed quietly. PARIS, TUESDAY. The Paris journals this morning are unanimous in con- demning the action of Great Britain towards Portugal as being a violation of the Act of the Berlin Conference. The "Journal des Mats" says :—" Portugal had no power to resist, as she would in that case have furnished England with a pretext for seizing the mouths of the Zambesi as well as Delagoa Bay; but the opinion of Europe will pass severe judgment upon the proceedings of the British Government.'

SIR WILFRID LAWSON AND THE PUBLICANS. A CHARACTERISTIC LETTER. The following correspondence will be read with in- terest : Crosby Hotel, Manchester. Sir W. Lawson.—Honoured sir,—Are you correctly reported in the enclosed cutting ("Manchester Guardian, January 8). My impression is that you (although an honest opponent of my trade) never used the word.—' am Sic., LAURENCE FLOOD. Sir W. Lawson, M.P. Brayton, Carlisle, January 10, 1890. Dear sir,—You are quite correct in your impression. I never called the licensed victuallers "scoundrels." The speech to which Mr. Millar, the assistant secretary of the Liberty and Property Defence League, refers' may be found in the" Alliance News" of September 8, 1881, and the passage on which Mr. Millar bases his allegation is there reported, as follows. I was explaining that the House of Commons has a strong desire to compensate all interests which can make out any kind of a ease for compensation, and the passage runs thus :—" The House of Commons has an affection even for scoundrels. Surely there can be no doubt that such men as the publicans are will get what they deserve, and perhaps rather more." It is obvious that I was placing the publicans in contra- distinction to the "scoundrels," and I remember explain- ing this to some official of some " Trade " association who had seen the words and had at once gratuitously fitted on the cap. The prohibitionist must indeed be a bungler who attacks the characters of the publicans. Those who have studied the question know that they are the only tradesmen whose characters have to undergo a searching examination beforethey are allowed to enter on business. The great point is that even these very good men, selected from their fellow-citizens for their worth and virtues, are unable to benefit the public by carrying on a trade which Lord Randolph Churchill has explained to be in itself devilish and destructive. I shall be glad if you will publish this note, as I should be grieved to think that anyone should believe me to have been guilty of calling the publicans " scoundrels " —language which, I am sure, the public would consider little short of blasphomy.—Yours truly, Mr. L. Flood. WILFRID LASVSON.

div.head: LONDON SCANDALS.
div.p: THE LONDON SCANDALS.

-- -- The charges against Arthur Newton, solicitor ; Freder- ick Taylerson,his clerk; and Adolphus de Gallo, an inter- preter, of conspiring together to defeat the due course of law and justice in proceedings relating to what are known as the West-end scandals were further investi- gated et Bow-street, before Mr. Vaughan, on Saturday. Inspector Abberline, of Scotland-yard; Luke Hanks, a Post-office constable ; and other witnesses were ex- amined, and the case was adjourned to Thursday next, when the defence will be opened. ALLEGED LIBEL ON LORD EUSTON. At the Cptral Criminal Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins, Ernest Parke,editor of the" Noah London Press;" was indicted for publishing a libel con- cerning Lord Euston. Defendant pleaded not guilty. Sir Charles Russell appeared for Lord Euston, and Mr. Lockwood for the defendant. Sir Charles Russell, in his opening iitatement, said there was not a word of truth in the allegation that Lord Euston visited a house in Cleveland-street for the immoral purpose suggested in the libel, though he he had gone once to view some poses plustive,es. It was perfectly untrue also that a warrant had been issued against him resulting in his leaving the country. Mr. Lockwood, for the defence, called wit- nesses to prove that on the dates mentioned in the plea of justification Lord Euston was in the habit of going to the house inCleveland-street and remaining there, and that he had been seen in the company of some of the boys who were at the house. The case for the defence having closed, Sir Charles Russell called Lord Euston, who stated the, he visited the house in Cleveland-street only once, and left it in indignation when he discovered its character. The court adjourned until next day. RIMMING UP AND VERDICT. At the Old Bailey on Thursday morning, Justice Zawkins summed up the evidence in the trial of Ernest I 'Parke for publishing an alleged libel on Lord Euston. ,e said the question for the jury was not whether 'others had committed these abominable crimes. The judge expressed approval of the action of the prosecution in not calling Lord Euston until the end of the defendant's ease, otherwise Lord Euston would not have known what to answer. His lordSbiki pointed out that the witnesses for the defence had not remarked upon Lord Easkon's unusual height, but had described a man of much less stature. As to the evidence of that revolting creature Saul, the jury Must say which they believed, him or Lord Euston. New- love, who was now in prison, and who was said to be in the house when Lord Ruston visited it, had not been called. The same observations applied to all the in- mates of the Cleveland-at, house. It was inexpedient and unjust to make serious reflections upon individuals without good and solid foundation.—The jury retired at five minutes past one o'clock. They found the prisoner guilty, and lie was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATUIMAY, JANUARY 18, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATUIMAY, JANUARY 18, 1890.
TIIE SUPPOSED CHILD MURDER AT BIRICDALE.

At the County Police Court, on Thursday morning, before the Rev. T. Sutcliffe and other magistrates, Hannah Woods, a young woman, was brought up on a charge of murdering her child, aged two months. the facts of the case are that the child was found in a shed in ! course of erection behind We.stbourne-road, Birkdale, • and at the inquest Dr. Charlick said the infant had died from exposure. Shortly afterwards the prisoner was arrested, and admitted that she had placed the child in the shed, but that it wits dead before she did so.— Inspector Jarvis said as the order for exhumation of , the body had only been received that morning, he asked for a remand till Saturday, when he would he prepared to go into the case and finish it. His request was acceded to

BOAT ACCIDENT ON TIIE DONEGAL COAST. ' LOSS OF NINE LIVES. A sad disaster 13 reported from the Donegal coast. A fleet of fishing boats, which went out from Dunaff Bay for the herring fishery, encountered a severe storm. The ; nets, which had bceu shot, were hauled in, and all the boats, with one exception, succeeded in reaching the harbour in safety. One boat went down, and nine men wore drowned.
rHE SOUTHPORT BABY FARMING CASE.

The magistrates at Southport on Saturday, after a four days' hearing, committed for trial William Pearson and his wife, of Birkdale, on a charge of manslaughter. May and Rosina Oldfield, the daughters of Mrs. Brade, formally Oldfield, were put out to nurse with the pri- soners, and the allegation is that the children died owing to the ill-treatment they received from the accused—that they were really starved to death in a dwelling th;t reeked with illth and was a travesty of home.

div.head: MR. STANLEY AT CAIRO.
div.p: MR. STANLEY AT CAIRO.

CAIRO, TUESDAY. Mr. H. M. Stanley, Surgeon Parke, Mr. Mounteney Jephson, and Lieutenant Stairs arrived here this after- noon, and were met at the station by the Khedive's Grand Master of the Ceremonies, the Egyptian Ministers, Sir E. Baring, Signor Maceio, the Italian Minister; Mr. Schuyler, the American Consular Agent General; Sir F. W. Grenfell, and the British and Egyptian Staff officers. Mr. Stanley proceeded to pay his respects to the Khedive. The Egyptian Government gives a banquet in Mr. Stanley's honour next Monday. CAIRO. WEDNESDAY NIGHT.—Sir E. Baring entertains Mr. Stanley and his companions on Saturday ; the Egyptian Government on Monday. The Khedive has decorated Mr. Stanley with the Grand Cordon of the Order of the Medjidieh, and Messrs. Parke, Nelson, Stairs, and Jephson with the Order of the fourth class, and Mr. Bonny with the Order of the fifth class. Emin's refugees, to the number of 250, arrived to-day. lIEBLIN, WEDNESDAY NIGHT.—The statement that the Khedive will request Emin Pacha to enter the Egyptian service again is calculated to destroy the hopes of many German colonial politicians. These were confident that Germany would succeed in gaining Ernin Pacha for her purposes in East Africa. RELAPSE OF EMIN PACHA. ZANZIBAR, JAN. 15.—Emin Pacha has had a relapse, and his condition is declared to be very unfavourable.

div.head: REVOLUTION IN BRAZIL.
div.p: THE REVOLUTION IN BRAZIL.

--- ACCOUNTS OF THE RECENT REVOLT. 100 IMPERIALISTS KILLED AND WOUNDED. NEW Vona, JAN. 'ls.—An officer of the steamer Herschel, which left Rio de Janeiro on the 20th ult., and has now arrived here, giies the following particulars of the revolt against the Provisional Government at Rio de Janeiro on the night of Dec. 18th. From their berths on board the ship the crew heard almost incessant *ring, which had not ceased at daybreak. In the course of the morning a number of citizens loyal to the Emperor, who had been watching for a suitable opportunity assisted by the 2nd Artillery Regiment, marched to one of the palaces, where they pulled down the new flag and hoisted the Imperial ensign. Intense excitement prevailed, and the news of the revolt spread rapidly. The soldiers supporting the Provisional Government were ordered from their Barracks to the scene of the rising, and on their appearance firing recommenced, men on both sides being killed. The Artillery Regiment and Imperialists were soon overcome, and the civilian ringleaders and Artillery officers arrested and imprisoned, while the common soldiers were confined to barracks. The new flag was replaced on the Palace amid cheers from the Republicans. During the rest of the day soldiers paraded the streets in detachments and companies, but there was no renewal of the outbreak, and all was quiet when the Herschel left. A Commercial house in New York received a letter from a correspondent in Rio de Janeiro stating that the outicok there was not reassuring. eOne hundred Im- perialists were killed or wounded before the rest surren- dered, and 21 of the ringleaders were shot by order of the Provisional Government. The letter states that no com- missioned officers were concerned in the meeting, the leaders of the insurgents being all non-commissioned officers.

div.head: WORK IND WAGES.
div.p: WORK IND WAGES.

THE LONDON GAS STOKERS. Fifty-four gas stokers have come out of the Rother- hithe works, being dissatisfied with the labour. Another crew is reported to have left a South Metropolitan steamer. ADVANCE OF MINERS' WAGES. The miners throughout the North Wales coalfields on Saturday received an advance in wages of 10 per cent., according to the agreement effected with the coalowners on the Ist inst. The wages advance affects upwards of 10,000 men. A WELSH STRIKE AVERTED. A delegate meeting, representing nearly 70,000 steam and house coal miners of South Wales and Monmouth- shire, on Saturday decided to accept the employers' pro- posals to abide by the amended sliding scale. The voting stood, for accepting 48,228, against 20,289, majority 27,929. A great strike is therefore averted. DURHAM MINERS' HOURS AND WAGES. At a meeting of miners held on Saturday at Ryhope Colliery, in Durham, delegates representing 50,000 men being present, resolutions were unanimously agreed to that a further advat ce of 15 pr cent, in wages be asked for, and that the agitation be continued for a limitation of the working days to ten per fortnight, with seven hours as a day's work, and ten hours from bank to bank.

THE REVIVAL IN TRADE. Mr. J. W. Sidebotham, M.P., speaking at Gee Cross on Saturday, referred to the steady trade revival, and pointed out the importance on the part of both masters and men of care and conciliation, so that the commercial prosperity could be retained and expanded. Working- men, he said, were now better informed than formerly, and he did not anticipate any prolonged bitter labour struggle, but he warned workers against the Socialists, and said, notwithstanding modern teachings, there would always be class distinctions in this country.

div.head: EPIDEMIC OF INFLUENZA.
div.p: THE EPIDEMIC OF INFLUENZA.

Reports of the influenza continue to be less serious, though fatal cases still occur, among the latest being that of Mrs. Blundell, wife of Colonel Nicholas Blundell, of Crosby Hall, near Liverpool, who died from the malady, which it is believed was introduced into the hall by scme visitors from London. Colonel Blundell is also ill, his condition being such that it has been deemed ex- pedient to keep from him the news of the death of his wife. The influenza epidemic has ablted considerably in London, there being fewer applications at the hospitals on Monday. The case of Mitchell v. the Queen, a petition of right, had to be adjourned in the Queen's Bench, on Monday, the Attorney-General, the leading counsel in the case, being a sufferer fromthe prevailing epidemic. An appeal by Dr. Barnardo against a writ of habeas corpus was to have been heard in the Appeal Court, on Monday, but 'was adjourned, Dr. Bamardo being laid up with influenza. The Limerick Quarter Sessions were adjourned on Monday, County Court .Judge Purcell being a sufferer from influenza. In London and the country the influenza epidemic continues to abate. Two deaths were, however, reported on Saturday in the Receiver and Accountant-General's office : Mr. Arnold, who had been on duty in the earlier part of the week, and Mr. James. A Plymouth corres- pondent states that Inspector-General Fisher, of the Royal Naval Hospital, Stonehouse, was attacked by influenza on Saturday. Lord Salisbury is fast gaining strength, and is almost restored. Sir Francis Knollys is much better. Lord Spencer has practically recovered. He drove out in a closed carriage on Saturday. Mr. Chaplin is rapidly recovering. Mr. E. Heneage, 'Tr., is recovering. Princess Louise of Schleswig-Holstein is ill with influenza at Darmstadt: The Duchess of Man- chester was prevented by influenza from joining the party to meet the Prince of Wales at Merton. The influenza is increasing in West Middlesex and about Arundel, Sussex. Mr. Walker Blaine, son of the American Secretary of State, died at New York during Wednesday night from pneumonia, supervening upon Russian influenza.

div.head: GREAT GALE.-WRECK AND LOSS OF
div.p: GREAT GALE.-WRECK AND LOSS OF

LIFE. WRECK OF A YACHT OFF CONWAY. No doubt now remains that Mr. Thomas Marsh's , yacht. the Heather Bell, went down in a gale, on Mon- , day morning, off Conway, and that its owner has . perished. On Tuesday Mr. E. Evans, harbour master, Conway, discovered where the yacht lay, and after con- , siderable exertions was able to recover the deceased gen- tleitan's gnu and revolver, but obtained no trace of the body. SHIPPING DISASTERS OFF THE MANX COAST. A Ramsey correspondent, telegraphing on Tuesday night, says .-:—The gale raged in Ramsey and neighbour- hood all day, and still prevails with hourly increasing violence. A strong south-west wind lashed the waves into spray, almost continuously obscuring from view vessels sheltering in the bay. Over fifty North Sea and Fleetwood trawlers were safely berthed in harbour. The Manchester lifeboat, Two Sisters, was launched at noon, in response to signals of distress, and amidst great ex- citement, proceeded to sea, returning in the afternoon with four of the crew of the W. M. J., of Swansea, in ballast. After landing the crew, the lifeboat imme- diately proceeded to answer signals from a lugrmr an- chord and riding heavily. The rocket brigade was also summoned, and rescued the crew of four men from the trawler Surprise, of Fleetwood, which was driven ashore about two miles north of Ramsey harbour. Communication by means of apparatus was promptly .effected. The crew, on being rescued, reported that one William Jackson. of Preston, had been washed overboard and drowned, whilst off Maugholcl Head, the crew being powerle.s to render assistance, in consequence of heavy sea and wind. Considerable damage has been done to property. The gale is the most violent that has been experienced here for over twenty years. BOAT ACCIDENT ON THE DONEGAL COAST. ' LOSS OF NINE LIVES. A sad disaster is reported from the Donegal coast. A fleet of fishing boats, which went out from Dunaff Bay for the herring fishery encountered a heavy storm. The nets, which had been shot, were Hauled in, and all the boats, with one exception, succeeded in reaching the harbour in safety. One boat went down, and nine men were drowned.
