div.head: DIVORCE CASES: HEAVY DAMAGES.
div.p: DIVORCE CASES: HEAVY DAMAGES.

In the Divoiv Division, on Monday, a petition for divorce filed by Mr. Herbert Gorringe, a manager in a brewery at Eastbourne, was heard. Petitioner alleged adultery on the part of his wife with Barton Norris Olney, now in the Dragoon Guards, the son of a brewery pro- prietor, at Hailsham, Sussex. Petitioner and his wife were married in 1883, and they had at first lived at a house in the brewery kept by the co-respondent's father. The co-respondent had apartments with them, and the wife attended upon them. Eventually she left her husband, and evidence was given that she had since lived with the co-respondent near Brighton. A special jury found the allegations proved, and assessed the damage against the co-respondent at £1,250. In the Divorce Division, on Wednesday, Mr. Justice Butt granted a decree nisi, on the petition of Mr. Walter Travers, provision broker, Liverpool, for dissolu- tion of marriage on the ground of his wife's adultery with Mr. Robert Gladstone, member of a firm of Liver- pool wine merchants. The jury assessed damages against Mr. Gladstone at £4OO. In the same court, Mr. Abney Hassall, chemical manufacturer, King's-cross, formerly of Eccles, obtained a decree nisi for dissolution of marriage, on the ground of his wife's adultery with William Briggs, managing clerk to a firm of London solicitors. The jury assessed the damages against the co-respondent at £1,400.
FUNERAL OF THE IMPRESS AUGUSTA.

The funeral obsequies of the late Empress Augusta were held at Berlin on Saturday, in conformity with the official programme. The weather was bright and clear. After a religious service in the castle chapel, the proces- sion started about noon for the mausoleum at Charlotten- burg, amid the tolling of the church bells. The route to the Bradenburg Gate was lined by troops, the various trade guilds, and the Veterans' Associations, behind whom thousands of people thronged. In the avenue Unt,er den Linden the houses were draped in black, and displayed also a profusion of mourning ensigns, while the electric light posts and gaslamps were shrouded in crape. At the crossings of the Charlottenburg-road and Lieges Allee the cortege disperned, and the imperial and royal personages proceeded in carriages to the mausoleum, the funeral car being escorted to Charlotten- burg by a detachment of the cavalry of the Guard. At the religious service in the Castle Chapel, Chief Court Chaplain Dr. Keogel delivered the funeral oration, in which, basing his text upon the late Empress's motto, " Be joyful in hope, patient in adversity, and gteadfa.st in prayer," he reviewed the life of the deceased, extol- ling her great virtues, her fear of God, her devotion and sense of charity, and the sincerity with which she loved her husband and the Fatherland. After exhorting the mourners to be mindful of the serious gravity of the time, to follow high ideals in their lives, and to rely upon the strength affArded by prayer, he concluded with the words "Depart in peace." STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. Edward Walsh, Mayor of Wexford, and proprie- tor of the " People" in that town, was on Wednesday committed to prison for two months, without hard labour, for publishing in his newspaper a paragraph which related, without comment, the proceedings of a League Committee meeting, at which a Mrs. Wadden complained that her derelict farm was about to be "grabbed." Mr. Walsh is highly esteemed by the people of Wexford, who have repeatedly elected him to the office of Mayor. At Sligo on Tuesday Mr. M`Hugh, proprietor and editor of the " Sligo Champion," on the charge of pub- lishing boycotting notices was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, without hard labour, and ordered to give at the end of that period security for his good behaviour, or go to prison for two months longer. Notice of appeal was given. The Conservative electors of East Manchester m.y need reminding that Sligo is not in Russia but in Ireland. At the meeting of the central body of the Irish National League in Dublin on Tuesday, Mr. D. Crilly, M.P., re- ferring to the rumoured dissolution of Parliament, said they would heartily rejoice at such an event. One of the considerations said to be influencing the Government towards this step was the success of Mr. Balfour's policy in Ireland, but the rapid growth of the National League formed a curious commentary on the Government boast. A branch of the Tenants' Defence Association was formed, on Wednesday, for county Mayo, at a Conven- tion held at Castlebar. Letters expressing sympathy with the movement were read from the Archbishop a Tuam, the Bishop of Killala, and the Bishop of Achonry. Mr. Balfour, at Dublin Castle, on Wednesday, received the members of a deputation from the Ulster Land Com- mittee and Antrim Central Tenant Right Association, whose object was to urge the adoption of compulsory sale of land as the remedy for Irish discontent. The right hon. gentleman, while promising that the state- ment of the deputation should have careful considera- tion, said he could not meet their views on the main question discussed. SUPPOSED MURDER BY A SON. An old woman named Carmody, residing at Charle- mont-place, Dublin, has been murdered at her residence, and her son, an engine-driver on the Dublin, Wicklow, and Wexford Railway, is suspected of having committed the crime. It is stated that two persons saw him beat the old woman with a piece of furniture about the head. Re afterwards went in charge of the goods train to Cray, where he decamped, and has not vet been arrested.

MORE COERCION. Eleven persons charged with unlawful assembly and, further, with assaulting the police on the occasion of a demonstration to celebrate the release of Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., from goal were dealt with by a Coercion Court, at Mallow, on Thursday. Several of them got off with finding security for good behaviour, two were sentenced each to a months' imprisonment, and a man named Donoghue, a private in the 101st Regiment, who was alleged to have been an active enemy of the police, in the occasion, and to have assaulted them with stones, was ordered into imprisonment with hard labour for Seven months.

DEATH OF THE WIFE OF THE DUKE OF CAMBRIDGE. The " Daily Chl•onicle " obituary of Monday contained the name of Mrs. Fitzgeorge, wife of his Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge. The deceased lad, who was in her 75th year, was the daughter of the late Mr. Fare- brother, a London printer, and previous to her marriage was an actress of considerable promise. For a consider- able time Mrs. Fitzgeorge has been a sufferer from acute rheumatism. In consequence of her illness her Royal husband has for some weeks past been unable to accept any public engagement. Although Mrs. Fitzgeorge was not received at Court, she was a general favourite in Court circles, and the Doke was devotedly attached to her. A London correspondent says :—No record appears in any of the books of the Mrs. Fitz George whose death has deprived the Duke of Cambridge of his wife. She was not Duchess of Cambridge. ' The Royal Marriages Act prevented the Duke from raising her to his own station. She was not received at Court. She had none of the honours paid to her which some of us think nevertheless to have been her due. But her marriage with the Duke was recognised by everybody outside the official circle. Though she was not received at Court she was received by the Queen, and was said to have been a great favour- ite in the Royal Family. She was a Miss Fairbrother. Opinions differ about looks, but she was not strikingly bsautiful. Her intelligence, brightness, and vivacity were remarkable. She was acting, I think, at the Princess's, when the Duke of Cambridge fell in love with her and married her morganatically. She was often in his company even on public occasions, and the affection between them was deep, and has proved to be lasting. The Duke's sons, Colonel Fitz George and Cap- tain Fitz George, are very well known in London society, and they have sometimes taken part in political move- ments. They are very like their father In manner and in character, even to the emphasis of the Duke's style of conversation. The obituary notices of Mrs. Fitz George do not, I think, record the fact that the Duke of Cam- bridge married her on the -ea -of his departure for the Crimea. As the nuptials were a breach of the Royal !Marriage Act they were conducted in secrecy, and how either banns or license for the marriage of such an illustrious bridgrootn could pass unnoticed by the offi- ciating minister was always a puzzle to contemporary observers. The body of Mrs. Fitzgeorge, was interred at Kensal Green Cemetery, on Thursday. The Duke and the three sons of his Royal Highness and the deceased lady were the chief mourners, and the inscription on the coffin described Mrs. Fitzgeorge as "the beloved wife of a.R.H. the Duke of Cambridge."

div.head: MR. PA.RNELL AND THE "TIMES."
div.p: MR. PA.RNELL AND THE "TIMES."

--- In the Queen's Bench Division, on Saturday, Mr. Lumley Smith, Q.C., appeared in support of an appeal by the "Times" against an order in Chambers that the "Times" should furnish answers to certain interroga- tories, which sought to obtain information as to the cir- culation of the " Times "on the days when the alleged Parnell letters and the articles on " Parnellism and Clime" were published, the names of the persons who supplied the " Times " with information upon which these articles were founded, the money paid for the information, and what steps were taken to verify the information. The Master's order was allowed as to the first interrogatories, and disallowed as to the others. Costs to be costs in the cause, and the answers to be delivered in a week.
TFiE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS CALAMITY.

Mr. C. C. Lewis, coroner for South Essex, resumed the inquiry concerning the deaths of twenty-five boys during the fire which occurred at the Forest Gate Indus- trial Schools on New Year's morning. The proceedings took place on Wednesday in the girls schoolroom. While the jury was assembling it was reported that another fire had broken out, and for a time considerable excite- ment prevailed. This fire broke out in the kitchen, but was kept within the smallest limits by the activity of the servants. With regard to the calamity Mr. Cook, chairman of the Board of Management, said the locking of the front doors of the dormitories was necessary to prevent boys from absconding, and Mr. Duncan, super- intendent of the schools, gave his opinion that the boys who died could not have lived in the smoke five minutes. The inquest was again adjourned. Next Monday some of the lads who escaped will be called. TERRIBLE BLIZZARD IN AMERICA.

A telegram from New York, on Monday morning, stated :—Throughout the Western States a terrible blizzard of snow and hail, driven before a strong wind, has prevailed. The storm was cyclonic in character, and has caused an immense amount of damage to property, besides considerable loss of life. The city of St. Louis (Missouri) has suffered severely. Many buildings there were partially wrecked. A woman was killed by the collapse of the roof of her house, though, strangely, her infant, whom she held in her arms, was unhurt. At another house, a children's party was in progress when the storm broke. The wind wrecked the roof, which fell inwards, causing the deaths of the hostess, one of her children, and a male relative. Four of the little guests were badly injured. In other parts of the city injuries were inflicted on persons in a similar manner. In the north-West all the trains are blocked by the heavy snow. Over Kansas city, the storm burst as a blizzard of sleet, which broke down the overhead wires, scatter- ing them in confusion into the roadw aye. Telegraph, telephone, and lighting wires then became entangled, and several persons received severe electric shocks.

div.head: MORE PLOTS AGAINST THE CZAR.
div.p: MORE PLOTS AGAINST THE CZAR.

-- A St. Petersburg correspondent telegraphs that the political atmosphere there is heavy with rumours of fresh plots and discoveries. It is known that numerous arrests have been made recently, and it is no secret, despite the enforced silence of the Press, that several officers of the garrison here have committed suicide, I notably Colonel Voieikoff, of the Imperial Horse Guards, ' who shot himself through the head with a revolver on Sunday. It is believed that this distinguished officer and the other unfortunates were implicated in the plot against the Czar's life recently discovered, but no one dare discuss the matter in public. It is reported that one of the Czar's brothers is about to be banished for ever from the capital, together with his family. It is not suggested that his Imperial High- ness had any share in the recents plots, but he is accused of mixing himself up in politics, by which, of course, is meant Liberal politics. Everywhere there is discontent and vague fears, even in the Imperial palaces. "Truth" says :—During the last three weeks the Emperor of Russia has been in a state of insane panic, the result being that he has sunk into th 3 deepest despondency, and constantly insists that his end is i approaching. The Emperor s not likely to rally from this miserable condition while he continues to soothe Ms nerves with injections of morphia.

div.head: DEATH OF EARL CAIRNS.
div.p: DEATH OF EARL CAIRNS.

News was received at Bournemouth on Tuesday after- noon of the death of Earl Cairns, at his London residence frotn inflammation of the lungs. The news caused a most painful surprise. His aunt, Mrs. M'Calmont, suc- cumbed to Russian influenza ten days ago. He was in constant attendance on her, and before the funeral caught the malady himself, but he insisted on attending the funeral at Gatton on Saturday week. He returned home very ill, but declined to send for a medical man, thinking the illness would go away, but the following day the temperature rose to 104, and Dr. Manley Sims was called in. Two days later bronchitis set in,and I 'though no serious apprehension was felt for his welfare, 'he was carefully tended. He became worse on Monday, inflammation and pneumonia supervening, and his strength gradually leaving him he passed peacefully away at five o'clock en Tuesday morning. Lady Cairns. who is only 21 years of age,was constant in her attention but shetwas almost alone, as almost all the members of the Earl's family were absent through illness. Dr. Manley Sims and Dr. William Ord were in constant at- tendance to the last. His Lordship married in 1887 Miss Olivia Berens, and leaves one daughter. He is succeeded in the title by his brother, the Hon. Herbert Cairns. The late Earl Cairns only attained his twenty-seventh year last December. As Lord Garmoyle he attracted a good deal of public attention in consequence of the action for breach of promise brought against him by Miss Fortescue, the well-known actress. The action was abandoned on pay- ment to the plaintiff of £IO,OOO. The late Earl, the most notable incident in whose career as Lord Garmoyle has . just been described, was son of the first Earl Cairns, and • succeeded to his father's title in 1885. In Jane of that year he was appointed private secretary to the President • of the Board of Trade. His father, Hugh M'Calmont Cairns, P.C., N. 8., D.C.L., LL.D., and first Earl, was 1 born in 1819. He was Lord High Chancellor of England % In 1867-88 and 1874-80. This eminent lawyer, statesman, 1 and judge was oducAted in Dublin. KILLING MEXICAN JOE'S HORSES.

At the Liverpool County Sessions, on Wednesday, James Wright, 25 years of age, a painter, pleaded guilty to an indictment charging him with having, at Warrington, maliciously killed two mares belong- ing to Jos Shelley, otherwise known as Mexican Joe. Mr. Collingwood dope, who appeared on behalf of the prosecutor, said that the prisoner had been in the employ of Mexican Joe as a signwriter, &c., and had attended the circus from town to town. He had killed two of his employer's mares under circum- stances of the grossest cruelty. One of the animals was a valuable performing mare, being priced at -£5OO. When atVigan, Mexican Joe had found fault with the prisoner, who thereupon threatened that If he were discharged" he would be even" with him. At Warrington the prisoner turned up \ late, and the prosecutor said that he would have to be discharged. Later on the prisoner was seen under the influence ot drink in the circus stables. He had no business to be in that part of the establishment, and it was noticed that he had a stick in his hand. The two mares were later on found in great agony, and upon being examined by a veterinary surgeon, they were found to be suffering from frightful in- ternal injuries. Both animals died within twelve hours. The prisoner told a fellow-lodger what he had done.—On his plea now the prisoner said that he was madly drunk at the time.—After the magis- trates had privately consulted, Mr. Perkins said they could find nothing to mitigate the offence, and as for the plea of drunkenness, they could think nothing of that. The prisoner had admitted his guilt ot a most awful offence. • They desired to make evrry allowance that was possible, but could not overlook the malice which was shown. The sent- ence of the court was five years' penal servitude.

div.head: LECTURE ON FLOWEILS.
div.p: LECTURE ON FLOWEILS.

-7 The opening meeting ..f int second session of the Warrington:Field Club de:- held on:Montlay evening in the Lecture Room at the M useum. A lecture was given by the Rev. Joseph Freet.ton. of Maccles- , field, on "Flowers, their loan and structure." and ' the lecture was illustrated by some large models ot glowers, &c., which have been in the Museum as a loan from the Science and Art Department at South Kensington. These models are singularly ingenious and faithful representations of the natural objects, and are so constructed that they can be taken to aces to display the various organs of the plants and flowers. The lecture was thrown open to the public, and it was very largely attended. Mr. F. W. MONIES, the president of the Field Club, briefly introduced Mr. Freeston. He said that the arranging for that lecture was something of a new departure for the Warrington Field Club. Ile hoped, however, that it was departure the right direc- tion, because it had for its object the giving to the, general public of valuable information on scientific and botanieal subjects. He was pleased to see so many persons present,and he should be glad if they could see their way to continuing that series of
teces

leetures. (Applause.) The Rev. J. FRZESTON, 'who was received with ap- plause, said it was a great treat to the inhabitants of Warrington to have the opportunity of examining so splendid a set of models of plants as he had before him. He had never before seen anything equal to them in accuracy and beauty, and as they were not made of sOme delicate substance they could be handled without fear of breaking them. It would have been a shame to have returned those models to London without making use of them, and he should be glad also if that lecture would contribute to new members joining the Field Club. He should be delighted if he could be the means of in- ducing only one or two to take up the study of botany, or natural history in anyslepartment, during the coming summer. He would say to those who were ma the least degree inclined to begin the study of botany that this was just the time of the year to do it. If during the next two or three months they got what they could from books and aroused an interest in the subject, they would be in just the right condition to go out with the mem- bers of the Club in April, and being ready for the study they would feel a real delight in it. Mr. Freeston then took to pieces the model of the Common Stock, pointed out the various organs of the flower, and explained in a very interesting manner the functions of these different organs. The tnodel:of tha Sweet-pea was dealt with in a similar manner. With regard to this order of plants he might, he said, get enthusiastic in des- cribing its immnese importance. It included the peas, the beans, the gorse, the broom, the clover, the lotus tree and many other plants. They got from it not only timber but valuable dyes—such as the indigo and logwood—gums and perfumes, and food, such as beans, peas, and lentils for man, and clover and vetohes for cattle. A beautiful model of the Ox-eve Daisy was next explained, and likewise the flower Of the Common . Two of the models which excited the keenest interest were those of the fruit of the moss, and of a grain of wheat. Both of these models were of course very much enlarged. The embryo of the wheat was displayed, and the process of germination described. In the same family of plants as the wheat were the barley, the rye, the rice, maize, and millet, so that they would see how vastly important that humblefamily—having no pretensions to fine appearances—was in the world In tropical countries the palm family was just as important as a means of nourishment as the family to which the wheat belonged was in temperate regions. The model of an acorn which had just shot forth the roots in one direc- tion and the tiny stem of the future oak in another, was next considered, and the lecturer asked the audience to consider that the oak which sprang from a common acorn might go on growing for four or five centuries, and it VMS not at all impossible that a thousand years hence the wood of a tree planted in our own days might form part of some dark and fashionable old oak furniture. (Hear, hear and applause.) In conclusion, Mr. Freeston again urged upon those present who had not already done so, to take an interest in the study of bo.any.
Dock.

div.head: WARRINGTON HIGIIWAY BOARD.
div.p: WARRINGTON HIGIIWAY BOARD.

-- A meeting of this body was held at the offices in Sankey-St., Warrington, on Wednesday afternoon, the chair being occupied by .Ntr. W. Royston (Poulton;, the vice-chairman. There were also present Captain J. Withington (ex-officio), and Messrs. P. J. Bate (Kenyon), J. Davies (liollinfare), R. Owen (Croft), J. lierfoot (Winwick), J. Hough- ton (Woolston), J. Grounds (Orford), H. B. White (clerk), E.A. White (assistant clerk,) and Thompson

(Bury-- eior.) Tam Lays CHAIIMAN.—The Chairman said he thoiight that before a new chairman of the Board was appointed, some notice should be taken of the loss sustained by the Board through the death of the late chairman, Mr. Joseph Hartley. Their late chairman was one of the oldest, and cue of the most useful members, and his death was indeed a great loss to them. He thought that some action should be taken by the Board, either by writing to the family of the late Mr. Hartley, or by plazing a resolution on the minutes.—After a little further conversation had taken place, the chairman proposed that a record be made in the minute book regarding the loss that the Board had sustained.—This proposition was seconded by Mr. Owen and carried unanimously. ELecricee OF A CRAIRMAN.—Mr. R. Owen then pro- posed that Captain Withington be appointed chairman of the Board for the remainder of the year. Captain Withington, he added, was willing to take the office if it was the unanimous wish of the Board ; he would be the right man in the right place.—Mr. J. Davies seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously; , and Captain Withington briefly aekuowledged the honcur. DIVERSION OF A FOOTPATH.—Mr. Price, one of the agents on the Ship Canal Works, wrote asking for per- mission to temporarily divert a public footpath at Wilde.grave, which was granted on the proposition of Mr. J. Houghton, seconded by Mr. J. Davies. LOCAL BILLS IN BARLIAMENT.--The surveyor reported that he had received four Parliamentary notices relating to the Manchester Ship Canal, one relating to the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company, and one to the Widnes brine supply. The first notice referred to abandonment of the swing bridge for carrying the Rix- ton and Warburton bridge road over the canal. The second referred to the diversion of the road in question, and the third had reference to a diversion of footpath near Walton Arches. a matter which had previously been settled by the Board. The fourth proposed to repeal sub-section 1, of section 92 (for the protection of the Board). There was nothing objectionable in the first three notices. The repeal of the sub-section mentioned appeared to be the only matter of importance which would require the con- sideration of the Board, as it seemed singular that the Company should wish to nullify the only clause the Board had for the protection of footpaths. The fifth notice referred to the intention of the London and North Western Railway Company to construct certain news railways at Arpley, which would necessitate the stop- ping up of Slutcher's-lane,and the construction of a new diversion road in lieu thereof. He had examined the deposited plan, and, as far as the Board was concerned, saw nothing objectionable in it. The sixth notice had reference to the Widnes Brine Supply. He had examined the deposited plans, and found that it was intended to lay a line of pipes along the centre of Ferry-lane and Tannery-lane, in the township of Penketh and along the centre of Widnes-road, through the township of Cuerd- ley, . He saw nothing objectionable in this, only perhaps it would be better to lay the pipes along the side of the roads, and the roads should be thoroughly re-instated. THE BOARD AND THE WARRINGTON EXTENSION The Surveyor, who reported that he had been informed by the Borough Surveyor of Warrington that the pro- posed extension of the borough would take 1,300 statute acres from Warrington extra-municipal area, and 84 stat- ute acres from Poulton-with-Fearuhead,theirateable value being £9,789 10s. and £387 respectively. The loss to the Board would be £42 Bs. for every penny in the £, con- sequently with a 7d. rate the Board would lose £296 16s. per annum, less the cost of the maintenance of district reads to the extent of about £6O per annum. Therefore the net lose would be £236 16s. The length of roads taken were as under—main roads, 1,9001 yards ; 4istrict r0ad5,1,3321 yards, total £3,233 yards Referring to the main roads, the extension would make no difference as far as rating was concerned, unless the borough was made a county borough.—The Chairman said he thought that the Board should take some steps for their own protection. The Bill in question would seriously affect the district. It would nearly take Orford away.—The Surveyor said that rather more than half the rateable value of Orford would be taken away.—lt was decided, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. J. Houghton, to refer the matter to the Finance Coimmttee, giving the Committee author- ity to petition against the Bill if that course should be thought desirable. FINANCIAL.—The Clerk reported the balance in hand to be £516 19s. Id., and cheques were signed for pay- ment to the amount of £Bl2 6s. This was all the business.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIAN.

The fortnightly meeting of the Board of Guar- dians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, anti there were also present Messrs. Blaekli urst,T. Jones, Heaton, Davies, Dobson, Harrison, Humphrey% Wright, Clarke, Ratcliffe, Jolley, Gill, J. Houghton, I). Jones, Smith, Aukland, Hibbert ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superinten- dent of Padgate Schools). APPOINTMENTS. The House Committee recommended the appointment of Miss E. Wilson, of the Wayland Union, to be children's caretaker and general assistant at the workhouse; and also of Miss J. It. Davidson, of Maidstoae, to be nurse at the Workhouse hospital.—The minutes were adopted. PREPARING FOR A BIG FIRE. The Workhouse Master reported that since the recent disastrous fire took place at the Forest Schools, London, he had beem thinking more seriously of the position they were placed in if .s fire occurred at the Workhouse. it was a matter he had mentioned casually a number of times in going round with different members of the Board, but, as no one seemed to take the matter up, he had determined to call their attention as guardians of the poor to the situation as it stood. All the protection they had at night, should a fire occur, were two buckets of water on each landing, the water contained in the pond in front of the house and a foot or twe of water ia the large tank tin the tower. The whole supply would be exhausted in a very short time, and as they had no means of getting the town water except from a fire- plug outside the boundary of the workhouse premises and not connected with their mains, he was fearful they should stand a very great chance of being burned rout. If the Hoard thought that a matter too large for them to consider as a body, he should feel thankful if a small Committee were appointed to thoroughly go into the matter and see if something could be done for the greater safety of the people in the House and hospital. De also suggested that the superintendent of the fire- brigade of Warrington should be asked that some time when he was going to take his men and engine out for practice he should imagine that a fire was at the Work- house, go there, and make himself well acquainted with the premises and its resources.—The CLERIC said that he believed powers were likely to be obtained by the Cor- poration for the extension of their fever hospital, and, as probably the hospital was very much in the position the Workhouse was in, if a main could be placed between the two establishments it would serve for either in case of need.—Mr. HEATON moved, and Mr. RA'TCLIFFE seconded, ' that further consideration of the matter be referred to ' the House Committee, and this was agreed to.

FADOATE SCHOOLS. It was reported that Mrs. Blakemore, mother of No. 4 home at Padgate Industrial Schools, had scut in her resignalion of this post. The resignation was accepted. Mr. Naylor, assistant schoolmaster at the schools, also sent in his resignation, he haying bees appointed school- ' master at the Dutton Workhouse of the Runcorn Union. The health of the children at the schools was reported to be very good. A GIFT. The IVosicsonss MASTER acknowledged a gift to the inmates of the Workhouse of illustrated papers per Aar. A. Jolley.

SCHOOL FEES. It was reported That school fees had been allowed in 94 cases, 84 of which were old and 10 new. Mr. BLACK- HURST, in MOVin the adoption of the minutes said there had been a great decrease in the application for school fees. A TESTIMONIAL ASKED FOR AND GRANTED. MISS Scott, the porteresq at the Workhouse, wrote to the Guardians asking for a testimonial as she was apply- ing for an improved position. The application was I acceded to.

MEDICAL authorities are undecided as to the specific cause of the epi- demic of influenza from which Europe is suffering ; but there is no reason to conclude that the disease is a new type. It has been called Russian, because it appears to have originated in Russia; but it is very much like the epidemics which have preceded it. Dr. Aiken, in his "Science and Practice of Medicine," says: "In 1311 influenza was very fatal throughout l'lmme. In 1403 the Courts of Law in Paris were Closed, on account of the deaths." Paris has suf- fered severely during the present epidemic, for the mortality returns show that the deaths for I)ecember, 1889, are 2,000 in excess of the number for Dec., 1888. Dr. W. J. Russell, the author of ThediCal hand-book, states that "in St. Peters- burg in 1728, forty thousand people were taken ill in one day." Dr. PROUST, who, with other Specialists, writes on the subject, in the " Universal Review," identifies the present epi- demic with those of 1580, 1733, 1743, 1762, 1775, 1782, 1830, and 1833. The theory as to Propagation which is now most generally ac- cepted is that it has its origin in a living organ- microbe which travels with the wind, and 13 otherwise carried from centre to centre. The disease is not in itself directly fatal, but the danger to be apprehended is from resulting complications. ROW common it is to say of someone whose career has been suddenly cut short, that the illness com- menced with a neglected cold. There are two notable deaths this week resulting from the epidemic, the victims being Lord CAIRNS and _Lord NAPIER of Magdala. The old are particularly , I'able to what may be called aftereffects, and, as Lord NAPIER was in his eightieth year, it cannot be regarded as a matter of surprise that he should • have succumbed. Lord CAIRNS was, however, a Young man ;but, in the confidence of his strength, he seems to have disregarded early symptoms, and he has been carried off by a supervening attack of congestion of the lungs. It is possible, of course, to coddle one's self too much; but when the enemy has once got a footing, it is the highest wisdom to take instant measures to rout him out. It is especially true as to attacks of illness that it is the stitch in time that saves nine. As to warding off influenza, or any other prevailing disease, there is nothing better than keeping in "tip-top condition." A. low state of vitality means a high susceptibility to disease. This is a truth which many people learn, alas! too late in life to prevent constitutional Weakness. As to influenza, it is like fire; if taken in time and rightly dealt with, it may be put out, or suffered to burn out, but if neglected it gets the Mastery, and the consequences may be fatal.

Portugal conduct in the dispute with Portu- al• It will be necessary to see the despatches be- fore the last word on the subject can be said ; but it looks, on the face of it, as though the British '4overnment had played the part of a big bully in dealing with a small boy. Granted that Portugal Was in the wrong, the question which may legiti- inately be raised is—was it necessary at the present Stage to send such an ultimation as was presented (ni Saturday last? It is not to be denied that inquiry was proceeding in the ordinary way; that Portugal had promised redress, if it could be shown that injury had been done; and, further, that she Was willing to submit the matters in dispute to a e°l nference of the Powers, or to arbitration. That ord Salisbury would have none of these, and that ne would be satisfied with nothing less than abject submission within twenty-four hours of the pre- Altation of the ultimatum, argues a state of mind tw.ilich is not creditable to him as the representa- wl°ll °I a great Power in dealing with a small Power. inrl,d he have acted with such precipitation nad been dealing with France, or Germany, C iu,ssia ? We cannot think that he would; and "1 the very essence of diplomacy that the Le's should treat each other as on a footing of ,-,-,7437. There was in fact, an attack e"nday night upon the British Consulate at Alsb" ; the windows were broken, and the Royal jnis thrown to the ground. The authorities have fre°llrse expressed regret for this attack, and the enders will be punished; but there is something be said for the indignation of people who feel that might has been placed before right. .Equatorial Africa is Ur away, and the "spheres of 1"0el:ice" are so ill defined that Portugal might well urge that time should be taken for full l_nquiry as to the alleged outrage upon the British 1,1,4 g• As it is, by compelling her to withdraw from Ze whole region in dispute—South as well as worth of the River Zambesi—we may be doing an act! of injustice, and laying the foundation of a c;il,g and bitter quarrel. Having strength on his ~ ie and a just cause, Lord SALISBURY would have ..on no Well to have exercised more patience.
LORD DERBY was usefully employed, Watchmaking at on Saturday afterroon, in formally

Prescot. opening the New Watchmaking Works at Prescot. The factory which has been erected will give employment to over 500 operators, and there is every reason to hope that the under- taking will prove successful. Lord DERBY is by no means a sanguine man, but he has evident faith in the Lancashire Watchmaking Company. He said he did not think there was any need to go about imploring the public to take shares; the dividends would speak for themselves, and investors would regard themselves as fortunate if they held shares. Mr. A. B. FORWOOD spoke in a similar confident tone; he has some knowledge of the work already done ; and is so satisfied that the concern will be a paying one that he said, if lie could find anyone who wanted to part with his shares, he was quite willing to purchase them. It would seem there- fore that everything is being placed on a sound business footing. The factory is to be a relief to Prescot by holding its own in the market, and find- ing employment for skilled artizans who are willing to work for reasonable remuneration. As Lord DERBY truly remarked, every person carries a watch now-a-days who can afford to buy one; and this being the case it is i matter of course to say that there will be an unceasing and increasing demand for good watches which are not too high in price. The English maker has the benefit now of the Merchandise Marks Act. There will be no palming off of Swiss works in English cases; or, if it be done, there is the risk of punishment for the fraud. But there is an end of watchmakers working at home in what some would call "the good old style." The big factory takes the place of the little workshop; the principal of sub-division of labour is carried out in every department; and the result is time-keepers at low rate which will keep time. Still quality will always command a price in the market, and if the Prescot Company will take care, in the first instance, to aim at good quality rather than a good dividend, they may rest them- selves content that in the end a good name will be a source of riches to them. We congratulate the promoters upon having done so much in so short a time; and trust the undertaking will be alike beneficial to them and to the long-suffering peoplel of Prescot.

It is curious to read that the natives of Cairo, who at first showed little interest in the explorations, made daily journeys, from Cairo to the field of operations when it became known that one of the inscriptions on the lower half of life-size figure related to " Ra-ian " ---:who, according to Arab tradition, was "the Pharaoh of Joseph." It would seem that RAMESES 11. had usurped the statues of his predecessors, having in most eases effaced inscriptions and replaced them by his own name and titles. After commenting on this, the writer says If, however, the most conspicuous surfaces were thus usurped,some very precious original documents Were found on smaller blocks, many ot which had been re-used—perhaps more than once—for build- ing material. Up to 1889, for example, the earliest royal name discovered in the ruins was that of Pepi Merira of the sixth dynasty, [circa B. c. 3650] ; but two stones unearthed towards the close of last season (1889) showed the temple to have been in existence as far back as the time of the fourth dynasty, one block being sculptured with the ka- name of Khufu, [Khufu (Cheops), circa B. C. 4206] ; the builder of the Great Pyramid, and the other With the throne-name of K h afra, [K haf ra (Chephren), circa B. C. 4143] ; the builder of the second pyramid of Gizeh. The date of the Great Temple of Bubastis is thus carried back to a point some six hundred years earlier than the first esti- mate, and its period extended over nearly 3900 years. It will be seen from these details that the temple goes back to a period anterior, by more than 200 Years, to the date commonly assigned to the crea- tion ; and that it is a matter of course to say that laan must have been in existence for many genera- tions before, in the ordinary course of things, he at- tained such a high state of civilization as is repre- aented by the carving of these wonderful statues. According to the writer, the chronological data are finally brought down to same point interme- diate between B.C. 205 and B.c 182. "Last and latest, an inscription of the time of Ptolemy IX.

carri-.% the history of the temple forward to with- in less than one hundred and fifty years of the Christian era." That is to say, the Temple of Bubastis had completed a cycle of 4,000 years before the British cycle can be said to haw, begun!

The Home Rule movement is still active in Brazil. A Rome telegram says the Brazilian Government has officially communicated to the Vatican its decision concerning the separation of the Church and State. This is one way, shall we say, of disposing of " Brazilian bonds ?''

Mr. Stanley terms the abondonment of the Soudan a political crime. But if it had not been abandoned, it would have been "worse than a crime—it would have been a blunder." It would be as easy to annex the North Pole as the Soudan —and there would be just as:much sense in it.

Let it never again be said that a surgical oper- ation is required before a Scotchman can see a joke. He has at last made one; for we are told that the Prince of Wales has intimated his desire to drive the last bolt into the Forth Bridge, and that the structure will he opened on the Fourth March.

Mr, Henry Irving is said to be considering the suggestion to give two readings of " Macbeth " with Miss Ellen Terry as " Lady Macbeth," and with the assistance of an orchestra. But wouldn't it be as well to have the assistance, too, of a few actors, and call it a "performance ?"

The "Medical Press" has a sharp comment lon the practice which is said to be current in War- rington of mothers cultivating measles as some- thing which their children "have to have." It would be well if it could be ascertained how far such a practice prevails ; for we quite agree with our medical contemporary in saying that "so gross an exhibition of ignorance is a disgrace to the age."

-- Two boys brought before the Warrington magis- trates on Monday, for playing at " shinty " in the streets, were discharged after being cautioned. The game corresponds with what is known as hockey; but why is it called " shinty ? " Has it any etymological relation to "shindy," which is the Irish equivalent for a row? In the " Ingoldsby Legends," Barham says—" Hear them for miles kicking up their wild shindy."

Co-respondents in divorce cases, who are formd guilty—are from a pecuniary point of view—being severely punished. There have been three decrees during the present week in which damages have ranged from £4OO to £1,400. If this sort of thing goes on—and it is to be hoped it will—the roving gentry will perhaps begin to count the cost before they to quote Byron's phrase—go "poaching upon nature's manor."

It is stated that "the Solicitor-General, Sir Edward Clarke, has, in consequence of his position as a law officer of the Crown, declined the leading brief for the Times' in the libel action brought against that paper by Mr. Parnell for the publica- tion of the Pigott letters." The Solicitor-General has shown more discretion than the Attorney- General ; or can it be that the Government find themselves sufficiently tarred with the Pigott brush?

It is quite a relief, all the world over, to know that the young King of Spain is at last out of danger. Royalty has been lost in the nobler sight of the tender mother devotedly nursing her sick child. It is the one touch of nature which has made the whole world kin. It would make a charming picture, that of the young King in the height of the fever throwing his arms round his mother and exclaiming—" Mamita, how I love you!"

The Emperor of Germany is not like his father —he is something of a fire-eater. It is true that at a reception, on Sunday, he said that" the general political situation appeared to fully assure the world's peace " ; but his idea of preserving the peace is to be incessantly occupied in sharpening the sword. Russia shows herself less disposed to spend on her army, and, if Germany would follow suit, it would have a better effect than empty talk.

Rumour is busy with her hundred tongues in reporting that the Government have had it under consideration to dissolve Parliament soon after the Budget has been passed. It is known that there will be a large surplus, and the idea is that John Bull will be so pleased with it that he will give Lord Salisbury authority to hold the reins for the next half-a-dozen years. But John didn't rise to the occasion when Mr. Gladstone tried to tickle him with a large surplus. -- • There are, however, other things to take into account; the Commission of Judges may report against the National League; and Mr. Parnell may be kept under a cloud with the O'Shea divorce proceedings. The Tories have always great hopes of finding a good thing by stirring up mud. So they may, after all, face the constituencies during the present year, and Liberals would therefore do well to look to their firearms and keep their powder dry.

Free Education is likely to be the trump card of the Tory players. Indeed, as there will be a good surplus, we do not see how they can avoid playing it--after Lord Salisbury's speech. It is true they might " revoke," but to revoke jiast now might mean throwing the game away. Free Education is good, but it may be accompanied with mall pro- visions as will make it had; and it will be bad if it is unaccompanied by popular control. This par- ticular" gift" horse must be looked in the mouth; for" give "it as they may, the Taxpayers will have to pay for the animal and they will have it to keep. , A Link;

The Rev. CF. Aked was right in condemning gambling in his sermon at Earlestown, on Sun- thy; but we cannot think that he was right in suggesting that the Prince of Wales was "a black- guard" because of his association with gambling on the racecourse. There are ministers of the Gospel who gamble, in a small way, and they set a bad example ; but it does not follow that they are blackguards. Calling a spade a spade is undoubt- edly legitimate—when you are quite sure the article is a spade.

• The Warrington Branch of the National Union of Teachers are a persevering body of men. They have failed once in their endeavour to obtain an interview with Sir Gilbert Greenall, but they are again "on the job." If at first you don't succeed,
Try, try, again. :It is to be hoped that when they have elicited the opinion of the borough member on "the ne:v code," they will find it worth the trouble they have taken to obtain it.

By the death of Mr. Daniel Adamson, another striking figure is removed from the stage of the Ship Canal. It is true that Mr. Adamson had not for some time been a member of the Board of Directors; but he lives, and will long, survive in popular imagination as an heroic figure battling with difficulties, when difficulties well-nigh over- whelmed the great project. It would be appropri- ate if the Company would in some form or other permanently associate his name with the canal. Why not have an Adamson Dock?

Mr. Asquith has written to protest against "distorted construction" of what he said the other day as to considering the details of the next Home Rule Bill. He says "the whole question is one of tactics which ought to ba freely debated and as to which we shall all loyally acquiesce in Mr. Gladstone's decision." Quite so, and, as there is a Government in office, it seems to us that it would be more pertinent to demand to know the details of the Local Government Bill for Ireland, which has for three years been promised, but which is not yet forthcoming.

div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY AT HALEWOOD.
div.p: SHOCKING FATALITY AT HALEWOOD.

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy-coroner, on Mondav afternoon held an inquest at the Derby Arms Hotel, Halewood, on the body of Benjamin Lawrinson, farmer, of Halewood Lodge, Halewood. It appeared that on Tuesday evening the deceased, and a man in his employ, were engaged leading a part with potatoe tops. The deceased was standing on the top of the load when the horse moved forward unexpectedly and the deceased lost his balanco and fell to the ground. He alighted upon his head and died in a few minutes. He was 37 years of age.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death" and expressed deep sympathy with the widow and family. READ the wonderful discovery on page 4.—Advt. CANNIBALISM AT WIDNES. Patrick Scanlan, of 44, Midwood-st., was brought before the Widnesmagistrates, on Monday, to answer a charge of wounding a youth named Thomas Haverty._ The families of Scanlan and Haverty lived together in Midwood-st., and on the 4th inst., a row started because an allegation was made that the prosecutor's father had got half a sovereign belonging to another lodger named Murphy. In the course (a f the disturbance the father was struck on the head with a poker, and the prisoner seizing the son knocked his head through a window. Afterwards he held him down on the sofa, and bit a piece out of his cheek.—Dr. Hutchinson deposed that he was called in to see the injured youth, and found that blood poisoning had set in and continued until Friday last. For three days he was in considerable danger. A portion of theflesh affected by the bite had sloughed out and the youth would bear a mark for the rest of his life. The ! prisoner, who was defended by Mr. Knowles, was com- mitted to the Quarter Sessions for trial. if CU -

Samuel Ellison, gardener, of Overton, brought an action against Samuel Spruce, labourer, Overton, to re- cover 75., the value of eleven rose trees' destroyed by defendant's donkey, and burleyman's fees. div.head: DEATH OF MR. SAMUFL WItITH, OF_RUNCORN.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. SAMUFL WItITH, OF_RUNCORN.

A well-known figure has been removed from our midst in the death of Mr. Samuel White,of Greenway-road, who breathed his last on Saturday, after a brief illness. He had attained the age of 77. Commencing life as an ordi- nay bricklayer, he by his shrewdness, and business capacity, became a large owner of property, and died 'comparatively speaking a rich man. The West Bank estate, at Widnes, has been covcred with cottage pro- perty built almost exclusively by the deceased, and he has carried on extensive building operations in Runcorn. Perhaps his greatest work was building the chimney at Weston Chemical works, which until recent years was the highest chimney in Great Britain. His mortal remains were interred at Runcorn Cemetery, on Wed- nesday afternoon, and he was followed to the grave by a considerable number of relations and townspeople

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCOR;. About half-past eleven, on Thursday night. P.C. Rat- cliffe was called into the house No. 7, Wilson's-row, and on proceeding upstairs found a bricksetter's labourer, named Joseph Mann, lying in bed, and bleeding from a wound in the throat. Mann had a short time previously come downstairs, and asked the landlady, Mary flig„nett, for a knife. She handed him an ordinary table knife, when he said he was going to commit suicide. She told him to "get off to bed," and he left her. A few minutes later she found that he had attempted to take his life by cutting his throat. Dr. McDougall was called in and stitched the wound, which is of a serious nature, although the windpipe is not severed. The unfortunate man told the constable the knife was not sharp enough. For some days Mann has been drinking heavily, and has been strange in his manner. He has been removed to the workhouse.

THE LATE MR. J. B. IMISON, OF WIDNES. The Vicar of Widnes,on Sunday, preached two sermons having reference to the loss the Church and the town had sustained through the death of Mr. J. B. Imison. In the morning the Vicar preached at the Parish Church, and in the evening at St. Paul's Church. There was a crowded congregation at the latter place of worship. The pulpit, reading desk, and choir stalls were draped in black. At several of the Nonconformist places of wor- ship reference was also made to the sad event. At a meeting of the Widnes Church Council, it has been unanimously resolved "That the members of the Widnes Church Council desire to express their deep sor- row at the death of Mr. J. B. Imison, honorary organist of St. Paul's Church, and formerly churchwarden. They feel that they have lost a true friend, and a most earnest and able fellow-worker, and one whose early death they deeply deplore. They beg to express to Mrs Imison their heartfelt sympathy with her and her family in their be- reavement." FATAL LEAP FROM A RBDROOM WINDOW AT WIDNES.

_ . On Tuesdayevening an inquest wes held at he Golden Bowl Inn, Whines, before Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy- coroner, touching the death of Thomas Simcock, aged 76 years, who sustained injuries by falling from a bed- room window on the 24th of November last.—Al,ce Lightfoot said she was the landlady of the Golden Bowl Inn, Whines. The body on view was that of her father, Thomas Simcock. He lived with her, and was a retired provision dealer. On the 24th of November last he went to bed about half-past seven o'clock in the evening, and some time afterwards he must have got up and opened the bedroom window, for she heard a crash of glass and afterwards found the deceased in the yard. He was immediately brought into the house and put on the sofa. Dr. McDonnell, who had attended him till his death, was sent for, and it was found that his thigh was broken. He died on Saturday. Two years ago the deceased had a stroke, which had affected his memory.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. FUNERAL OF MR. W. BANES, 3.1'., RUNCORN. div.head: RAILWAY FATALITY AT WIDNES.
div.p: RAILWAY FATALITY AT WIDNES.

A shocking accident occurred at the Sheffield and Mid- land Goods yard, Moss Bank, on Thursday evening. Frederick Charles 13oulton,aged 14, of 168, Widnes-road, who is employed by the Company as a junior clerk, was in the act of attaching invoices on waggons, and while crossing between two sets of waggons, he was crushed between the buffers. The waggons were set in motion through shunting operations. The boy, was carried into a cottage in the vicinity, but he died before the arrival of Dr. MacLennan.

div.head: SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A WIDNES MAN AT WIGAN.
div.p: SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A WIDNES MAN AT WIGAN.

An accident of a rather serious nature occurred to a man named Joseph Lllford, aged 27, living in Deacon- rd., and in the employ of Messrs. John Hutchinson and Co. About two o'clock on Wednesday aftern3on he was at Garswood Hall Colliery, near Wigan. After he had finished his work, and was making his way to the railway station from the siding, he had to pass a number of wagons, and while in the act of crossing the line, the engine at the other end started, and he was knocked down, some of the wagons passing over his left arm. He was speedily removed to the Wigan Infirmary, where it was found necessary, from the seriousness of the Injuries he had sustained, to amputate the arm from the shoulder joint. div.head: COLLIERS WAGES IT ST. HELENS.
div.p: COLLIERS WAGES IT ST. HELENS.

The colliers of St. Helens anddistrict are express- ing considerable dissatisfaction in consequence of certain employers not having given the:full 10 per cent, advance, which was promised to them from the Ist of January. It was stated that when the men at a few Of the collieries Were paid on Friday and Saturday they found the advance given was in some cases only five per cent., and in others 7i per cent. On Monday afternoon the ,day-wagemen at the White Cross Collieries placed the matter before their employers, who promised to give the full ten per cent. In the evening a meeting of the day- wagemeu employed at the St. Helens Collieries was held at the Green Dragon beerhouse, and it was decided to meet the employers and place the matter before them. It was also decided that in the event of the employers not acceding to the men's wishes, notices should be sent in terminating all contracts until the full advance is made. _ _

THE HOME IRON TRADE. Mainly owing to ''',ambling in Scotch warrants, the regular course 01' business in the iron trade was somewhat interfered with last week, but the market once more emerges from the ordeal in a steady con- dition, a sign that trade generally is still in as healthy a state as it entered the new year in. Pig-iron has been depressed by the operations in Scotch warrants ; but although the latter have experienced a considerable drop, prices of Scotch makers' iron, for which there is a fair demand, have remained steady. Middlesbrough pig has lost 3s. 6d. a ton since last week, but hematites in the north-west remain unchanged with makers, while in other districts the value of pig-iron is fairly well and in some stiffly maintained. In finished iron, business is pretty active, and rates are steady, the result of the quarterly meetings being to confirm the stability of prices. Steel is slightly quieter, but there is no going back from recent advances. Shipbuilders are busy, but no fresh orders are reported this week. Engineers are briskly engaged, with plenty of fresh work offering. A WRINKLE FOR TITHE-PAYERS._

At the -Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before Judge Ffoulkes, Thomas Hewitt, farmer, of Burtonwood, sued John Kenwright, a carter, living in the same township, for .C 4 18s. 4d., in respect of a payment of tithe. Mr. H. J. Longton appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. P. Davies for the defend- ant. It appeared from the evidence that Ken wright bad previously occupied the farm which was now tenanted by Hewitt. Prior to his leaving iR March last, the sum mentioned had become due for tithe and had been demanded but not paid. After Hewitt had entered upon 'the farm, he received a demand for the payment of the money from the re- ceiver of tithe at Warrington, and was threatened with a distraint in default of payment. Under this compulsion he paid the money, and afterwards Mr. HaNall, the agent for the estate, wrote to Kenwright demanding that the amount should be refunded by him. Kenwright decline qto pay, and hence this County Court action. His Honour, in giving judgment, said the obligation to pay tithe was on the laud and not on the tenant. There was no personal obligation on the defendant to pay tithe after having lett the land. Tithe was a charge upon the land, and if there was nothing on the land to distrain upon, the tithe would have to go unpaid. There never was, his Honour repeated, any personal liability for tithe. He gave a verdict for the defendant with costs. ANNUAL CLEARANCE SALE now on, J. -W. Dutton, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adet.
THE ARCHDEACON OF WARRINGTON ON CHURCH
REUNION.

The Archdeacon of iffir-rington read a paper, on Wednesday, at the conference of evangelical clergy- men now being held at Islington, London, his subject being "Reunion Is it Desirable? Is it Possible ?" and to both questions, on the basis laid down by the Lambeth Conference, he gave a decided negative. He said the question was a difficult one. What was desired was the restoration of the organic unity of the Church ; but the demand of the Lambeth Con- ference for a recognition of the historic Episcopate rendered reunion impossible; for the Presbyterians. who had as truly as ourselves an historic ministry, would not be likely to unchurch themselves and commit ecclesiastical suicide. He would like tn open wide the gates of the national establishment of religion by a broad and liberal comprehension, so' as to include all who were willing to accept the doctrines of the Church of England while retaining their own freedom, though acknowledging a funda- mental agreement with the establishment. Ile would net, however, admit them tothe endowments of the English Church, unless they conformed to her rules. With a greatphilosophic statement hewould lay the foundation of the Church broad and deep, so that she might crush the powers of darkness, and have no breaches in her wall or traitors in her cita- del. Ile would like to see the stringency of the Act of Uniformity relaxed; and steps taken to prevent all counterfeit of the Roman Mass, so that the National Church might be a bulwark against unbe- lief and superstition.

div.head: NEW Sr. HELENS RAILWLY.
div.p: THE NEW Sr. HELENS RAILWLY.

A sleeting of the directors of the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway Co.. has been held at St. Helens, under the presidency of Mr. U. Seton-Karr, M.P., at which there were also pre- sent Lord Gerard, Mr. W. J. Legh, D L and Mr. Joseph Beecham. It was reported that everything was in a satisfactory condition, and if the weather continued favourable, the contractor would, in a short time, have five hundred men at work. It was considered that the improved state of trade warran- ted the directors in proceeding with the construc- tion of the line as rapidly as possible. • ANNUAL CLEARANCE SALE now on. J. /4 W. Dutton. Sankey-st., Warrington.—advt. THE ROYAL MILITARY EXHIBITION . .

Some local interest will attach to the forthcoming Royal Military Exhibition, as, we understand, some volunteers of the Eight-Fortieth regimental districts, which include Warrington, St. Helens, &c., have come forward with exhibits. The Exhi- bition buildings are to be finished by March 25th. They will form an irregular quadrangle, enclosing the Gordon Home and grounds, about three-and- half acres, with one entrance in Tite-street and one on the Thames embankment. These build- ings will contain the exhibits for the Soldiers' Industrial, Loan, ..nd Trade sections, the refresh- ment-rooms, offices for the staff, band-stands, &c. On the eastern side, about four acres of the Royal Hospital Park has been by the kindness of the Commissioners, appropriated for military sports and amusements. Here there will be a hand-stand cap- able of containing 500 performers, the Ambolance exhibits of the Medical Department, and of the Order of St. John, a shooting gallery, end a concert, hall. The electric light will render this portion of the Exhibition an attractive feature by night. His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales has consented to open the Exhibition on a day early in May, to be notified hereafter; and her Royal Highness the Princess of Wales has also promised to be present, and at the opening ceremony to receive the purses, which are now being collected by ladies from all parts of the United Kingdom, through the organis- ation of the district and local committees, of which 112 are in working order. These purses will be devoted to Church of England Soldiers' Institutes, as also will any surplus lands at the close of the Exhibition.
