div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.-IMPORTANT MEETING."

A meeting of this body was held at the offices at the Town Hall, Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon, under.the chairmanship of Air. T. H. Gossage. There were also present Messrs. E. Carey, T. Handley, J. Midwood, D. Wright, H. S. Timmis, S. Sadler, J. Houghton, H. Gaskell, J. Taylor, F. Heyes, F. C. Liddell, R. , Cook, Dr. O'Keeffe, J. T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr (engineer), and J. Dickson (inspector).

THE NOTIFICATION OF MEASLES AND WHOOPING COUGH. Mr. Carey proposed that whooping cough and measles be added to the list of diseases that are scheduled under the Compulsory Notification of Diseases Act, that was recently put in force by the Board. He said that he thought that the members were agreed that the notifica- tion of certain diseases was desirable. If good was done in this way with regard to some diseases, the same effect would be obtained in regard to others. It was at first suggested that the compulsory notification of measles and whooping cough should be adopted for a period of twelve months, but it was now thought advis- able to propose that it be tried for nine months—from , the month of March next to the end of the year. During the last four years there had been 79 deaths from scarlet fever, 93 from measles, and 33 from whooping cough. He thought that when he mentioned those figures, there would be no hesitation on the part of any member of the Board in considering that it would be advisable to have compulsory notification of the two diseases in ques- tion.—The proposition was secended by Mr. D. Wright, and carried unanimously.
THE MOSS RANK SEWER AND THE 'WORK OF THE SURVEYOR. THE QUESTION OF EXTRAS.

Among the letters that were read by the Chairman was one from S. Cowburn and Sons, Hindley, near Wigan, with regard to the Moss Bank sewer, a subject which was the catne of a subsequent protracted discus- sion. The letter said that Mr. W. Cowburn had informed the firm of the result of his interviews with the Sewage Committee of the Board,durina which,he stated, the Committee came to the conclusion 'to offer £5OO in settlement of their account of £773 is. 4d., in connection with the Moss Bank portion of their sewage contract. In answer they begged to state that they could not at present see their way to accept the offer, as they believed the work had been carried out faithfully to the wishes and instructions of the surveyor, and they were at a loss to understand why the Committee should wish to make such a reduction from the account, as on glancr ing over the account it would be seen that the major portion of the amount charged was comprised of extra costs for steel pipes, and work in connection therewith, brickwork, supports to water and as mains, culverts and railway crossing, and deviation of and widen- ing the line of sewer in sundry places, so as to admit sewer pipes between water pipes and sides of sewer trench. In reply to some remarks made by the Committee on several items of the account, they begged to explain as follows. Length of sewer on Marsh.—ln the original line of sewer marked on the plan it was intended to lay a length of 82ft. of iron pipes, which they would find mentioned in the schedule, at the end of the sewer next to river estuary, but this was not done. If they added to this the length of sewers which had been relaid, it would make up the difference complained off. 100 item of 9 inch drain, laid in river estuary (included in of 190 i yards in account,—Owing to the increased depth of sewer across the marsh they pointed I out to Mr. Campbell, the then clerk of works, that this work was necessary, and he quite agreed that it was, as I otherwise the main sewer could not have been laid, as the tides for a considerable portion of the time during the laying of the sewer were of such a height as to completely submerge that portion of the marsh. Thereupon their Mr. W. Cowburn and I Mr. Campbell went to the Surveyor on the matter, and after explaining to him he agreed that it was neces- sary and woula allow for it, and they therefore contendel that this item was a proper charge. Item 534 I yards and altering line and level of sewer, and for sup- port walls on account of water and gas pipes. They con- tended that it would be most unjust to make this work part of the contract, as suggested, as it was necessary I owing to the zig-zag course of the pipes, and as it was impossible for a contractor coining strange to the iis- trict to estimate the probable inconvenience and extra cost in supporting the pipes, they could not allow for this item without losing all possibility of their tender being made favourable for acceptance. And, again, I were they to have kept clear of the pipes it would have necessitated a number of extra man- holes on account of the altered line, which would have been more expensive still. Item, 484 i Yards excavating to connect drains.—They could not at present recall to mind the exact position and dimensions of this item, but from the number, and extra labour attached to some of them (a watchman and lights having to be kept on them for two or three nights at a time), Mr. W. Cowburn said he was certain that the amount charged was under, rather than over, the actual cost. Item : Brickwork to support gas and water mains.—This item had all been put in to surveyor's orders, owing, in a a large measure, to gas engineer's objection to have the pipes dealt with anyother way. Item: Conductor to arrange with Canal Company for turning off the water. —As previously explained, the time for sending in ten- ders haying nearly expired before they received the quantities, no time was left to make the necessary in- quiry as to cost of saine,wnereupon the late head of their firm, and Mr. W. Cowburn, waited upon the Surveyor to point this out to hint, and he then said that the Board would attend to this item. Consequently, they did not Include anything, in the tender for that, and the reason why the matter had not been mentioned by them earlier, was that they never for a moment thought but it had been so arranged between the Surveyor and the Board, and that they were fully aware of it at the time. Item Steel tube.—They gathered from what Mr. Cowburn said, that under the circumstances,. the Board were kind elough to allow this item. They assured the Hoard that they were very much out of pocket by the above item, having made something like twenty journeys and attended at the works to ensure its being got ready in tune, besides laying out of the money from then until now. Item: written orders. from Surveyor for extra work.—On first page occur the follow- ing words," who," meaning the Surveyor, "shall also have full power, during the progress of the works,to add I to or deduct from the following quantities, such alter- ations to be executed by the contractor at prices set forth, in this schedule; any extra work not provided in such schedule shall be valued by the quantity surveyor; In the face of this, and the fact that they had before been required to produce written orders, always taking the different Surveyor's word, with the impression that everything would be right and in order as to payment, they hoped that the Board would be able to. grant them payment of their account in full. ' When the consideration of the minutes of the Highway Committee was taken, Mr. Sadler,. who proposed that they be adopted, referred to a recommendation to the effect that the Surveyor be asked, to resign. This had been brought about, he said, in connection with the Moss Bank sewer. The sewer had been completed for a long time, and the Committee had been consta Kay ask- iiag the Surveyor for the account, but had not been able to obtain it until recently. When the account was pre- sented the Highway Committee thought that it was not I satisfactory, and appointed a sub-Committee to investi- gate the matter. That Committee held several meetings, with the result that on every occasion they had not been able to get at the infortnation that they should have had. Mr. Sadler then enumerated a number of com- plaints against the action of the Surveyor. At one part, he said, the sewer had been made three feet deeper than was originally intended, and as the plans were lost a satisfactory solution of the matter could not be arrived at. With regard to the nine inch pipes they were unable to check that item, and the Surveyor pipes, allowed considerably more Per yard than the Committee

thought he should have done. There were numerous extras for brickwork, and it was decided to have three branches opened, to see if they corresponded with the items of account. In the first branch the Surveyor's measurement was 340 feet, and the actual measure- ment was 286 feet, making a difference of 51 feet. The Surveyor's measurement for the second branch was 260 feet, actual measurement 186, a difference of 74 feet; - and in regard to the third branch the Surveyor's measurement was 98 feet, and the actual measurement was 38i feet, a difference of 54 feet. Summarised, the amount of the account rendered was £2,433, and the amount of the original tender was £1,957, a difference of £476. The sum of £2lB had been allowed in the speci- fications for flushing tank and ventilating sewer, which had not been provided, this reducing the original tender by that amount. Deducting £343, difference between eost of steel pipes and cost of iron pipes, left a total difference of £351 not accounted for. The only reason of the Committee in bringing the matter forward was that they could not conscientiously pass an account like that.—Mr. Liddell seconded the proposition. Their prin- ciple complaint against Mr. Higginson was that they could not get any details from him. He sanctioned work being done without letting the Committee know about it—extra work. He. had continuously been told about allowing extra work to be put in, and keeping the Com- mittee entirely in the dark.—Mr. Taylor said that the 'Committee could get no information; and no figures, although they had had the contractor before them.—Mr. Wright said that the matter was one that the Board should carefully consider; bethought every member should have been supplied with a copy of the particulars. He was afraid that the Committee would have to take some blame upon itself, for, notwithstanding the great increase of the work of the highway department, the Surveyor had had it all to attend to. He thought that it was ins- 'possible for any man to carry out the work that had been carried out by the highway department within the last four years, and do it without making mistakes. They could not find that the Surveyor had ever received any bribe, 'Ur that he had in any way profited.—The Chairman: Ido not think that there has been the slightest imputation of anything of this sort. —Mr. Wright said that someone must have had the money, and his contention was that the Board and the ratepayers had got the benefit of it ; it was granted by the public that the Surve or had worked hard and made an excellent job of the sewering.—Dr. O'Keefe then proposed, and Mr. Wright seconded, an amendment to the effect that the minutes be passed with the exception of the one in question.—Mr. Brown said that in a contract like the one in question there must be a pretty large provision made for extras, -and it was quite possible that all the difficulties that the contractor would have to face could not be foreseen and provided for. In a job of the sort in question a larger amount of extra work would be required than in the (lase af an ordinary plain sewering job. With reference to the Surveyor not giving inform- ation to the Committee, he could not see any excuse at all.—Mr. Sadler: Our chief cause of complaint is that he should allow these extras to be incurred without bringing the matter before the Board.—Mr. Gaskell said that he thought the Board couldonly conclude that they had an incapable Highway Committee or an unsatis- factory Surveyor. He thought they were driven to the conclusion that theSurveyer was at fault.—Dr. O'Keeffe: It is because he has too much work. It is not fair to bring charges against a man who is expected to do three times as much work as he should do. He has been ex- pected to do work both inside and outside. How could he superintend everything, and be in two places at one and the same time. It is very unfair of the Highway Committee to bring these charges against him merely because he has spent a few pounds that could not be avoided.—Mr. Carey: I think it is only fair to give the Surveyor an opportunity of replying, either now or when he is ready.—The Surveyor : I would like to answer in writing.—Mr. Carey then proposed that a special meeting be held that day fortnight, for the purpose of receiving the reply.—Mr. Timmis seconded the motion, for which seven voted, the same number voting against.—The Chairman gave his casting vote in favour of the motion, and the other portions of the minutes were adopted.

div.head: DINSMORE PROCESS.
div.p: THE DINSMORE PROCESS.

Tho Gas and Water Committee reported that this process continued most efficient in its action, the average illuminating power of the gas supplied to the town for the last five weeks being 19.2 candles.

MOSES FOR FIREMEN AND WORKMEN. The Gas and Water Committee recommended that houses be provided for the Fire Brigade on the Board's land fronting Lacey-st., estimated to cost £l5O each, say 7 houses. Mr. Gaskell, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, said that it was considered advisable to have a certain number of the firemen living near to the fire station, so as to have a sufficient force ready in case of fire without risk of delay. Mr. Wright seconded the motion, which was carried.—it was also resolved, on the recommendation of the Highway and Health Committee, and on the proposition of Mr. Carey, that a number of houses bebuilt fronting Lacey-st., for highway and night soil workmen, subject to the consent of Leigh's Trustees.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that in future the fever hospital be free to the inhabitants of Widnes, other than pauper patients. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. Wright. The remainder of the business before the Board was of a routine character.

div.head: RUNCORN PARIS [I CPILTRCH TEA PARTT.
div.p: RUNCORN PARIS [I CPILTRCH TEA PARTT.

The annual tea party and concert was held in the National Schools on Monday evening. About 300 persons sat down to tea, "tables 'for which had been given by the Vicar, theßev. J. Holden, Messrs. J. Williams, W. Wigg, Mellor, Leicester, Lake. Buck, Rogerson, I. Speakman, Gregory, Towns, Barker, Crosby, A. Salkeld, J. Ball, Savage. Imison, W. Bate, J. Littler, George Hewitt, W. Frith, W. 41, hittaker, R. Abel, J. E. Meredith, John Johnson, J. N. Lello, Dugsdale, J. K. Diggs, W. Timmins, and E. Mar- wood; Mesdames Gorst, Statham, C. H. Hazlehurst, Hampson, Jones (South Bank) and A. Timmins, and the Misses Smith. After tea a sale of work was helld in an adjoining room, in aid of the District Nurse Fund. The articles offered for sale were the surplus of the recent bazaar, and Mr. E. Wynn Humphreys acted as auctioneer in capital style. The subsequent entertain- ment was given to a large audience by the Metropolitan Handbell Ringers who gave a number of selections of musicon the bells and contributed songs and duets. There was a numerous audience.—During an interval in the programme the Vicar (t'.e Rev. A. M. Wood, M.A.) delivered a speech in which he referred to the fact that he had had charge of the parish for the past three -ears. I Speaking of the past year's work, he said the Church Army since its introduction had done a great deal of good. Their Bishop had pah.... the Chairman a visit during the year, and he believed had taken away' a kindly opinion of the Runcorn people and had said he would be glad to come again. (Applause.> They had now got a nurse at work amongst them, and Runcorn having got her would not easily let her go away. (Applause.) Alluding to the School BoarclElection, he said he had not the slightest notion of what the members were going to do but they would all try to do their best for the town—(applause)-- without quarrelling with each other, if possible, anclhe hoped those present would back them up in that desir- able wish. With regard to the future, Major Orred had been good enough to let them have a house for nothing, and they were going to put it to a very good purpose. ' It was to be used as a house of refuge, and any articles of furniture they had to spare would be very acceptable. The next thing they wanted was to finish St. Michael's Church (applause)—and that could only be accomplished by appealing to the public. It would costa great deal of money, but it was essential that the edifice should be completed. In conclusion he announced that a- general mission would be held in the town shortly, and they had secured the aid of an experienced missionary. They wished to stir up the town from one end to the other. (Applause>. He was quite persuaded that with the blessing of God they would de very well in the coming year if they had a long pull, a strong pull, and a pull altogether. (Applause).

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARD/ANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARD/ANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon. 'rhere were present, the Rev. Dean Finegan (chairman), Rev. S. A, K. Sylvester, Messrs. W. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson, J. Leatherbarrow, W. Middlehurst, J. Marsh, J. W. Wareing, W. Ranson, G. Davies. N. Borrows, P. Longton, E. Syder, G. E. Chad- wick, J. Mercer, J. Griffiths, J. Ellison„ J. lienwright, J. Rirchall, J. Burchall, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). Itxtur.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 600 inmates of the house this week...against EX last week, • and 604 in the corresponding week last year ; 57 vagrants had been relieved during the. week, against 67 in the corresponding week last year. THE NEW RELIEF OFFICES. YO D Sr. HELENS.—At a. meeting of the Special Committee appointed to consider the question of the proposed new relief offices at St. Helens, held on the 13th January, the Uerk produced a draft plan ot proposed relief offices at St. Helens, pre- pared by Mr. Gandy, which was considered by the Com- mittee, and instructions were given to the architect to. see the owners of the land as to the terms upon which it could be obtained and to. prepare a detailed plan.—Mr. Longton asked if there had been any further communi- cation received on thesubject.—The clerk replied that he had not. A NEW NURSE.—The,lor'al Government Boatd wrote, on the 3rd inst. sanctioning the appointment of Miss Mary Ann Hughes as nurse of the Boys Home„ at a salary of £2O per annum, THE WOOLItOIi VACANCY.—Mr. Marsh asked if any communication had been received from the Local Government Board in regard to the resignation of Mr. Tuson,. one cif the Guardians for Much Woolton.—The Clerk stated that he had not; and explained that till course to be pursued was for Mr. Tinian to forward his resignation direct to the Local Government Board. TIIR SCIIOOI. ATTENDXNCE COISMITTEE.--The School Attendance Committee submitted an estimate of the amount they expected to require for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Education Act for the quarter ending 25th March next. The amount was £lO3 ss. This was the principal business>

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

THE STREET OBSTRUCTION QUESTION AGAIN. On Monday, at the Warrington rolice Court, Elizabeth Hallows, greengrocer, 56, Winwick-road, was summoned for having, on the 4th January, allowed a table upon which vegetables were exposed for sale to stand in front of her premises to the obstruction of passengers. P.S. Rowbotham gave evidence in support of the charge. Defendant said that the table was a small one, and on it were only nine cabbages. She was willing to pay a small sum for the privilege of putting out her table. The case was adjourned for a fortnight, to enable the matter to come before the Watch Committee.—A similar charge of obstruction against John Gregg, furniture broker, 35 Winwick-toad, in respect of furniture exposed for sale' was also adjourned. THE " SHINT'Y " SEASON IN FULL SWING. According to the Chief Constable of Warrington the "shinty" session commenced recently, and may be now considered to be in full swing. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, two boys, named John Hardman and Joseph Whitlow, were summoned for hiving played " shinty " in Brick-st., on the 2ndjanuary, and pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable observed that the " shinty " season was just commencing, and he wanted, if possible, to put a stop to the practice of playing the game in the streets. The Mayer said he had many a time had to leave the footpath, or he would have been struck by the missile which the "shinty" players were using. It was a practice which must be stopped in the streets. There was plenty of waste ground outside the town, where the police would not interfere with the players. The defend- ants would be discharged, but they must be careful not to again offend. AN EXTENSION OF HOURS FOR A BIRTHDAY SUPPER.— A MAGISTERIAL OBJEOTION. On Tuesday, at the conclusion of the ordinary business of the Warrington Police Court, Mr. George Lambert, of the Blue Lion Inn, Market-place, applied to the magistrates—Messrs. Robert Garnett, William Owen and E. M Crosfield—for an extension of hours on the occasion of a birthday supper.—Mr. Garnett (who was in the chair) : 'think public-houses are open long enough. That is my decided conviction, and I shall certainly not agree to this application. If persons cannot get drink enough by eleven o'clock it is a pity. I can manage in less than that time. My friends can do as they like, but I don't think—The Clerk : It is a supper.—Mr. Garnett : But I can get mine in less time than that. Eow2ver, I leave it to you gentlemen; I leave the responsibility to you.—Mr. Garnett then left his seat on the Bench, and Mr. Owen and Mr. Crosfield, after a short consultation, decided to grant the applicant two hours' extension of time, it having been stated that it was customary to grant such applications. DRUNKENNESS AND VIOLENCE: SATURDAY NIGHT ASSAULTS. Two cases of drunkenness, accompanied by acts of violence, were investigated by the Warrington magis- trates on Monday. William Miller, a tanner, residing in Lythgoes-lane, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Irlam-street, on Saturday night, and with having assaulted his married sister, Martha Richardson, at the same time and place. Prisoner went to his sister's house, and, as he was drunk, she ordered him out. He declined to go and struck her in the face. She went for a constable, and on the way back from the police station the prisoner met her, and assaulted her so badly that she became insensible. The Bench imposed a fine of 55. and costs for the drunkenness; and, with respect to the assault, bound the prisoner over in two sureties of £5 each to be of good behaviour for sixmonths. —ln the second case Thomas Burke, an engine driver employed on the Ship Canal works at Moore,was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Irlam-street on Saturday night, and with having assaulted John Finn at the same time and place. In the presence of Inspector Spinks and P.C. Taylor, the prisoner, who was drunk, knocked Finn down and kicked him whilst he was on the ground. The magistrates ordered the prisoner to pay a fine of 20s. and costs, or go to prison for a month with hard labour. A MARRIED COUPLE AT VARIANCE. A young married couple of the name of Woods aired their marital grievances before the county bench, at Warrington, on Wednesday. The husband, William Henry Woods, was summoned for having, on the 3rd inst., assaulted his wife, who met the charge with a cross-summons for assault, alleged to have been com- mitted on the same date. Mr. A. Browne conducted the ease on behalf of the husband. The evidence of Mrs. Woods was to the effect that she had been married twelve months. After five months experience of married life she and her husband separated, but subsequently they came together again. She ,complained that on the date mentioned in the summonses her husband caused the furniture to be removed from the house, and that when she asked for an explanation he replied rather too forcibly by striking her. In answer to Mr. Browne she admitted having broken a picture with a poker, and having smashed half-a-dozen cups and saucers. She, however, denied having made a wreck of the house. No evidence was brought in corroboration. Mr. Browne submitted that Mrs. Woods had neglected her household duties, and that on the day in question she assaulted her husband by throwing stones, half-bricks, and clinkers, at him. He allowed her Li a week, but she pawned things, and ran him into debt. The result of the hearing was that the Bench dismissed both cases, and advised the two to endeavour to live comfortably together. A DISCHARGED SOLDIER'S FUTILE EFFORTS TO OBTAIN WORK. At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, a young man of good appearance, named Charles Turner, who wore the uniform of the Liverpool regiment, was brought up on a charge of having fraudulently enlisted in that regiment, on the 9th of last November, by giving a false answer on attestation. On enlistment he said that he had never before been in the service of her Majesty, and subsequently he admitted having. served with the 11th Hussars. Prisoner, who soon gamed the sympathy of the court, told the magistrates that when he left the Hussars for the Reserve he found It very difficult to obtain employment. His reserve pay was soon gone, and for nine months he was knocking about until he was really sick at heart :he could get no per- manent employment. He would have rejoined the colours, but could not do so without refunding the reserve pay, and of course that was impossible. He handed to the magistrates references from officers under whom he had served, and asked the Bench to take into consideration the fact that he had been in confinement for 14 days awaiting trial. Replying to the Bench, the prisoner said he had served five years and 87 days, and left the Hussars on the 30th January, 1889. His de- ferred pay amounted to £l4 145., and his reserve pay was Bd. a day. He tried for a number of situations—as groom, porter, clerk, and berths of that kind. He was 24 years of age, and belonged to Liverpool. He tried to enter the police force in Liverpool, Leicester, and Nottinghamshire, but was below the standard ' • he sft. Sin, In height. The Chairman observed that the magistrates were of opinion that it was a rather hard lease, and they had decided to deal with the prisoner as ightly as they could. Ile would be committed for seven days, without hard labour. ALLEGED PICKING OF POCKETS IN THE MARKET. At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday morn- ing, Thomas Marshall and Annie Marshall, husband and wife, were brought up on remand from Monday on a charge of having been found loitering in the Market. place on Saturday for an unlawful purpose, with intent to commit a felony by picking pockets. Tney were also charged with having stolen a purse containing Ts. sd. in money, from the person of Clara Shaw. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. A witness named Sheldon deposed that he saw the prisoners picking pockets in the Market; questioned, he positively affirmed that he saw them pick the pockets of from "six to a dozen" persons. Other witnesses were called who said that they saw the prisoners acting in a suspicious manner in the Market, and Clara Shaw, a married woman, who lives in Cart- wright-street, deposed to having lost her purse on Satur- day evening, in consequence of which she had to go without any Sunday's dinner. She did not feel anyone abstract the purse from her pocket, but saw the female prisoner standing near her. She identified a burrit'penny that had been found in the possession of the prisoners as being like a coin that was in her purse on Saturday night. The purse contained two half-crowns, a two- shilling piece, a threepenny-piece, and twopence, one of the pennies being a burnt one. Constable Monoghan said that when prisoners were arrested they had, amongst other money, two half-crowns, two florins, a threepenny piece, and a burnt penny. The latter was found on the male prisoner, who was not identified by Mrs. Shaw. Mr. Browne, for the defence, admitted that the case was one of suspicion, but contended that there was not sufficient evidence upon which to convict. He thought that there was no case, unless absolute proof was brought on behalf of the prosecution. The Bench thought that the charge of attempting to pick pockets was sustained, and committed the male prisoner for one month, with hard labour, and the female for fourteen days, with hard .abour.

MINOIt CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Councillor Voisey. A DESERTER.—John Collins, a desertor, was remanded to await escort. DRUNICENNP.SS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—David Taylor, in Scotland-road, fined ss. including costs ; James Lavell, on Town Hill, on Saturday night, fined ss. and costs; Mary McLough- lin and Sarah Quinn, in Old-road, Latchford, on Satur- day, each fined ss. including costs. He was fined 20s. and costa for the latter offence. A SLEEPY CABDRIVER. Frederick Robson, a cab- driver, was summoned for having been asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cab, on the sth inst. Ile was ordered to pay the costs. DISTURBING THE PEACE.—James Gleeson, for creating a breach of the peace, in Winwiek-st, p oil the 4th inst.

was ordered to find two sureties for his good behaviour, or go to prison for a month. UFREGISTEILED LODOINGS.—James McCann, Welsh's- yard, Old-road, was summoned for having, on the 7th -January, kept lodgers without having his house regis- tered. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. ' CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Abraham Thornley, summoned for having allowed the chimney of his house to be on fire, was fined one shilling. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett, W.:Owen, and E. M. Crosfield. MISCELLANEOUS. Richard Dobson and Catherine Brown were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness. Margaret O'Brien, charged with having used obscene language, was dismissed with a caution. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes, Mr. John Fair- . . . .

dough, and Capt. Nicholson. DRUNKENNESS .—William Conroy was fined ss. and costs / for having been drunk and disorderly in Church-st. on Monday, and for having been drunk and diforderly in Buttermarket-st. on Tuesday evening; Joseph Bayliss was fined 55., including costa. DESERTRR.4.—Harry Samuel Malin, a deserter from the Royal Dublin Fusiliers, and William Robinson, a deserter from the sth Dragoon Guards, were remanded to await escort. They were apprehended on attempting to enlist at Orford barracks. THDRSDAY.—Before Major Litton, Alderman Sutton, • and Captain Ridgway. DammeNwess.—Margaret Fryer, charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Battersby-lane, was dis- missed on promising to leave the town at once, FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White, Alderman Harrison,

MISCELLANEOUS.—A navvy named W. Pugh; and a woman of bad character named Harriet Carter, were each sent to prison for a fortnight, for sleeping out at Arpley- on the previous night.—Annie Holmes, a young woman, was sent to prison for a week for indecency. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—A young man named W. Spiers. was summoned fer having assaulted Sarah Brown, a married woman, who lives in Lengford-st., on the 7th , inst., Mr. A. Brown defended. Complainant alleged I that defendant struck her on the head with a brick, but the magistrates, after hearing evidence, dismissed the CUE.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Edward Greenall, and J. Marson.
DIWNICENNESS.—Thornas -13-u-s.hell, a farm labourer, charged with being drunk and disorderly at Stretton on the 11th January, was ordered to pay a fine of ss. and costs.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Capt. Withington and Mr. Matson. _
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Capt. Withington and Mr. Matson. _

DRUNKENNESS.—The following were dealt with for this offence :—James Ince, at Burtonwood, on the 21st ult., fined ss. and costs; Samuel Wilkes and Abraham Wilkes, at Sankey, on the 12th inst., each fined 2s. ed. and costs; and John Perk, at Sankey, on the 30th ult., fined ss. and costs.

ASSAULT.—John Taylor, a railway ballast man, was summoned for having, on the 3rd inst., at Padgate, assaulted a signalman named George Pritchard. A cross- summons charged Pritchard with having assaulted Taylor. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the latter,and Mr. A.Browne for the former. Taylor was fined ss. and costs, and the case against Pritchard was dismissed.

LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. G. B. Dewhurst, (in the chair), Mr. H. Stanton, and Dr. Brabizon. DRUNICENNESS.--ThOMM Holt, drunk and disorderly, at Lvmm, 21st Dec., ordered to pay costs; Peter Walsh, drunk and disorderly, at Warburton, 23rd June, 1889, ordered to pay costs ; Robert Taylor, drunk and incap- able, 20th Dec., 1889, ss. and costs; Wm. Ravenscroft, drunk and disorderly, at Lymm, 4th Jan., is. and costs. Doo OFFENCEB.—James Gould, farmer, Bollington, was charged with having allowed his dog to be at large, unmuzzled on the 12th January, ordered to pay costs, 4s. 6d. Frederick Clarke of High Leigh, was charged with allowing his dog to be at large insecurely muzzled, and the case was dismissed. REFUNDING POOR RELlEF.—Patrick Hirley, was Sum- moned by the Altrincham Board of Guardians for not repaying some relief which had been advanced to him in the way of loan. An order was made for the payment of 2s. a week. Defendant stated that he was a farm labourer and he only received 12s. a week wages. ASSAULT.—Edward Holt, a volunteer bandsman, at Lymm, was summoned by Robert Oldfield, farmer, Lymm, for having assaulted him on the 18th Dec. A fine of ltis. and costs was imposed. POACHING .—Thomas Evans, a young man employed on the Ship Canal, was charged with trespassing in search of game, at Warburton, on. the 28th Dec. A gamekeeper stated that Ship Canal men went about poaching in groups of five and six and defied anybody who went near them. A fine of 20s. and costs us., was im- posed. A &Hoot CASE.—Charles Broddell was charged with not having sent his son regularly to school, and a fine of , ss. was imposed. INDECENCY.—CharIes Jackson, of Altrincham, was charged with having behaved indecently at Bowdon, I towards a girl named Maud Bannister, on the previous day. It was stated by the police that they had obtained information of previous similar offences by the prisoner both at Altrincham and Lymm. He was committed for trial.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL-RUGBY.
To-day's matches :—Warrington V. Rugby, at War- rington ; Runcorn v. Bradford, at Bradford ; Widnes v. St. Helens, at St. Helens (League match) ; St. Helens Recs. v. Kendal Hornets, at St. Helens.

The Lancashire fifteen did a good stroke on Saturday when they defeated Somerset by two goals and two Tries to one goal and one try. This is better than either Yorkshire—the "champion county "—or Middlesex did against the same county, for the latter had to be con- tent with a draw, while Yorkshire were lucky in winning by a try near the call of time. Valentine was very much in evidence for Lancashire, scoring three out of four tries, and the well-known Swintonian was never seen to better advantage than on Saturday. Whittaker is to be credited with the fourth try. It is worth noting that all the Lancashire major points were scored in the first half, and those of Somerset in the second half. It seems from this that Lancashire went off with a lot of dash, and that, on the other hand, Somorset displayed a lot of staying power.

Runcorn gave Broughton Rangers a taste of their quality, on Saturday, when the Manchester men, although assisted by the redoubtable.Royle were unable to score a single point of any description. One of the Runcorn contingent did not turn up and Hughie was entering the field with 14 men, when a fiatman named Basnett, who is pos.se.ssed of only one arm, pleaded so hard to fill the vacant place, that the Captain consented. "All I want you to do" said Hughie "is to get down in the scrimmage and push," and the recruit worked like a trooper throughout the game. At one point he collared Royle close on his own line and brought him to Mother Earth much to the county man's disgust.

The Ran,gers were beaten both forward and behind and they were kept busy defending their line from start to finish, but in the first half Runcorn could make no im- pression. In the second half they ran up a score of a goal and two tries; Hampson, W. Hughes, and Daniels, being the scorers.

Under the pretence of giving the portraits of the players in the Runcorn first team, a Liverpool evening journal, on Saturday, exhibited to the public a veritable chamber of horrors. The sketch of Broady was a fair likeness, but the mother of any of the other 15 would never have recognised the lineaments of her son in the portraits given. The artist had apparently seen the difficulty that might arise, because each player was care- fully labelled with his name twice, so that there might be no fear of mistaking who the picture was meant to represent.

Warriagton scored a double victory over Widnes, on Saturday. At Widnes the " wirepullers " made another step upwards in the West Lancashire League, and at Warrington the" A" team beat the "chemicals" second string. In each case, however, the victory had to be strongly fought for. Widnes first team are clearly in much better form now than they were at the beginning of the season, and the combination and dash they dis- played, on Saturday, was very creditable.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

A team will be sent from the Warrington gymnasium next Saturday, to try conclusions with the Exeter Hall team in the first round for the English Challenge Shield. The Exeter Hall team is a strong one, as may be judged from the fact that they have twice held the shield, but the local gymnasts are in good condition, and they may be relied upon to do their best against their formidable opponents. I may also mention that it is intended to hold an assault at arms in connection with the Warring- ton gymnasium on the second Monday in February.

FOOTBALL.

"..* Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY. RUNCORN HORNETS V. WIDNES VICTORIA.—At RUGCOII3. Result Victoria 3 minors, Hornets two minors. .RUNCORN TRUE BLUES V. DITTON RECS. "A."—Played on Saturday at Ditton and a good game resulted in a draw of two tries each. Hill and Brereton were scorers for the Blues and Gilbody and Nixon for the Recs. RUNCORN A V. BROUGHTON RANGERS k.—ln this match, which was played at Runcorn on Saturday, Novell kicked off for the visitors, and play of a very even character prevailed 'for some time. "Davies broke away from the line out, and Woods received a neat pass, and the latter put in a fine kick. Relief was given by Ward, and in the course of really smart passing the visitors were pressed by the home forwards and had to resort to defensive play. The visitors played with much dash, mad Wood and Pendlebury showed prime form. A drop at goal by Houghton compelled the visitors to kick dead, and at the close of play, a goal having been kicked in the second half by Runcorn, the score stood: Runcorn one goal, two minors; Rangers, three minors. WARRINGTON 2ND V. TRANMERE WANDERERS.—This match was played at Traamere. The visitors rushed the leather over the line, and Williams scored, Oxley placing a goal. With this advantageends werechanged, and Tranmere again defended. Warrington again got over the line, but the point was disallowed. Minors fell in quick succession to the visitors, and a good game ended in Warrington one goal four minors, to Tranmere nothing. 'this is the first time that the Wanderers have been beaten for two seasons. Heosom, Knowles, Berry, Barnes, Wilkin, and Oxley all rendered invalu- able aid for Warrington. Warrington team: A. Newton, back: three-quarter backs, Bibby, Heesom, and Lalley ; half backs, Williams (captain) and Knowles: forwards, Berry, R. Barnes, Wilkin, Russell, Woodward, Reynolds, Welsby, Johnson, and Oxley. RUNCORN V. BROUGHTON RANGERS.—The Cheshire champions, on Saturday journeyed to Broughton to meet the Rangers. The home team kicked off, and Evans soon obtained possession of the ball, and it was kicked into touch by Crompton, to whom it was passed. Re- lief was shortly afterwards given by Boyle, who put in a good kick, and almost immediately the Runcornians secured a free kick. Again Royle was equal to the occa- sion, and prevented anything alarming from taking place by judiciously returning. Again Evans gained possession of the ball, and a neat pass was made to Crompton, who showed a determination to improve mat- ters by putting in a magnificent run. Gresty, however, was on the alert, and brought Crompton up somewhat sharply. But the Cheshire men were not to be daunted, and at once by strategetical and fineplay, during a sharp dribble, succeeded in crossing the line' and thus com- menced the scoring. Gresty showed good running form, and the ball was kicked into touch. Hughes passed the ball to Crompton, and he made a splendid drop at goal; but the sphere was kicked dead by Royle. After the Broughton Rangers had dropped out, Runcorn hurried the ball over the line near the touch line, a try being secured by W. Hughes. Brazendale, however, failed to convert. Quinney put in a smart dribble,but Brazendale checked the ptessure, and returned the ball into touch. Then followed some neat kicks on the part of Hurst; but once more Crompton obtained possession,and passed to Davies, who ran in his accustomed form and scored. Brazendale then scored a splendid goal, and at the close of play the score registered was: Runcorn, 1 goal, 2 I tries, and 3 minors ; Rangers, nil. Teams :—Runcorn: J. Brazendale, back ;T. H. Davies, Crompton, and H. [ Hughes, three-quarter backs ; W. Evans, and S. Abrams, ' half backs; W. Hughes' Riley, Hancock, Gayter, Broady, Rigby, Hampson, Hulse, and Basnett, forwards. Rangers: Royle, back; Gresty, Kennedy, and Hurst. three-quarter backs : Higginbottom, and Roberts, half backs ; Moxon, Jackson, Skidmore, McGowan, Wheeler, Squires, Quinney, Fitton, and Smith, forwards. WARRINGTON " A " v. WIDNES" A."—Notwithstand- ing the threatening weather, a very fair muster of spec- tators assembled to witness this fixture on the Wilders- pool enclosure on Saturday. It was considerably past the advertised time when Widnes commenced, and play settled down in earnest at the home quarter, until Molyneux, Lawless, and Rowe started a dribble, which resulted in the visitors being slightly pressed. An im- mense kick by Jolley followed, but a free kick toliVidnes found play contested at midfield. A grand screw scrim- mage by the home van was stopped by McGurl, but a momentary advantage was gained by some passing of the Widnes backs being intercepted, and Webster getting a pass almost dropped a goal,a minoraccruing. Following the drop-out, Tonkies and Wright spoiled the return, and a strong rush by the visiting forwards quickly found the ball at their opponents' 25. Here Daniels strove hard to get away, but was overtaken at centre, and the game was stoutly contested for some period at neutral territory. Ultimately Peters ran very well, but the rush wasstopped by Sampson. McGurl was now very prominent, getting clean away, and throwing widely to the wing, but Webster stopped his man in fine style. This was soon neutralized by a splendid pass from Mather to Daniels, who made considerable headway, and Barnes, Eyre, and Davies by some good play further improved the position. Then followed a splendid run by Mather, hut selfishness spoiled a certain try. Directly afterwards Mather was again conspicuous, and Isherwood, Rowe. and Thorniley dribbled to the line. The ball was soon got out of danger, however, and Widnes in turn attacked strongly, a bad pass enabling Warrington to relieve. Some exceedingly fine kicking by Jolley and Bates followed, and a minor was only obtained after Lawless and Thorniley dribbled over the line. A good dribble by Kenyon, Ridgway, and Wright was stopped by Sampson, this being replied to by Isherwood, Eyre, Davies, and Howarth, starting a rush which was only saved under the posts. A bad piece of play by the home team lost the advantage gained, but following some more good kicking Lawless again missed scoring, a minor accruinz. From the drop-out Widnes attacked determinedly, but short rushes by Eyre and Beard gradually relieved to the 25, where some pretty passing by Parr, Abbott, and Peters was witnessed, half- time arriving with Warrington 3 minors to nil. On re- starting Davies showed up with a good kick, and Barnes by a fine punt nullified some smart work by Abbott. By a strong rush of the visiting forwards' the game was transferred to the opposite end, the ball hovering danger- ously near the line. Relief at length came by Beard, Howarth, and Molyneux rushing to the quarter flag. A free kick to the home team was finely returned by Abbott, and a bad mull being made of the kick, Mullinger who had followed at top speed gained an easy try, the place failing. Put on their mettle by this unexpected reverse, the home forwards played updesperately, and had the ball at the Widnes quarters in quick time. Davies then stopped a rush, but Eyre, Thorniley, and Isherwood dribbled to the line, and a nice pass by Lawless to Mather enabled Beard tc gain a try, a capital attempt being made to convert. The drop out found no relief, until Parr being tackled, quickly put the ball in motion' and started a pretty cross dribble, which took play to the home 25. Some more good kicking by Daniels, Peters, and Samp- son followed, the result being a minor to the home team. Free kicks were now the order, and a sharp pass by McGurl enabled Abbott to kick to midfield. This was replied to by Webster running well, and a spell of passing by Lawless, Mather, and Daniels took play to the line, and Lawless giving Mather a short pass enabled him to cross, Webster converting. The kick off was finely returned, and Abbott failing to reply, Mblyneaux was enabled to run well into ' his opponents quarters. I Subsequently Mullinger put in a fine run, and when looking extremely dangerous, was safely pulled up by Jolley, aril relief was brought about by a fine kick from Jolley. Widnes again attacked, and the home team had a rather anxious-time of it until Lawless dribbled from a pack, and the visiting backs making a bad mull, Mather obtained possession, and ran in a splendid try from half-way flag, and although far out Webster kicked a goal, leaving Warrington winners by 2-1-4 to 0-1-0. Teams :—Warrington: Sampson, back;.* Webster, Jolley, and Daniels, three-quarters; Mather and Law- less, half backs; Barnes, Thorniley, Molyneaux. Howarth, Evre, Isherwood, Rowe, Davies, and Beard, forwards. Widnes: Bates, back; Peters, Abbott, and Mullinger, three-quarters; McGurl and Parr, half backs; Wright. Tonkies, Kenyon Farmer, Ridgway, Pearson, Cook, Minton, and Hartland, forwar is. WARRINGTON v. WIDNES, WEST LANCASHIRE RUGBY LEAGUE.

What might be termed a " Derby Day" in West Lan- cashire football occurred on Saturday, when the above clubs met in their return fixture at Widnes. The first game this season had resulted in a decisive victory for Warrington, but on the present. occasion, the Widnes ! men evidently meant business, for a strong team had been whipped together, whilst Warrington on the other hand, had to deplore the absence of Barnes, who had , not recovered iron' his injury received at Devasbury ; and Bandies at the last moment failed to make the journey through indisposition. This match on Saturday being a League match inure than ordinary interest was taken in it, and judging from the speculation which was rife, the chances of Widnes were highly fancied. Ample train accommodation had been provided for the War- rington enthusiasts, it being estimated that some 1,500 journeyed to the chemical town. Both teams met with a hearty reception on entering the arena, and, Turner having won the toss, Parkinson started towards the pavilion goal, Massey returning to the half way flag. A rush by the Widnes forwards was cleverly foiled by Nevins, and from some loose play Morris was the means of Improving the position of Wid- nes. It was left to Massey to relieve by a tall kick, and smart following up by the same player prevented Parkinson from placing his side in an aggressive atti- tude. The game continued of an exciting character, each side striving hard to gain a footing in their opponents quarters, but beyond a slight pressure at the opening of hostilities, midfield was chiefly the scene of operations. Brennan was now at fault with a pass from Laws, and Evans intercepted, but Warrington failed to take a splendid chance. From a free kick taken by Fair Turner the Warrington forwards, headed by Donohoue and Dillon, again took play tothe half way flag,and after Massey had again foiled Parkinson. in his endeavour to
.M
- :124TER, SATURVAY, JAN'

feply to a kic,k, Evans ran along the touch until Hartles deposited him in touch ii . close proximity to the Widnes quarter flag. Massey. to whom the bulk of the work had so far fallen, punted grandly up the field, and from a pack a rare exhibition was witnessed between Antro- bus, Bate, Evans, and Lawless, the last-named being tackled before he could fairly get into his running. Another similar exhibition was witnessed immediately after, but this time Lawless punted high up over the line. The Warrington forwards were well up, and Law- less racing up at top speed took advantage of Widnesians hesitation, and placing his men "on side" with a clever piece of play Frank Turner pounced on the leather, and scored an unmistakable try. The simplicity of the point made it all the more ridiculous but it was un- doubtedly the result of tricky play and excellent judg- ment. Frank 'Turner was entrusted with the place kick, and a neat goal was the result. On the restart, Lawless put in a strong kick along touch. and Fair. Turner charg- ing Clarke's kick, matters aeain assumed a dangerous aspect for the honeesters. Dillon, Nevins, and Little- wood each became prominent with capital pieces of work, and then Stubbs and Smith by a well-executed dribble caused BOSCOW a little auxiety. The visiting custodian was as safe as could be, and after he had effected a smart save of the Widnes forwards, yr. Dillon and Frank Turner raced away, and although Clarke tried to effect an opening, he found more than his match in Nevins. Hartles here receivcd from a long kick by Massey, and failing to pick up he dribbled grandly through the opposing forwards, and the movement was not checked until Fair. Turner saved at the visiting quarter flag. Bate and Antrobus each in turn tried to effect an opening, but it was to no purpose. From a rush near the line the visitors saved. Exchanges fol- lowed on the popular side immediately on the re-start, the final operator, Nevins, directing the oval in touch at the half-way flag. Some smart passing by the Widnes backs resulted in Warrington defending, and only by degrees were the visitors able to relieve. Massey and LittlewoOd in turn worked the oval to the half-way flag, and then another brilliant exhibition by the Warrington half-backs was loudly applauded. Judicious kicking by the Widnes backs once more took play to the War- rington end, and although Littlewood, Donohue, Povey, and Nevins found their way through a pack, Parkinson neutralised by a dodgy run, until Massey barred his progress. The tackling powers of Warrington were re- peatedly called into requisition, and Laws made a good bid for a tangible score with a strong run from the quarter flag. A free kick fell to Widnes, but the eval grazed the posts on the outside, Boscow running the ball out to the 25 flag. Half-time was then called, Warring- ton leading by one goal to Widnes one minor. On resuming, exchange kicks at once followed between Nevins and Brennan, with advantage to the first-named. A fine piece of work by' Antrebus and Bate resulted in Evans putting in a strong run to the lk idnes line, Hartles pulling him up a yard from the goal. From a pack which followed, the ball was sent to Lawless, who dropped the leather over the bar, but through some informality the, point was over- ruled. Warrington would not be denied, and a vigorous assault was kept on the Chemicals citadel. Massey apparently got a fair try at the corner flag, but still the point was overruled. From a wide pass Clarke got away,and putting in a brilliant run effected capitarrelief by taking the oval to the half way flag. Widnes new seemed to revive, and aide,' by the smart play of Hartles the Warrington goal was placed in jeopardy. Nevins came in for special notice repeatedly, with capital returns and effective tackling. The play was chiefly of a give-and-take nature, and was confined to the -for- wards, and despite this the game never flagged in the least. The interest was maintained all through, and when any individual player accomplished anything out of the ordinary he was the subject of a round of ap- plause. Clarke made several attempts to score, but the smart play of Boscow and the remaining Warrington backs frustrated all efforts, and a good game ended in favour of the visitors by one goal to one minor. A more even game we have never witnessed, and both sides are to be complimented on their display. The game throughout was conducted with a spirit that is becoming to all footballers, and during the whole of the game there was not a single instance where one could point to direct rough play. Boscow played capitally at full back, whilst Massey was the best back on the field. I Both Antrobus and Bate worked capitally together, and Nevins and Fair. Turner were the pick of the good set of forwards. On the Widnes side, Stubbs, Clarke, Hartles, and Smith were the pick. Teams :—Warrington : Boscow, back : P. R. Lawless, J. W. Evans, and J. T. Massey, three - quarter backs; W. Antrobus and J. T. Bate, half-backs; Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, W. Dillon, E, Dillon, W. Nevins, J. Holmes,T. Donohue, W. Povev, and A. Little- wood. forwards. Widnes: J. Hartles, back ;J. Clarke, J. E. Parkinson (captain), and D. Brennan, three-quarter backs; G. Howard, and T.. Laws half backs; G. Hewitt, W. Barber, J. Gandy. W. Stdbbs, J. H. Smith, E. Gordon, P. Tickle, S. Morris, and J. Holt, forwards. Referee, Mr. Higson, Salford F.C. ASSOCIATION. HAYDOCE V. WHISTON.—These teams met at Haydock on Saturday. Haydock started, and had the best of play for some time. Smith opened the scoring from a pass by Tunstall and Chisnall followed with another soon after. These reverses woke up Whiston, but they could not make headway against the defence of the homesters. A combined run by the home forwards re- sulted in Taylor scoring a third goal, and at half-time the score was Haydock, 3 goals; Whiston, 1 goal. After a very brief interval, Haydock again pressed, and was in the Whiston goal. Final result :—llaydock, goals ; Whiston, 1 goal. Sr. BEL ENS ASSOCIATION V.POLICE ATHLETIC.—These teams met in the West Lancashire Association League contest at Cropper's-hill, St. Helens, on Saturday after- noon. There was a good attendance of spectators who witnessed a well-contested game. Thehome team won the toss and played downhill in the first half. At the start St. Helens had the best of the play but shot badly, and threw away several easy chances. The visitors played a strong game and at half-time led by three goals to one. The period, was evenly fought and both sides alternately pressed. At the call of time the Police were the victors by five goals to 2.

div.head: DEATH OF LORD APIER OF MA.GDALA.
div.p: DEATH OF LORD APIER OF MA.GDALA.

Lord Napier of Magdala, Constable of the Tower of London, who has been suffering for some days from an attack of influenza, died on Tuesday afternoon at twenty minutes past four, at his residence, 63, Eaton-square, London. His lordship was quite well on Saturday last, but late in the day caught a slight chill, whieh developed into an attack of influenza. On Tuesday evening, after the announcement of his lordship's death, there were many callers at the Tower of London, under the impres- sion that his lordship resided there. The distinguished general, who was born in 1810, was consequently in his

reightieth year. The Emperor William, in a telegram in which he signs himself " Admiral of the Fleet, has expressed his sympathy with the British Army on the loss of Lord Napier, of Magdala, "one of its ablest and bravest soldiers."
LIBELLING MR. HERBERT GLADSTONE.

DAMAGES £l,OOO. At the Sheriff's Cotht, London, on Thursday, a jury sat to assess damages irt the action brought by Mr. Herbert Gladstone. M.P., against Colonel George Bruce' -Malleson, a correspondent of the " Allahabad Morning Post," for libel in suggesting in that paper that plaintiff had narrowly escaped appearing as a co-respondent in the Divorce Court at the suit of a Gladstolitan leader not far from Leeds, and that the matter had only been hushedup through the exertions of plaintiff's father. Plaintiff claimed £s,ooo.—Sir Charles Russell stated the case for the plaintiff, and said the defendant was a gentleman of position and fortune. Defendant did not deny writing and publishing the libel, and the only question was the assessment of damages. The news- paper had since published an apology.—Mr. Herbert Gladstone was sworn, and gave an emphatic denial to all the suggestions.—Mr. Gill, for the defence, submitted that nominal damages would be sufficient.—The jury gave a verdict for £l,OOO.

COLLISION IN THE CHANNEL. LOSS OF FOUR LIVES. The steamer City of Rotterham, which arrived at Belfast on Thursday, had on board the sole survivor of the three-masted schooner Mary of Hale, bound from Rrussels with a cargo of China clay. When off the Isle of Wight,on Saturday night,the schooner was run into by an unknown steamer and cut in two, and four other sailors were drowned. The rescued seaman, who was at the wheel, had only time to cut the lashings of the life- boat when the vessel went down. A coroner's jury, on Thursday, returned a verdict of accidental death in the case of Mr. Morgan, manager of the Festiniog Gasworks, who was suffocated on Tuesday by an escape of gas while he was endeavouring to improve the service to the street lamps. The Hampshire, an iron barque of 1,214 tons, owned lin Glasgow, and which left Bangor, Maine, for The Clyde lon September 22, has been posted as "missing." She is nearly 90 days overdue, and there is too much reason to fear that she has been lost with all on board.

Craig Sellar, M.P. for the Partick Division of Lanark- shire, died in Edinburgh, oil Thursday, at the age of 55 yeart. Previous to the general election of 1855, he sat as a Liberal for the Haddington District of Burghs. He was then returned for Partick as a Liberal, and in 1886 won the seat as a Liberal Unionist, by a majority of 800. Lieutenant Henry Maxwell Buller Triton, of the 14th Lancers, stationed at Brighton, was killed on Wednes- day, whilst hunting with the Southdown foxhounds. His horse, in taking a five-barred gate, caught its hind feet, , and throwing its rider, rolled on him. Lieutenant Triton sustained terrible injuries, and died on Wednes- day night. The condition of Mr. C, R. M. Talbot, M.P., is con- sidered hopeless. He is suffering from bronchitis.
