div.head: FitODSIIAM.
div.p: FitODSIIAM.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A MASTER PAINTER.—OD Wed- nesday afternoon a somewhat serious accident occurred to Mr. F. W. Spencer, painter, of Main-street. He was engaged with some of his employes repairing the spout- ing at the Town Hall, when the ladder broke near the roof, and Mr. Spencer was thrown to the ground. He fell on to his side on the stones with which the road is paved, and was immediately conveyed in an armchair to his residence, where he was subsequently seen by Dr. Weaver, who discovered that his left wrist was broken, and his right leg severely injured. He was also injured internally.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held on Tuesday, when there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. P. Speakman, H. Aaron, Lewis, Bretlierton, Smith, P. Hall, J. Hall, Jeffs, J. Monnfield, C. Mounfield, Lowe, E. Jackson, W. Whitlow, T. Forster, D. H. Jones, Hewitt, Bran- dreth, Stokes, J. Baguley, Grice, Taylor, Parr, J. W. Baguley, Weir, Haywood, Dansey (Local Govern- ment Board Inspector), IL Linaker (clerk). The chief business of the Board was the appointment of a schoolmaster, of which three notices of motion had been given. Referring to Mr. Jeffs proposition that Mr. Stubbing, the former schoolmaster, be allowed to com- mence the duties to which he had been appointed by the Guardians, the Chairman pointed out that the Local Government Board had refused to sanction the appoiet- ment, and if this motion were put and carried, he asked how could Mr. Stubbing be allowed to take the post of schoolmaster in the House. The Guardians would be surcharged for his rations, and whoever signed the cheque for his salary would not get the money remitted. He suggested that Mr. Jeffs should alter his motion to the effect that the Local Government Board be asked to reconsider their decision.—Mr. Jeffs said lie had no wish to fly in the face of the Local Goverment Board, and his intention was to 'ent that Board's sanction.—Mr. Dansey agreed with the Chairman, and said they were asking him to put before them something which he could not legally do. Whether right or wrong ; whether they got a good schoolmaster or a bad schoolmaster, the sanction of the Local Government Board was neces- sary to the appointment before they could employ him, and if they employed a man who was not sanctioned then the Local Government Board had power, under an Act of Parliament, to apply for a mandamus to compel the Guardians to appoint another. He was giving them the legal aspect of the thing. It would be unwise to ask the Chairman to put anything before the meeting, which they could not legally act upon.—Mr. Speakma n said if there was no chance of getting the appointmen t sanctioned it was no use wasting time in going into the matter at all.—Mr. Jeffs said he fancied the Local Government Board would give way.—The Chair nan suggested that Mr. Jeffs should accept the following pro- position. That at a meeting of which doe notice was given, and at which 30 Guardians were present, Mr. Stubbing was elected by 17 votes against eight for Gleave and five for Naylor, and that the Local Govern- ment Board be urged to sanction the appointment of Mr. Stubning,.—Mr. Jeffs adopted that motion, and said he considered the reasons of the Local Governina nt Board for not sanctioning the appointment were very unsatisfactory. He made inquiries and had come to the conclusion there was nothing very serious in the Doncas- ter business, and even supposing there had been some- thing in it, after his services in that union for the past six years, he (Mr. Jeffs) did not see why that should come against him. As a Guardian he knew what took place at Runcorn, and Mr. Dansey had said that it was nothing very serious, but it was evident the Master and schoolmaster had got across and could not agree, and it would be better if the schoolmaster would resign. The schoolmaster had resigned and had been re-appointed by the Guardians, out of a num- ber. of others, as having the best credentials and he thought they had chosen the best man. When the Local Government Board learned that it was the wish of the Board that Mr. Stubbing should have the appoint- ment, they would give way as they had on previous eccasions.—Mr. Smith seconded the motion.—Mr. Dan- sey congratulated Mr. Jeffs upon the temperate manner in which he had brought forward the matter, and refer- ring to Doncaster, said after an inquiry there in 1883, the Committee reported that the schoolmaster frequently absented himself and was in the habit of frequenting public-houses on both Sundays and week days, and " is not in their opinion a fit and proper person, to have the care and charge of children. The e ommittee there- fore recommended his discharge. An extract from that report was sent to the schoolmaster, and in the ordinary course of things he sent his explanation and resigned. In his explanation, Mr. Stubbing said he had to some extent visited public-houses, but he denied that he had ever neglected his duty. This was the reason why Mr. Stabbing left Doncaster. When he applied for the situa- tion at Runcorn shortly afterwards, one of the queries "cause of leaving last situation," and he replied" Be- cause children attend at school in Doncaster." This was deception, and it was owing to that that the Local Government Board hesitated about sanctioning his appointment to Runcorn, but ultinneely they yielded to the , unanimous wish of the Guar- dians. In February last year at the request of the Guardians he (Mr. Dansey), made an investigation into complaints made by the 'nester against the school- master and vice versa—The complaints were not of a very serious nature, but tended to show that the two officers were getting on anything but well with each other, and the Guardians reprimanded them both. He was requested to see the schoolmaster privately and he did so and advised him while he had a good chance to get another situation, because he (Mr. Dansey) felt sure that if he stayed he would be in danger of ha eing a stigma thrown upon his character. He did not get another place and again in August an inquiry was held and the Guardians unanimously- requested him to resign.—Mr. Jones: They did not. It was four votes to two. Mr. Baguley and myself objected to it.—Mr. Dansey said however he was called upon to resign. The charges were not serious ; but he had been guilty of insurbordination to the master, whom it was his duty to assist, and his conduct in that room showed that it was impossible to expect the two men to go on together. He (Mr. Dansey) thought it was the duty of the Guardians to support the superior officer unless some- thing grave was brought against him. He had the task of maintaining the peace of the Workhouse, and it was against him they must find fault if anything went wrong. This matter had been considered by Mr. Ritchie himself, and the appointment if persisted in would not have the sanction of the Local Government Board, as they could not feel that it was to the interest of the Workhouse that Mr. IStubbhag should continue the schoolmaster.— Mr. Speakman said it was evidently hopeless to insist upon the appointment and the Guardians would do the man a serious injury by prosecuting the matter further. —Mr. Dansey said there was nothing at present to pre- clude Mr. Stubbing being appointed elsewhere.—Mr• Whitlow said for three years previous to Mr. Cunnali coming to that House, Mr. Stubbing did his duty with- out complaint and worked amicably with the late master, but he could do nothing right for the present master. There was no doubt 'that the te'o had got on badly together, and they were as nearly ff and 6 as lie could compare them.—lf the Guardians did their duty they would ask both the officers to resign. He resided in close proxmity to the House and knew that the schoolmaster had much to put up with. With regard to his food, he had to pay for a portion out of his own pocket not being able to eat the food sent to him by the master.—Mr. D. B. Jones contended that there was no charges of neglect of duty against the schoolmaster and the School Inspec- tor had just been down, and said Mr. Stubbing had passed the boys better year by year since he had been there. The behaviour of the boys had also been better outside the school. He further contended that Mr. Stubbing had not been insubordinate,but he did not think that he as a schoolmaster was to bow and scrape and fall dowa at the feet of anyone, and he was of opinion that if one officer went the other ought to go.—Mr. Smith said he did not know why one set of Guardians had so much ill-feeling towards Mr. Stubbing. He had been a good servant to the Board, and he (Mr. Smith) did not see why they should dismiss him.—Mr. Jones : Best we ever had.—Mr. Grice said there were none so blind as those who would not see. (Laughter.) In the interests of the house and the ratepayers, it would not do to continue Mr. Stubbing in his position as school- master. They had no charge against the master, there- fore why should they ask him to resign? He was res- ponsible for the conduct of the house, and a complaint of insubordination was a proper one to make.—Mr. Brandreth : We cannot do with two masters in the !lout°. (Me. Jones : No one wants two.) One will be sufficient, and if we get this schoolmaster we shall have two. Mr. Braedreth went on to state that the school- inaster had altered keys.—Mr. Jones: They were not altered by him.—Mr. Taylor: Mr; Chairman, will you allow Mr. Jones to make another speech, please. (Laughter.)—Mr. Brandreth said the schoolmaster altered keys so that he could go into any part of the house, and had he been his servant, ho should Rave dis- charged him at once.—Mr. Whitlow : If you were locked up at nine o'clock you would find keys.— Mr. Parr said lie should not know Mr. Stubbing if he met him, but he thought he had been badly used. He had been treated as if it were determined to throw him out of the House. and why it should be he did not know. lie asked how many old servants there were in the House that were there then when Mr. Jones left. None, lie believed, except Mr. Stubbing, and he argued that, ae a proficient man, they ought to keep him.—Mr. Dansey asked whether Mr. Stubbing would like this matter to be pressed.—Mr. Jeffs: Yes, he would.—Mr. Dansey: It is only my opinion that it would be detri- mental to his future welfare.—The motion was then put and it was announced that 13 were for and 13 I against. It was found that there were 27 members I present and the voting was taken again with the same

div.head: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK.

The annual meeting 'Will; managers and trustees of this bank was held at the office, High-st., on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. J. Brundrit, J. P., the pre- sident, occupied the chair. The actuary (Mr. Handley) reported that during the year the number of personal deposits was 1,815, and the amount paid in £5,389 6s. 4d. ; 4 Penny Bank deposits, £4 2s. 6d. ; 72 charitable societies' deposits, £328 Bs. 11d. ; and 133 friendly societies' deposits, £1,693 is. 3d., the total deposits amounting to £7,406 19s. There were 607 withdrawals, amounting to £5,895 3s. 7d. The total number of transactions was 2,631, an increase on the year of 426. The increase on deposits was £731 19s. 11d., and the decrease on withdrawals was £1,358 12s. Id. Excluding the societies, the average deposit had been £2 19s. 411, and the average withdrawals £8 55. The expenses of management for the year had been £B4 , 7s. 6d.' being at the rate of about a .1 per cent. on the capital of the bank. The interest allowed by the National Debt Commissioners amounted to £786 23. 6d. ; 1 dividends on stock held for depositors, £lO ; commission on purchase of stock, ss. sd. ; sale of pass books had realised £1 us.; total, £797 18s. 11d. The interest and dividend paid and credited to depositors was £692 3s. 11d., and adding the expenses of management, there was a surplus on the year's working of £2l 7s. 6d. With the surplus at the close of last year, there was now the sum of £76 19s. 11d, to the credit of the bank. The bank had now 1,001 accounts open amounting to £30,753 6s. 9d. an increase over last year of 112 accounts and in amount of £2,213 19s. 4d. To meet this indebted- ness the National Debt Commissioners held £30,482 6s. 4d. ; and there was in the hands of the treasurer the sum of £348 Os. 4d. total £30,830 6s. Bd. showing the surplus previously mentioned. In addition to the above the Commissioners held in Government stock for three depositors £4OO an increase over last year of £2OO. The actuary showed that notwithstanding the reduction by the Government in the rate of interest from 21 to 21 per cent., the number of depositors of small sums had con- tinued to increase.-The Chairman proposed the adop- tion of the report, and said he was glad to see that the change of premises, which they did not at the time desire to make after having tenanted them for 50 years, had, they were pleased to see, been appreciated by the public and had been altogether an advantage as was proved by the increased business conducted during the year. The bank being now in a more public position seemed to have attracted greater notice, and he was glad to see that at least4ne of the old institutions of the town was prospering and doing well. He thought a great deal of the prosperity of the bank was due to the constant care of the treasurer, (Mr. Simpson) over the funds. He did his utmost for it fina.nci- ally, and also lent it the weight of his name, which had ever been of the greatest service to the Bank. The Actuary, too, was very painstaking and thoroughly alive to the welfare and interest of the Bank as his satisfactory figures of progress showed. He was glad to see present Mr. Salkeld, the former actuary, who had relinquished the office on account of advancing age, and who must rejoice to see that the Bank was not dying but carrying on a course of increased usefulness.-The Rev. Dr. Preston seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr. Salkeld, seconded by Mr. Whittaker, the Treasurer (Mr. Simpson), was cordially thanked for his services during the past year, and a similar compliment was paid to the auditors, Messrs. J. H. Salkeld, G. M.arwood, W. William son and C. rownall, who were re-appointed. The list of trustees and managers being reduced by removals, deaths, &c., it was decided to request the following gentlemen to accept the position of additional trustees :-Messrs. E. Thnmins E. Imison, J. Meadow- croft, Dr. McDougall, W. Fidler, T. Handley, J. R. Frith, James Pritchard, Samuel Taylor, F. A. Lake, and S. C. Beckett. The following gentlemen were requested to act as additional managers : Messrs. G. Surnmerfield, r John Wilson, John Birkett, Joseph Pritchard, Michael Barker, D. H. Jones, W. Hankinson, R. Morris, W. E. Lea, Thos. Booth, Charles Garnett, Edwin Marsh all,John Littler, Robert Norman, and W. B. Kay.-Acting on a suggestion from the Chairman, Mr. W. F. Salkeld moved and Mr. Whittaker seconded and Mr. W. Littler supported that the salary of the actuary be increased from £5O to £6O per year.-1 hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proceedings.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.

The first lecture of-t-li-e-s-;c-o-ti:d series of lectures under the Oxford University Extension Scheme was delivered in Bethesda schoolroom, on Tuesday even- ing, by Mr. H. J. Mac Kinder, M.A., F.R.O.S. The title of the second course is Physiography, and the particular subject of consideration on Tuesday was "The Earth's Crust." The room was crowded with an attentive audience. In introducing Mr. Mac- Kinder, the Vicar (the Rev. A. M. Wood), compared the earth to a prison, whence none wished to escape and said there were times when people thought they knew all about the surface of the earth on which they walked, but since then they had learned that rocks were seful for other purposes besides building and were in fact the leaves of a wonderful book, which taught us something about the wonderful universe in which we lived. About these and about other things affect- ing the welfare of the inhabitants of the world Mr. Mac Kinder would have much to tell them. Mr. Mac- Kinder then delivered his lecture in which he described science as "common sense at its best" and Physiography simply meant the scientific description of nature. PhysiographY was not a science, it was a bit of all sciences, brought nicely together to explain the world which we saw around us every day. He went on to describe the formation and construction of rocks,and how they were found in nature, and the important position on the earth's crust. His descriptions oxy-hydrogen limelight views, thrown they occupied aided by upon a screen, by means of a lantern manipulated by Mr. Horace W. Handley.—At the conclusion of the lecture, Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, the hon. sec. t 3 the local committee, announced that the examination of students of the course of lectures, on "Socialßeformers," would be held in the National Schools," on Tuesday evening next. With respect to the present course it was decided to form a "Student's Association," to meet on alternate Tuesdays, to the present lectures to discuss any points of difficulty that might arise' and Mr. T. H. Annett had promised to attendand give his aid. Students would have the privilege of borrowing books from a travelling library, which was in the care of Mr. J. D. Jones, the librarian.--The Lecturer expressed his approval of the proposed Student's Association and said they wanted an honest attempt to learn something. Since the lecture, on Tuesday evening, 45 ladies and gentlemen have signified to Mr. Humphreys, the secre- tary, their willingness to join the proposed Students' Association, and a meeting will be held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Tuesday evening next, to formally inaugurate the association. The whole of the students are cordially invited to be present. During the present course of lectures, the travelling library will be restricted to the use of members of the Students' Association, and a small charge will be made to defray incidental expenses.

div.head: MARRIAGE AT WIDNES.
div.p: MARRIAGE AT WIDNES.

On Thursday morning a large congregation assembled in St. Patrick's Church to witness the marriage of Mr. .James McMahon, Moor-lane, assist— ant manager of the Lancashire Alkali and Sulphur Works, Ditton-road, with Miss Maggie llewitt. second daughter of the late Mr. John Hewitt, grocer, Waterloo-road. The service, which included a special nuptial mass, was conducted by the Rev. Father Chap- man, assisted by the Rev. Father Kenny. The bride was given away by her uncle, Inspector Drysdale, of Manchester. She wore a beautiful dress of white silk, with tulle veil and a wreath of myrtle, jessamine, and orange blossoms. The bridesmaid was Miss McMahon, sister of the bridegroom, and she wore a costume of electric blue, with hat to match. Mr. Barry Hewitt, brother of the bride, was the best man.
RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TUESDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Wynne Foulkes. - THE CAUSE LIST _ .

Comprised one adjourned plaint, seven default summonses and 112 original plaints. Even DRINKERS. The Boddington Brewery Company Limited, Strange. ways, Manchester, had issued 40 summonses against householders for small barrels of beer. The Registrar (Major Jolliffe) made orders for payment in 23 cases; the others had been settled out of court.

div.head: INSURANCE POLICIES.
div.p: INSURANCE POLICIES.

The Refuge Assurance Company Limited, of 89, Corporation-Bt.. Manchester, sued Albert Edward Penny. agent of 5, Belvedere, Runcorn, for the return of £3 18s. SI money raid to defendant for new business to be lapsed.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys defended. It appeared that under arrangement the defendant was responsible for new business up to a certain period,and it was alleged that the defendant was responsible up to the extent claimed before he left the Company's service. The defendant's contention was that business lapsed after his connection ceased, and that Mr. Thornton one of the directors of the Company gave him 10s. on their separa- tion and said he was sorry they were parting.—The plaintiffs' representative put in a number of letters written by the defendant in which he promised to pay as soon as possible, and pleading that he was now very badly off.—The judge after investigating the papers ' put before him gave judgment for the plaintiffs for 13s. lid., the amount which he thought was due.

LEPERS.

--- Sir,—We have during the past few months been often reminded of Father Damien and his work, as though therewere not any other persons working amongst them. We are now officially informed that the Lepers them- selves are carefully and duly cared for by the authorities. The Moravian Missionary Society, 29, Ely Place, Lon- don, were working amongst the Lepers before Father Damien was born, attending to their bodily and spiritual wants, feeding them with the " Word of life," a society older than any other in England, one deserving of sup- port. The R.C. cry is evidently to further the cause of Mother Church; their word is not to be relied on, for Cardinal Newman (in the controversy with W. E. Gladstone) says "no pledge from R. Catholics was of any value to which Rome was not a party." The disease is not contagious, P.Xcept through inoculation, and not the same kir4d of leprosy as named in Leviticus.
ROBERT FOULKES.
Frodsham, January 13, 1890.

-- OUR NATIONAL POVERTY AND GOVERI\ MENTAL EXTRAVAGANCE. Sir,—ln the last letter you kindly allowed me space for in your columns, I showed that our Royal Family were costing the nation too much, considering that they do very little for the huge sums spent annually upon them, and that cur future king was setting a very bad example to his future subjects by drawing, pay for work which he did not perform. Not only that, but another bad example is in being colonel of a regiment which he seldom sees. If a colonelcy is only an ornamental office, then the sooner it is abolished the better, and the money saved. His Royal Highness has cost the country, in hard cash, considerably over ai millions, besides living rent, rates, and taxes free, with travelling expenses also free, the nation providing luxurious steam packets for his and his family's conveyance to wherever they want tq ge. The Duke of Cambridge, Colonel and Majer-General, Field Marshal, Commander-in-Chief, and Ranger of the Green, St. James', and Hyde Parks—has drawn in cash for these offices, somewhere about £700,000, besides having Gloucester House rent, rates, and taxes free, with special packets for his own personal and exclu- sive use. Instances might be multiplied to tediousness; let us summarise, and say that ten individuals of the Queen's family, exclusive of her Majesty, have cost the nation up to now, five millions sterling, independent of rent, rates, taxes, ships, and repairs to palaces and dwellings. Three members of the Cambridge family cost close upon a million, exclusive of rent, rates, and taxesfree. Thirteen other individuals, her Majesty's re- latives, including kings, queens, dukes, duchesses, and princesses, have cost close on nine millions. Then we have perpetual pensions to the descendants of individuals whose names and characters are disgrace- ful, who left the world worse than they found it, and whose advent to life is clouded with shame, and yet the descendants of these profligates are called noble, wearing titles, though they have developed from bastardy to nobility, with no more moral right to the pensions they enjoy than the offspring of Dick Turpin or Jack Sheppard. There are men in the aristocracy of England who have cost the country untold millions, wrung from the blood and labour of the toiling millions, who, if brought to book as to what service they had rendered to the State for what they enjoy, the answer would be nil. And worse ; many of their lives have been mischievous and profligate, and a power for evil. The root of their genealogical tree would rival that of Judas Iscariot. Where are the descendants,of profligate Charles Second by Nell and Barbara and Louise? They are among our old nobility ; more precious than "learning, wealth, and commerce,"—so sung a sprig of their class. They can hold up their proud heads and say, "My father was king, but my mother was a courtesan, and a grateful country pays me well to keep their memory green." We turn from these ; but let them stew in their own juice ; their time will come. How fares it with the men who laid their lives upon the altar of duty, who yielded up their lives, or saved them only by the skin of their teeth—the survivors of Alma, Inkerman, Balaclava, the Redan, and other hard-fought fields, for 13 pence a day, and who bear the marks of their valour and devo- tion to duty on their persons ? Where are the sur- vivors of the Six Hundred? They, I believe, are pen- sioned—save the mark ! Just enough to starve on, if they get any at all. They eke out (those of them who may not be in the workhouse) a supplement to the ' wretched pittance the Government grudgingly gives them, by such work as they can get ' • men who per- formed some of the noblest feats of valofir the world ever saw, and a grateful country allows them to starve— unmolested and unhonoured (except by a few) in shame- ful obscurity. Surely, if we can spend millions—seven millions a year—in perpetual pensions upon the orna- mental and useless, we can do something for those who have put their lives in jeopardy, and for the widows and children of those who fell in their country's cause, instead of allowing them to perish in neglect and poverty. I am, sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, January 13th, 1890.

div.head: CYNIRO.
div.p: CYNIRO.
A RUNCORN BEERHOUSE KEEPER SUMMONED.

Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Henry Wood, a middle-aged man, was summoned for being drunk on the licensed premises of the Rose and Crown beerhouse, on the 9th inst., James Taylor, the landlord of the house, was also charged with being drunk, and with permitting drunken- ness on his premises on the same date.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys defendehil Taylor. Inspector Bowyer deposed that at a quarter to ten on the 9th inst., he visited the Rose and Crown be.rhottae- in Church-st., in company with P.S. Woolley and P.C. Woodrow. In the bar he saw Taylor sitting there with his head hanging down. He was drunk. In the tap- room he found Wood, who was also drunk and' had glass half filled with beer before him. Before witness spoke, Wood stood up and said "Do yeu say I am drunk." The Inspector replied that he was, and leav- ing the room saw Taylor standing in the lobby. He was steadying himself by the wall. The Inspector told him he was drunk, and not in a fit condition to conduct the house, and then left the premises. Shortly afterwards Wood came out, and staggered along the street. Taylor then came out and the Inspector advised him to go to bed out of the way. The Inspector said he went to the house because a man was brought to the police station charged with being drunk on the premises, and he then visited the place. '/hat man was fined on the following morning.—P.S. Woolley corroborated, and in answer to Mr. Humphreys, said Taylor was much mere drunk than the man who was previously turned out. He had cautioned Taylor on previous occasions.— P.C. Woodrow also corroborated, and P.C. Benfield and P.C. Taylor also gave evidence proving that defendant Taylor was drunk. For the defence Taylor was called, and stated that he had kept the house for 15 years, and during that time had never been charged with miscon- ducting the house. On the night in question a man entered the house drunk, and he used bad lan- guage because he would not serve him. He went out- side, and asked P.S. Woolley and two constables to eject the man,because he was drunk. Two constables ejected the man, and told him (witness) that he was drunk. He denied that he had any cause to support himself. He was not drunk then nor at any time in his life. Wood had only had one glass of beer and was quite sober. He (witness) locked the house up himself at 11 p.m.—The aefendant Wood also denied that he was drunk, and said during the whole of that day he had only had two pints and one gill.—Thomas Ashbournes, salt boiler. Percival-lane, said Wood lodged with him, and he was quite sober when he returned home on the 9th.—Samuel Hayes, shoemaker, Church-street, said Taylor was read ing the evening newspaper for him from about half-past nine to 10 o'clock. Ile was sober.—John Griffith, salt boiler, Mill-street, and Edward Farrell, a sailor, gave evidence as to the defendants sobriety.—Mr. Humphreys, in his address, said in the multitude of councillors there was wisdom, and in the multitude of police witnesses there was contradiction. He contended that the evidence of the police was contradictory, and unreliable, and was controverted by the evidence for the defence.—The Bench retired to consider their decision, and on return- ing, Mr. Reynolds said the evidence was so contradic- tory that both summonses would be dismissed.

div.head: LAD KILLED.
div.p: A LAD KILLED.

Fred Griffiths, a lad 18 years of age, was engaged on the Canal at Warburton, on Thursday, when he met with a sudden end. He was picking up a piece of iron from the side of a stationary wagon when another wagon, which was being drawn by a horse, jumped off the metals and fell on him. His head was crushed and death was instantaneous. ACCIDENT.

On Saturday, a middle-aged man, named William Torrington was admitted into the Thelwall Hospital, suffering Torrington, a broken leg. Whilst employed on the Weston Point section, a travelling crane toppled over and fell upon him, smashing his leg, in such a manner that it was deemed advisable to amputate it. Torrington is now an inmate of the hospital, and under the care of Dr. Byrne is doing well.

A MECHANICS' INSTITUTE. A mechanics' institute has been commenced at Morris- brook, in connection with the number 6 district of the Ship Canal contract. Mr. J. Price, is president ; Mr. J. ,Lewis, vice-president; Mr. A . Robins, treasurer; Mr. G. Manning, secretary and librarian. The Council con- sists of Messrs. J. A. Ewart, H. A. Dicks, G. W. Raby, W. Browning, J. Lythe, E. Collins, and G. Harlock. There are already thirty members enrolled. The Institute will be located at the Coffee Tavern, and it is intended to take in morning, evening, and weekly papers, and also illustrated and trade journals. The institute will be opened on Tuesday next. FATAL ACCIDENT AT RIXTON.

An accideat happentd on Thursday, upon No. 6 section at Rixton. A steam navvy was at its usual work, at- tended by a coal wagon that is always placed at the end of navvy for tke purpose of supplying the navvy with coal. In bringing up the empty wagon with horse- power, the wagons have to move from one set of rails to another by means of pints. The coal wagon not being quite clear of the points an empty wagon caught one end of the coal wagon and forced it against the steam navvy, James Knight, wagon filler, being caught between the coal wagon and the navvy. Death appeared to be instantaneous. He was aged 21, and the sole support of his widowed mother. The body was removed to Latch- ford awaiting the inquest.

div.head: MOTHERS' MEETING AT THELIVALL.
div.p: MOTHERS' MEETING AT THELIVALL.

For a considerable time past a mothers' meeting has been carried on by Mrs. Price at the huts, Thelwall, and it has been a great success amongst the navvies' wives. The meetings having been discontinued for a short time were re-commenced on Monday, when Mrs. Price pro- vided a very substantial tea, to which thirty-six sat down. Ample justice was done to the excellent repast, and afterwards songs, &c., were rendered and a very enjoyoble time spent. There were many expressions of gratitude for the great sympathy shown to the mothers and children by Mr. and Mrs. Price, and hopes were expressed that they would long live to continue their good services amongst the workpeople. The remains of the provisions were distributed amongst the children in the Coffee Tavern, which under the new management is giving satisfaction to both workpeople and visitors.

div.head: MR. LEADER WILLIAMS ON THE MANCHESTER
div.p: MR. LEADER WILLIAMS ON THE MANCHESTER
SHIP CANAL.

On Monday evenin-g--M;'..-Z-I:eader Williams, the engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal, delivered a lec- ture in the Manchester Town Hall on " A visit to the Ship Canal works." Mr. Lees Knowles, M.P., presided, and said that when one considered that it was only in November, 1887, that the first sod of the Ship Canal was cut, it was simply marvellous to see what progress had since been made with the work. When they con- sidered the enormous amount of money spent upon the plant, they would recognise the present advantage of the Canal, and still greater advantages in the future. It was one of the greatest undertakings of modern , times.—Mr. E. Leader Williams said that the totai length of the Ship Canal was 351 miles, and the fact that it was not of great length was one of its main advantages. Vessels would be able to steam up in a few hours, and so compete successfully with the railways. (Hear, hear.) The width of the canal at the bottom would be 120 feet ; the bottom of the Suez: Canal was 78 feet wide, and the Amsterdam Canal was somewhat larger. The Board of directors of the Manchester Ship Canal were, however, making their waterway so wide that steamers would be able to pass at any point. From Barton to Manchester k2imiles) it was to be made 170 feet wide, so that vessels could lie along the Salford side I and yet two vessels could pass at any point. The mini- mum depth would be 26 feet.

The total fall from the level of the water in the Man- chester docks to the level of the tide rising 14ft. 2in. above the old dock sill at Liverpool would be 60ft. 6in. Vessels would corns up the canal as it were by a series of steps, and warehouses and mills erected on the banks could converiently load at any point. The area of water space in the Manchester and Salford Docks would be 114 acres, and the area of quay space 152 acres. The length of the quays would be 5t miles, or equal to the present quay space at Glasgow. The Warrington docks would cover 23 acres. The plant at work on the canal to-day comprised 96 steam navvies, one floating dredger, 169 locomotives, 166 steam cranes, 128 portable and other engines, 18 steam pumps, 5,900 wagons, and 40 pile engines. There were 213 miles of temporary railway, the number of men and boys em- ployed was 11,489, and of horses 182. The quantity of coal consumed on the works in a month was 10,000 tons, and 8,000 tons of Portland cement were dealt with in the same period.

, RU/SCORN RIMAL SANITARY AUTHORITY: The fortnightly meeting was held at the Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present Messrs. Stokes, Aaron, Baguley,l3retherton, P. Hall, Lowe, Brandreth, Parr, Lewis, J. Mounfield, J. Hall, C. Mounfleld; Weir, H. Linaker (clerk) ; H. G. Linaker (assistant clerk) ; Dr. Adams (medical officer) ; and . J. .Farrington (nuisance inspector) ; J. W. Dankly, Lbeir Govern- ment Board Inspector, was also present.

WIDNES BRINE SCHEME. A letter was read from Mr. J. L. Trafford, addressed Westminster Palace Hotel, Victoria-st., London, in re- ference to the Widnes Brine Scheme. He stated that he was getting up an opposition to this Bill on Standing Orders , and it would be very desirable to have the memorial signed by any public bodies whose districts are in any way affected by,the Bill, in which category might be included, he thought, the Runcorn Rural Sani- tary Authority and the Dgesbuty Highway Board. He would send a copy of the memorial as soon as it was settled with Parliatnentary Agents.—Mr. Aaron: I can- not see that we should; interfere with it at all. The scheme will bring this Union In a great deal of money if it goes on. They would lay their pipes a long way through the Union, and these would have th be assessed to the rates. He proposed that the letter should lie on the table.—Mr. Parr: I think it should: be signed. If it brings in a great deal of money it takes from other places.—Mr. Aaron : It doesn't take from our Union.—Mr. Stokes: I don't see what we have got to do with it.—Mr. Aaron: No. We have no more right to look after Northwicia than Northwich has to look after us.—Mr. Stokes: Northwich are afraid of losing their trade.—Mr. Parr: With regard to the high- ways, they will do more damage than they will pay us. The road will be oinking twelve months through the lay- ing of the pipes.—Mr. Aaron : We must compel them to make the roads good again. We have the power.— The Assistant Clerk said there was a clerk from the office of Messrs. Trafford and Cook, of Northwich, and they had better hear what he had to say before deciding the question.—The gentleman was called into the room, and he handed to the Clerk the last sheet of the memo- rial for signature or seals. He said the memorial was in course of being lithographed,and would be forwarded I as soon as possible.—The Clerk said there were nine I paragraphs in the memorial, some of them lengthy, and he could not ask the Chairman to attach the seal of the 1 Authority to a blank document in favour of a memorial they had not seen.—Mr. Dansey said it was like asking I the Chairman to sign a blank cheque.—Without any formal motion being put, it was understood that the seal should not be attached under the circumstances. THE SHIP CANAL PLANS. Mr. Aaron asked if the Clerk had heard anything mord. about the plans of the Ship Canal Company with regard to the sewerage outfalls of the .Union.—The Clerk: Not yet.—Mr. Aaron: What istO be done.—The Assistant Clerk: We can write and ask them to push on the plans.--Mr. Aaron: It is quite time this Board were supplied with the information. ' OUTBREAK OF FEVER. The Medical Officer reported six cases of scarlet fever at Frodsham, Frodsham Bridge, Helsby, Norley, and Appleton. There was a case of typhoid fever at Main-st:, Frodsham, and there were three cloldren attacked by the same disease at Wood's Row, Halton. The general insani- tary condition of these cottages called for improvement. NEW PROPERTY AT WESTOWPOINT. Certificates of occupation were granted to nine houses at Weston Point, belonging to Captain R. Clark, the. water supply being satisfactory. t NUISANCES AT HUSBY.
A letter was read from Mr. U. C. Taylor as to nuisances at Helshy, and the Sanitary Inspector reported that the work of remedying the nuisances had been placed in the hands of a contractor.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
BY. AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

That it was expected that Mr. Brunner would have addressed his Runcorn constituents on the 21st inst., but through his unavoidable absence in Egypt, the meeting has had to be postponed. That Mr. T. E. Ellis. whose illness is the cause of the failure of the arrangements for the meeting, is progressing rapidly towards recovery, and his numerous admirers will rejoice at the fact. That the services of the Right Hon. James Stans- field, M.P.. who was to have been the principal speaker, will be available for a future occasion. That the Runcorn Guardians have at last solved the difficulty in which they were involved by the re-appointment of Mr. Stubbing to the position of schoolmaster,which ho resigned some three months ago under pressure. That the incident has given rise to great warmth of feeling, and the meetings of the Board have been more numerously attended during the agitating period than for a year or two past and on Tuesday a member put in his first appearance since he was elected in March of last year. Could be not have been spared to his retirement for a couple more months? Opinions were so evenly divided that the casting , vote of the Chairman was required to seal Stubbing's fate, and another close fight took place in filling the , vacancy, Mr. Naylor, of Warrington, who was ap- pointed gaining the verdict by the narrow margin 1 of one rote.

Mr. Naylor is highly recommended, and it is to be hoped that the peace of the Workhouse will be re- stored, and that the ratepayers have heard the last of Government inquiries into official conduct for a long time to come. That the proceedings of Widnes Local Board revealed a nice state of affairs axisting between the Highway Committee and the Surveyor, Mr. Higgin- son, and the serious proposal to at once dispense with the services of that official was made.

That the specific charge brought against the Surveyor was with regard to the carrying out of the Moss Bank Sewer, but it would seem that the Committee have been dissatisfied with his method, or want of method, of working for some time past, and either they have acted with careful consideration to the Surveyor,and have neglected the interests of the ratepayers by allowing matters to reach such a serious crisis, or the Surveyor is a much abused individual. That the Surveyor is to be allowed to answer the allegations of ,the Committee in writing, and in the meantime judgment ought to be suspended. That the roads in Widnes are not a credit to any- body,whoever may be to blame in the matter.
RESIGNATION OF THE TOWN CLERK OF WARRINGTON.

We understand that Mr. W. 11. Brook has sent a letter to the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), in which he tenders his resignation of the office of Town Clerk. The letter will in due course be submitted to the consideration of the General Purposes Committee, and afterwards to the Town Council. Mr. Brook has for some time , contemplated resigning, his object being to devote himself exclusively to private practice The office cannot be said to have been particularly remunerative to him, as he employs Mr. J. Lyon , Whittle, the deputy town clerk, and another clerk, to assist him in the performance of the duties de- volving upon him. Mr. Brook is an experienced and able lawyer, and it is a matter of course to say that the town will lose not a little in failing to have the benefit of his large experience and sound advice. It is, however, satisfactory to know that Mr. Whittle, the deputy town clerk, who has had an admirable training under Mr. Brook,' is an applicant for the office ; and, judg- ing from the high regard in which he is almost universally held by members of the Town Council, there is every likelihood of his securing the appoint- ment. Mr. Whittle is thoroughly conversant with every department of the work, having, in fact, had control of it, under the supervision of Mr. Brook, for a considerable number of years. It may be mentioned as evidence of his general qualifica- tion that, some months ago, he was one of three—out of 77—applicants who were taken into special consideration for the town clerkship of Carlisle. On that occasion he withdrew his application, believing from what he had heard that he would have a fair chance of finally succeeding Mr. Brook. It is of interest to mention that both Mr.Collingwood and Mr.Mawdsley who, together with Mr. Whittle, formed a trio from which the town clerk of Carlisle was selected, now fill the offices of town clerks. Mr. Collingwood received the appointment at Carlisle, and since then Mr. Mawdsley has become town clerk of Dewsbury. The circle of appointments will be com- pleted should the present resignation result in Mr. Whittle becoming town clerk of Warrington. We believe that Mr. Brook speaks in the highest terms of the fitness of Mr. Whittle to be his successor, and of the way in which he has performed the import- ant duties allotted to him. There seems, therefore, to be a very general feeling that Mr. Whittle is in every way the , most suitable gentleman to succeed the present town clerk. It may be mentioned that it is the opinion of many members of the Town Council that, now that a change is being made, it would be advisable to make it a condition of the appointment, that whoever succeeds to the office should devote him- self entirely to the duties. pertaining thereto, as the duties have a tendency to increase in impor- tance, and as this is a course which is being taken in regard to new appointments throughout the country. We may add that Mr. Brook has held the office of town clerk since 1878.

DEATH OF NUL JOHN BENNETT, OF LATCHFORD' . On Sunday, Mr. John Bennett, one of the oldest V tradesmen in Widnes, died at his Latchford resi- dence, aged 63 years. Mr. Bennett was descended from an old Derbyshire family, and was ,born at Stockport in 1827. Having received a good edu- cation, he was apprenticed to his cousin, Dr. Brierly, of Ashton-under-Lyne. He had no taste, however. for the practise 0 surgery; therefore he took a situation with a chemist and druggist. In 1861 he commenced business at Farnworth, and shortly afterwards removed to Waterloo-road, Widnes. After conducting a most successful business there, for some 15 years, he built his present shop in Victoria-road, Widnes' where for the last 12 years, and also at,Albert-toad, Widnes, the business has been successfUlly conducted. Owing to ill-health he some years ago ceased to take any very active part in the business. He suffered greatly for the last three years from disease of the heart, and latterly from spasmodic asthma, to which be succumbed at his residence, Spring Cottage, Latchford, on Sun- day. He was attended by Dr. Starkey Smith, of Warrington. Mr. Bennett-did not take an active part in public affairs, but he was a staunch Liberal and a member of the executive of the Widnes Divi- sion Liberal Association. The remains were interred in Grappenhall churchyard on Wednesday, the officiating minister being the Rev. Canon Greenall (rector). t . °

ST. 'MARY'S MISSION Cntinau. :

On Wednesday evening, the bells which have been hung in the tower of the church were rung out merrily for the first tiroe,Under the superintendence of Mr. James Woodward and Mr. J. Forster. The chimes were highly appreciated by the inhabitants of Penketh. Mr. C. Mathews, cabinet -maker, was the conti actor for the woodwork, and the painting and staining was entrusted to Mr. S. Mainley. LECTURE ON AUSTRIA. On Wednesday evening, at a meetiug of the Mutual Improvement Association, bliss Dutton gave a lecture entitled " Austria, its capital, lakes, and salt mines." The lecture was very interesting, be- ing the outcome of notes taken during an extended Continental tour. Miss Dutton banded round several fine " photos" of the places of special in- terest on the journey. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer for her very interesting and instructive paper. , PENRETTI LIBERAL CLUB. .

, - The annual tea party and entertainment was held last evenipg, in the day school at Penketh. About 1001pbti6ns sat down' to a. substantial tea. After tea the following programme was gone through in a highly pleasing manner: piano solo, gavotte. Misses Hargreaves and Carter; song, Miss Broadhurst; recitation, Mr. Thomas Davies; election on a..the fairy bells, Mr. F. Sandalls ; piano solo,T Miss M: Garnett;' recitation. -" The house that 4,ack built," Mr. Robinson; song, Mr. A. Greenhalgh ; dialogue, "PllO Vill- age Schoolmaster," some friends from Penketh school. Apology was made for the absence of Mr. R. Garnett, who was unable to attend
LATEST NEWS.

BIRTH OF A PRINCE. A Vienna correspondent says that Countess Hartenan, wife of Prince Alexander of Battenberg, has been safely delivered of a soil, TIE ROYAL INVALIDS. On inquiry at Marlborough Hu se on Friday morning it was learned that both the Prjncess of Wales and Princess Maud were going on weir'
_ - THE POPE'S HEALTH.' A Rome correspondent says the announcement made by some of the French newspapers that the Pope is seriously indisposed is entirely false. His Holiness is in excellent health.

WRECK OF A STEAMER. Lloyd's agent at Galle telegraphed yesterday that the steamer Norsa, bound from Middlesbrough for Madras, struck on a rock off Akorella, and was abandoned. The crew landed at Galle.

--- STRIKE IN THE GRAIN TRADE. The strike in the grain trade of Liverpool is extend- ing. The porters at the Alexandra Dock came out yesterday. The grain traffic at the north and south docks is at a standstill, and it is feared the Grain Com- pany's Storage Company's men will come out. A MOTHER MURDERS THREE CHILDREN. A terrible crime is reported front Cannon, Minnesota. A mother shot dead three of her children with a revolver and forced another to join her in drinking carbolic acid. The mother and this child are expected to recover. Despondency on account of ill-health is assigned as the motive for the crime.

FIVE TAILORS ACCUSED OF MURDER. Yesterday, five tailors, named Meittle McVittie, Flowers, Oddie, and Sergeant, were remanded, at Black- burn, on suspicion of causing the death of Phillip Thomas, a publican. Thomas was sitting outside his house, yesterday morning, when the prisoners came along and a fight ensued. Thomas was badly beaten, and died shortly afterwards. Two men who assisted him were also much hurt.

TERRIBLE STRUGGLE WITH A BURGLAR. Early dia Friday morning Constable Beresford found a man in the garden of a house near Sheffield. The burg- lar attacked the constable with a crowbar, inflicting terrible wounds on the head. The officpr closed with his assailant, who fired two shots with a revolver, fortu- nately missing the officer. The latter became uncon- scious from loss of blood, and the burglar escaped. Beresford's injuries are very serious.

div.head: INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.
The Duchess of Marlborough as suffering f rom influenza.

The Rey. Aubrey Lackington Moore, hon. canon of Christ Church, Oxford, died on Friday morning from congestion of the lungs, following= attack of Russian influenza. In consequence of the influenza. epidemic, Eton College will not be re-opened until the 29th inst., THE LATE LORD hTAPIER OF MAGDALA. The remains of the late Field Marshal Lord Napier of Magdala will be interred at St. Paul's Cathedral, on Tuesday next, at half-past eleven o'clock. The funeral will be military, and will be made the occasion of an imposing military display; the whole route from the deceased's residence to the Cathedral will be lined with troops, and it is expected that ten or twelve hundred officers and men, in full uniform, will follow the hearse. THE ALLEGED BLACKMAILING CASE. The trial of Claude Marks, Woolf, and Marix on the charge of blackmailing, was resumed in the Queen's Bench, yesterday. Sir Charles Russell, for the defence, declared that the Crystal Reef Company was a bank- rupt concern, and that the object of including Marix in the prosecution was to get at Claude Marks and enable Bebro to gratify his unmitigated hatred of Harry Marks, because the latter had systematically denounced Bebro's shady undertakings.

SCENE AT AN IRISH BOARD MEETING. From Athlone, on Friday, was reported an extraordin- ary scene at the meeting of the Town Commissioners. The Chairman called in a sergeant of police to keep order. One member was about to be removed when the meeting broke up in confusion. An official then struck a member on the nose, causing him to bleed pro- fusely and to tumble on the floor, when the Chairman stumbled over him, and a struggle took place. The sergeant helped the bleeding commissioner out of the room, and the lights were extinguished. DECAPITATED ON THE RATLWAY. A shocking accident occurred yesterday morning at Moston Station, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Rail- way. A young man had booked from Middleton, and was told by the booking clerk not to cross the line; as an., express train was due to pass at the time. Disregarding the warning, he ran across the line just aS the express train came up, and before he could regain the opposite platform he was caught by the engine an'd knocked' down, the whole train passing over his body. His head was severed from his body, and his brain scattered on the line. I per)
THE DOUGLAS TRAGEDY. PAINFUL SCENE IN COURT.

At the Court of General Goal Delivery Welditt Douglas [yesterday by his Excellency Lieutenant-Governor Wal- Riole, and three inshlar juilgeWintliam Kelly pleaded guilty .to the manslaugther of his wife, on the 26th November, by cutting her throat. Mr. Ring, advocate, called Witnesses as to character, and asked tor mitigation of the sentence owing to the intense provocation received by the prisoner from the deceased, who, after making the vilest charges against him, had flung herself on a chair, put her head back, and dared him to cut her throat. The judges were absent thirty-fie minutes con- sidering the sentence, and upon returning Kelly was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude. Prisoner's four daughters were in court ; one fainted and the other three screamed and cried and hadto be removed. Kelly will be sent to an English prison to work out his sentence. DEATH OF MR. C. R. M. TALBOT, MX, A Bridgend correspondent telegraphs that Mr. Talbot expired at Margam House, at an early hour yesterday morning. The hon. member died at 2.20 a.m., the immediate cause of death being inflammation and con- gestion of the lung. His death causes a vacancy not I only in the parliamentary division of Mid-Glamorgan I "shire, but also in the lord-lieutenancv of the county. He I was born in 1803, and was educatea at Harrow and at Oriel College, Oxford. A peerage was offered to Mr. Talbot, in November, 1869, but he declined the honour. The deceased gentlemen, who was eighty-seven years of age, was chiefly kn)wn akthe "Father of the House of Commons," having sat uninterruptedly for the mid- division of Glamorganshire since 1830, a period of sixty years. He was elected without oppos.tion at both the general elections of 1885 and 1886. Mr. Talbot was a Liberal in politics until Mr. Gladstone introduced his ")IHome Rule Bill in 1886. Subsequent to that event, how- ever, the deceased gentleman had associated himself ; with the Liberal Unionist party. . ,
